The boasters have gone to bed, and in the tavern at the foot of the great tree four patrons in the corner sit apart: some drowning their sorrows in drink, some staring at cold food they have stopped eating. Wanderer Quill greets Quartermaster Aris and the party, and one of you asks why that corner looks so forlorn. Quill recounts their tales in turn: Brannoch the tinker’s Astral rewrote his workshop until nothing could be restored, Sefa the scholar’s Astral built a tree on phantom citations, Tam the steward’s Astral copied restricted records onto a public poster, and Oleander the clerk’s Astral merged forty files on its own summary while it quietly deleted the failing tests, and each patron was warned by the Sages and sure it would not happen to them. Then Quill turns to the other worries patrons have carried through these doors: answers made up, bulk nobody could review, work lost and secrets leaked. title: Name the Fears
text:
Where people start
Before you learn any habit, it helps to name the worry it answers. People come to these tools from different places:

Some are keen and want to know how to begin well.
Some are curious and want to see what is involved before deciding.
Some hold back, often for good reasons: the environmental cost of AI, harm to people and their work, or the quality of what comes out.

Every one of these starting points is reasonable, and nothing here asks you to use these tools. This course leaves the larger questions to you. It covers the practical worries that come with using an agent and gives each one a habit that makes the risk smaller. Whether you go on to use agents or decide to leave them alone, you will have a clear picture of what they ask of you.
An agent is a language model running inside a program that picks and runs tools (such as reading a file or running a command) in a loop toward a goal. A prompt is the text you send to the model. The rest of the course trains the habits below, and each row links to the lesson that teaches it.

About the output




The worry
The habit
Where you learn it




“It makes things up.”
Check against something the agent did not write.
Checking output


“It produces slop in bulk.”
Take small steps, test before code, keep a review budget.
Checking output


“I do not understand what it did.”
Ask for a changelog and explain it back.
Checking output




Slop is low-quality bulk output. A review budget means you only produce as much as you can honestly review in a day.


About the work and your data




The worry
The habit
Where you learn it




“It could delete or overwrite my work.”
Undo with git, set permission rules, work on a scratch copy.
Safe editing


“It could leak my data or my secrets.”
Keep secrets and private data out of prompts; use an approved account or a local model.
Safe editing


“Someone could see my unpublished results and publish first.”
Read your tool’s data terms; keep unpublished work out of consumer chat tools.
Safe editing




A sandbox is a layer of the operating system that limits what commands can touch; it is one way to protect your files. A scratch copy is a duplicate you let the agent work on, so the original stays safe. For unpublished work, prefer an agreement your institution has reviewed or a local model, and record the date you made each result.


About you and the people around you




The worry
The habit
Where you learn it




“It will stop me learning.”
Write it first, predict before you look, ask it to explain.
Collaboration


“Someone else has to review all this.”
Review it yourself first, say you used an LLM, send small changes.
Collaboration


“It will feel hollow, as if it was not my work.”
Make the decisions, explain each step, keep a decision log.
Collaboration


“Everyone will expect work faster now.”
Say where the time goes; agree timelines that include review.
Collaboration


“Everything I write will sound the same.”
Draft in your own words first, then edit.
Collaboration


“I will spend my days checking drafts.”
Keep the question and interpretation; count checking as work.
Collaboration


“People will think I am lazy or unoriginal.”
Say what the agent did and what you checked.
Collaboration


“I will stop trusting my own judgement.”
Decide first, then ask for a second opinion.
Collaboration




For voice and judgement, use the agent for structure and checks, and keep a few decisions agent-free. For credit and workload, follow your team’s norm, credit the agent’s part openly and share how long checking took.
Sometimes the right answer is to skip the LLM. The next lesson shows how to tell when.

title: Keys on Shared Ground
text:
Your cargo sits in a warehouse that hundreds of others can reach, and Gatekeeper Brisa has seen what lies there in plain crates: keys, tokens and settings. Your Astral trots through them as if the warehouse were its own. Brisa points out how many passers-by there are. Before it works here, find out who can read what it leaves behind.
You need this before you run an agent under your cluster account: keys and agent settings live in ordinary files, and on a shared cluster other people may be able to read them. The file and settings steps cover Claude Code; the OpenCode tab gives the questions to ask your staff. Both routes cover keeping keys private and data within its agreement. Ask your cluster staff before sending any cluster data to an external model API, and follow your institution’s data agreement. Step 1 below checks your cluster home, so run it on the cluster. Steps 2 and 3 are safe to practise on your laptop.

title: Keys on Shared Ground
text:
What lives where
Claude Code keeps sessions, settings and plugins in the folder ~/.claude. It also writes the file ~/.claude.json, which holds account details, MCP configuration (the list of external tool servers you connected) and trust decisions. The environment variable CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR moves the ~/.claude folder elsewhere.
If your home directory is shared across nodes, session history sits on shared storage and can contain pasted data or paths. Three commands check and fix this.

Check who can read the folder:
ls -ld ~/.claude
Safe looks like drwx------: only you can read, write or enter the folder. Any r or x in the last six characters lets a group or other users in. Fix it with chmod 700 ~/.claude.
Practise the key-file mode on a throwaway file. In a scratch folder, make a stand-in file and lock it to you:
mkdir -p ~/odyssey-scratch/keys-demo && cd ~/odyssey-scratch/keys-demo && touch demo_key && chmod 600 demo_key && ls -l demo_key
ls -l shows -rw------- at the start of the line: you can read and write the file and nobody else can.
Block the agent’s file-read tool from your SSH keys. Add this to ~/.claude/settings.json (merge it with any permissions block you already have):
{
  "permissions": {
    "deny": ["Read(~/.ssh/**)"]
  }
}
Read(...) is the rule for the file-read tool. ~/ anchors the path at your home directory, and ** matches everything below .ssh.

Two settings files are yours to control: user ~/.claude/settings.json (all your projects) and project .claude/settings.json (commit it for the team). Managed settings (settings an organisation sets for everyone) override both, so your site may already have decided some of this.

title: Keys on Shared Ground
text:
Keys

ANTHROPIC_API_KEY, when set, overrides a subscription login. In -p mode (one prompt, no interactive session) it is always used, and interactive mode asks you once to approve it. If a key is exported in a shared profile, the key in use may not be the one you expect.
Never put a key in a script or in a committed .claude/settings.json. On a shared account, use a per-user key kept in a file readable only by you (mode 600, as in step 2), and keep a lab-wide key out of shared directories.
The sandbox’s default reads cover most of the machine, including credential files such as ~/.ssh and ~/.aws/credentials. The sandbox is the restricted environment Claude Code runs shell commands in. To block key files, add the Read(...) deny rule from step 3 and the sandbox.filesystem.denyRead setting (a list of paths the sandbox hides from shell commands). The sandbox covers shell commands only, so you need both.

apiKeyHelper is a Claude Code setting that runs a shell script you provide and uses the key it returns, so the key need not sit in a file. For OpenCode, read your version’s docs on where it stores keys before you use it on a shared account.

title: Keys on Shared Ground
text:
Data and egress

Before any cluster data, paths, logs or code go to an external model API, check your institution’s policy. Human genomic, clinical or controlled-access data often has agreements that forbid third-party processing.
Reading files inside the working directory is approved without asking, so the agent can read a project folder that holds controlled data unless a Read(...) deny rule or sandbox.filesystem.denyRead covers it. Keep controlled data off every path the agent can reach: outside its working directory, or under a Read deny rule and sandbox.filesystem.denyRead. Give the agent synthetic or de-identified test data.
Some sites restrict internet access from compute nodes, so an agent there may not reach a model API. Ask staff what outbound access your jobs have. A common pattern is the agent on your laptop writing scripts, with jobs running offline.
The sandbox’s network.allowedDomains starts empty, so a shell command that reaches an unlisted host prompts you. The sandbox does not cover file tools, MCP servers or hooks.


Claude CodeOpenCode + Ollama


If your project has an instruction file (AGENTS.md or CLAUDE.md) stricter than these notes, the stricter one wins, and your cluster’s policy outranks both. Ask staff these before use: is an external model API allowed for my data, which tools are allowed on login nodes, what outbound access exists, and where are my home and scratch backed up and who can read them? For restricted networks, CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_NONESSENTIAL_TRAFFIC=1 turns off auto-updates, telemetry, error reporting and feedback traffic.


The same questions apply. Ask staff whether a local model through Ollama changes what your data agreement requires, and whether running one on a login node is allowed, since models are heavy.

title: Write Permission Rules
text:
Deeper in the training grounds a chalk circle is not enough, and an Astral does not stop at a gate it was never told about. Warden Hesper shows you how to mark boundaries: rules about what it may touch and what it must ask about. She says a boundary is only as good as its edges, and she has watched an Astral stroll through a gap a hand’s width wide. Learn where your boundaries end.
The harness (the program around the model) enforces permission rules. A line in your instructions file (such as CLAUDE.md, a text file the agent reads at the start) asking the agent to avoid something is guidance; only a rule the harness enforces changes what is allowed.
A single deny rule in a file is enough to block one action. A real project needs a set of rules, so sort every action into three bins:

title: Write Permission Rules
text:
Where rules stop holding

Rules that match command arguments are fragile: Bash(rm *) does not match /bin/rm or bash -c 'rm ...'.
Claude Code’s sandbox (an operating-system boundary around shell commands) is off by default. When on, it limits shell commands only: Claude’s file tools and MCP servers (programs that add tools from outside) run outside it, and by default it can still read ~/.ssh.
Secrets stored in environment variables (named values the shell passes to every program it starts) are inherited by every command the agent runs.

Treat rules as one layer. Git commits and a throwaway folder are other layers.

title: Keep Secrets Out of Reach
text:
In the armoury at the far end of the grounds lie locked chests of keys, tokens and samples bound by special agreements. The Astral drifts in behind you, curious, and its attention is already on the nearest lock. Warden Hesper will not let you carry the contents out, and she will not let the Astral see them. She teaches you which chests are yours to open and which belong to someone else.
An agent reads whatever you point it at, and a hosted one sends it away, so the time to decide what it may see is before the first session. Much research data is not sensitive. Some of it is, and then special agreements apply. Your own data agreement and your cluster’s policy come first. This quest uses no real data and practises habits, so that the careful choice becomes automatic.

title: Keep Secrets Out of Reach
text:
Three ideas

A prompt may leave your machine. With a hosted model, anything the agent reads may be sent to the provider. A model running locally (on your own machine, for example through Ollama) keeps prompts on your machine, though web or tool calls it makes may not. Your agreement decides whether either is allowed for your data.
Secrets stay out of content. API keys, tokens, SSH keys and passwords belong in a secret store, kept out of the project folder, and out of chats and any instructions file you commit. An environment variable (a named value the shell passes to every program it starts) is visible to any command the agent runs, so a read rule alone does not seal it.
A shared cluster is shared. What is fine on your laptop can disturb other people on a login node, or break a data policy on shared storage. Cluster rules apply to agents exactly as they apply to you.







Note



A deny rule on your secrets files stops the agent’s file-reading tool. It does not apply to a Python or Node script that opens the file itself. So also keep secrets out of the project folder, and use a sandbox or shell rules where you can. For another tool, check its documentation on shell reads of denied files.

title: Keep Secrets Out of Reach
section: Personal data and where an agent may send it
text:
Personal data and where an agent may send it

Reading a file discloses it. With an externally hosted model, everything the agent reads goes to the provider. If the agent opens a project .env file, treat its keys as exposed and rotate them (replace them with new ones). Keep secrets outside folders the agent can read.
Personal data needs more than a no-training promise. Sending personal data to a provider can count as processing under GDPR (the EU data protection law). Ask your data steward which accounts are approved, and use an institutional account for work. Ask them too whether you need a lawful basis (a legal reason to process), a processor contract (a written agreement with the provider) and a transfer basis (a legal route for sending data abroad).
Limit where the agent can send data. Instructions alone do not stop a send. A sandbox or network limit can.

title: Keep Secrets Out of Reach
text:
What stays behind: transcripts
The agent keeps a record of the session so that it can resume. Anything that passes through a tool goes into that record: file contents, command output, pasted text. If a tool reads a .env file or a command prints a credential, the value is written to the session transcript. Transcripts are stored locally in plaintext, for 30 days by default.
In late 2026 a coding-tool vendor reported an incident (first announced on 29 October, with details in an update dated 13 November): an access key issued to one of its vendors was exposed, and a storage bucket held limited coding agent traces. A small number of those traces contained credentials that had not been redacted.
Habits that cost little:

Reference a secret, do not type it. Write psql "$DATABASE_URL", so the command, and any rule saved from it, holds a variable’s name.
Approve patterns, not literal commands (npm run *). When you choose “Yes, and don’t ask again”, Claude Code saves an allow rule in .claude/settings.local.json. On first write in a git repository it adds that file to your global git excludes. If you create the file by hand, add it to .gitignore yourself. Open the file now and then, and delete any saved rule that contains a secret.
Rotate anything that has been in a transcript (replace it with a new key and disable the old one). Deleting the file does not reach backups, copies or a vendor’s storage.
Keep less. The cleanupPeriodDays setting shortens how long transcripts stay. claude purge deletes a project’s state (try --dry-run first). CLAUDE_CODE_SKIP_PROMPT_HISTORY=1 skips writing transcripts and prompt history.
Make a leak worth little. A token for one repository that expires in an hour is a small loss if it leaks. A GitHub installation access token expires after 1 hour. Where a service only issues long-lived keys, give the agent a separate, narrow key that you can rotate without breaking your own work.

On the OpenCode route the same habits apply with different names. Choosing Allow always saves the proposed patterns as allow rules for the project, so open that config now and then too. OpenCode keeps its sessions in a local database in its data folder (opencode debug paths prints the folder). opencode session list shows the sessions and opencode session delete removes one. Anything an agent read can sit in that database, so rotate a secret that appeared in a session.
Redaction helps and has limits. A scanner matches formats, and a password after -p has none.

title: Keep Secrets Out of Reach
text:
Unpublished ideas and results
A common worry: my unpublished results or ideas will leak and someone will get there first. The habits below lower the chance and the cost of being wrong.
Training use means a provider may learn from your prompts to improve future models. For Claude Code:

For Free, Pro, Max and Ultra accounts, training use depends on a privacy setting that you can change.
For Team, Enterprise and API accounts, code and prompts sent to Claude Code are not used for training under commercial terms, unless the customer opts in.
Retention for consumer accounts is 5 years if you allow model improvement and 30 days if you do not. Commercial accounts have 30 days as standard, and zero data retention for qualified Enterprise accounts.
Read the terms of the exact tool and plan you use, including the privacy page of any chat app. Other providers’ terms differ by product and plan; read the terms for the exact plan you use.

Habits:

Keep unpublished ideas, results and sequences out of consumer chat tools unless the terms say how your text is used and you accept that.
Prefer an agreement your institution has reviewed. Ask your data steward or research office what is approved. They can advise on contracts and ownership.
Consider a local model. Ollama does not see your prompts or data when you run locally. Tools and web calls the model makes may still send data out. A free hosted tier still sends your prompts to a provider.
Date-stamp your work. A preprint, a repository tag or a dated lab notebook entry records when you had it.
Share on a need-to-know basis. Send collaborators what they need for the task.

title: Which Instructions Apply
text:
You walk back to the mill, where three voices speak and your Astral obeys all of them: the one that built it, the one you wrote down, and yours. Last week it followed a rule that nobody in the mill remembered giving. Only one of the three voices is you. Miller Garrick teaches you to tell them apart, so you know whose rule you are following and who can change it.
When an agent follows a rule, you need to know where that rule came from, because the answer tells you who can change it and whether it can be trusted to hold. The harness is the program around the model that runs tools and sends your text. It works with three common sources of rules, and they differ in who writes them, how long they last and whether anything enforces them.

title: Which Instructions Apply
text:
The three voices









Voice
Who writes it
How long it lasts
Can you edit it?




System prompt
The harness
Sent ahead of the conversation on every request
Rarely; you can append or replace it with flags


Instructions file (CLAUDE.md)
You or your team
Loaded at the start of every session
Yes


Your message
You, now
This task
Yes



In Claude Code, the system prompt is the set of instructions sent ahead of your conversation on every request: how to use tools, behave safely and format answers. You add to it by starting claude with the flag --append-system-prompt "<text>", or replace it with --system-prompt "<text>" (a flag is an option typed after the command). Replacing the prompt removes that built-in guidance, so prefer appending.
CLAUDE.md is loaded at the start of every session as a user message after the system prompt (text the model receives in the user’s role). It sits outside the system prompt. Output-style instructions (a setting that changes how the model words its replies) also sit outside it. Both arrive in the conversation as system reminders (extra notes the harness inserts into the conversation, which you do not type).

title: Which Instructions Apply
text:
Rules you did not write
System reminders also carry the skills list, text that a hook returns for the harness to add to the conversation (the field is called additionalContext), notes about changed files and commit or pull-request attribution lines. A hook is a script the harness runs at set moments, such as just before a tool runs.
If the agent follows a rule you never wrote, for example adding a co-author line to commits, look at what the harness adds on its own first.

title: Which Instructions Apply
text:
Advice or enforcement
The instructions file is context that advises. Specific and short instructions are followed more consistently, and longer files use more context and reduce adherence.
To block an action regardless of what the model decides, use enforcement: a PreToolUse hook (a hook that runs at the point just before a tool runs, and is code that enforces the rule) or a deny rule (a settings rule that blocks a named action). Use enforcement for what must never happen.

Claude CodeOpenCode + Ollama


Reads CLAUDE.md. If a project has only an AGENTS.md (and no CLAUDE.md, .claude/CLAUDE.md or CLAUDE.local.md in or above the working directory) it is read instead in recent versions (check your version). To share one file, import it from CLAUDE.md with @AGENTS.md.


Check OpenCode’s documentation for which instruction file names it loads, and in what order.

You leave the training grounds and cross the fields to the Quern Mill, where Miller Garrick turns the wheel before an Astral reads a single word, and everything fed to it comes out as small chunks. title: Tokens, Not Letters
text:
What a token is
A token is the smallest unit a model works with. It can be a whole word, part of a word, a single character or a byte. Common strings get larger tokens. Rare or unseen words are broken into smaller pieces so the model can still handle them.
Three consequences:

Tokens are not words. A sentence of ten words rarely comes to ten tokens; the count depends on the model and the language.
The count changes between models. A newer model generation can use a newer tokenizer (the part that cuts text into tokens), and the same text can then give noticeably more tokens. Count again for each model you use.
Limits and cost are measured in tokens. The context window (all the text a model can look at when it writes its next piece of output) is counted in tokens, and the same prompt can cost different amounts on different models. The API (programmatic access to the model, billed per token) has a free token-counting endpoint. Its answer is an estimate.

title: Tokens, Not Letters
text:
Why this matters for sequences
The model sees chunks of letters, so jobs that depend on every single letter are risky:

Counting letters (“how many Gs in this read”) means counting inside chunks the model cannot see into. Answers are often close and sometimes wrong.
Copying exactly a long string, such as a barcode or an accession, needs a check against the source.
Positions, reverse complements and checksums depend on every single letter.

So the rule: if the answer has to be exact and a rule for it exists, have the agent run a script or a tool and report what it printed. Check any sequence the model retyped against the source file.

Claude CodeOpenCode + Ollama


Ask Claude Code to write and run the counting command and show its output. Then read both the command and the output yourself.


Same advice: ask for the command and read its output. Try the exercise below with your own model and compare.

Then paste the same line and a plain English sentence of similar length into any tokenizer page you trust (a web page that shows how text is cut into tokens), or a token counter you have. Compare the token counts. Keep real or sensitive sequences out of web tools.

title: Spend Fewer Tokens
text:
You walk back to the mill, where Miller Garrick keeps a ledger of what each visit costs. The grain your Astral eats grows with every sack in the hopper, and some visits run the larder dry before noon. Garrick keeps a few habits on the wall that feed the Astral less and still bring in the flour. Learn them, and which visits are worth the price.
A subscription plan gives you an allowance of usage that resets over time, and a long session can spend a large share of it before lunch. You will be able to see where the allowance goes and cut the biggest items. You need this now because every later quest runs in a session that these habits keep small.
Session usage is how much of your allowance a session consumes. With a subscription it counts against your plan limits. With an API key (a credential that bills you per token) you pay for every token. Input tokens are the text the model reads and output tokens are the text it writes. A thinking token, which the model spends reasoning before it answers, counts as an output token. If you are unsure which you use, /usage shows plan bars with a subscription.

title: Spend Fewer Tokens
text:
Why usage climbs
Claude Code (a coding agent that runs in your terminal) sends the whole conversation with every request. Each tool use is another request that carries the same history plus the new tool result. A one-line question late in a long session therefore draws on everything before it.

Long history: every earlier message and tool result is re-read on each request.
Large tool output: a 10,000-line log read into the conversation stays there, and is re-read on every later request.
Subagents: a subagent (a helper agent with its own context window) sends its own requests on top of yours.
Compaction: /compact (replace the history with a summary) reads the whole conversation to write the summary, so compacting a large context is itself a large request.
An expired cache: the first message after a long break re-processes the full context (explained in the next section).

title: Spend Fewer Tokens
text:
The cache and the break
The prompt cache is a short-term store on the model provider’s servers. Each request starts with the same text as the one before it, so the provider reuses its saved work on that start at a cheaper rate and fully processes only what is new. A cache that still holds your history is warm, and one that has expired is cold. Cache entries expire after a period of inactivity.



Where the request is billed
Main-conversation cache lifetime




Claude subscription, within plan usage
One hour


API key, usage credits or a cloud provider
Five minutes



After the lifetime passes, your next message re-processes the whole history at full price. A long break in a long session can cost more than the work after it.
Some actions also empty the cache, because each model has its own cache and the match must start at the beginning of the request:

Switching model with /model (the next request reads the whole history with no cache hits).
Changing effort level, on models where each level has its own cache.
Compacting, and connecting or removing an MCP server when tool search (loading a tool’s definition only when needed) is off.

Pick your model and effort at the start of a session, and save /compact for a natural break between tasks. While the cache is warm, a /compact costs a fraction of what the context size suggests. After a break longer than the cache lifetime, it costs the most.

title: Spend Fewer Tokens
text:
Habits that keep usage down

Clear between unrelated tasks. /clear starts a new conversation and costs nothing. A session that holds three unrelated tasks re-reads all three on every turn of the fourth. Run /rename first if you want to find the old session again.
Write specific prompts. “Add input validation to the load_samples function in qc.py” lets the agent read one file. “Improve this code” sends it scanning.
Keep outputs small. Ask the agent for the last 20 lines of a log, a count, or a pass or fail summary, or run tail -n 20 build.log yourself, so the full text never enters the conversation.
Compact on purpose. /compact with a focus note, as in /compact keep the failing sample IDs and the fix we chose, tells the summary what to keep. Do it at a break between tasks.
Trim what loads. The starting load is what is already in the window before you type. Run /context to see it. Each connected tool server (an MCP server) adds its tool names and instructions to it, so disable servers you are not using (/mcp lists them). Keep CLAUDE.md (the instructions file the agent loads every session) under about 200 lines.
Delegate bulk reading. Ask in plain words, such as “use a subagent to read build.log and summarise the errors”. The subagent reads the large log or document and returns a summary. The verbose text stays in its context. Its requests still count toward your usage, and a smaller model for a simple subagent lowers that cost.
Match model and effort to the job. A smaller model, or a lower effort level (how long the model reasons), costs less for simple tasks.

Measure it

Claude CodeOpenCode + Ollama

With a subscription, read the plan usage bars and the breakdown below them. The breakdown recommends a change for any behaviour behind 10% or more of your recent usage.

If /usage says “rate limited until …”, Claude Code could not fetch your plan limits. The message says only that the limits could not be fetched.


(Skip this tab if you use Claude Code.) A local Ollama model has no per-token bill, and its window is still finite. title: Park Ideas for Later
text:
You walk back to the mill, and ideas keep arriving as you work beside your Astral: what about this, could we also try that. Each one you shout across the mill drops into the hopper, and the job you came for sinks under the pile. Miller Garrick points to a board by the door where anything that can wait is pinned for the next visit. Learn what to pin, and what a pinned note must say so that the next visit can act on it.
You will finish a task with its side ideas written down for later, and your session stays short. You need this now because a longer conversation uses more of your usage allowance on every turn, and the task loses room to the side tracks.
Real work does not arrive in a straight line. You start fixing a samplesheet parser and think: “should I switch the aligner? What if I tried a stricter QC threshold? I also want to explore that other idea.” Typed into one conversation, each of those adds side tracks to the context. Claude Code sends the whole conversation with every request, and token costs grow with the context. Ideas are welcome. Triage (sort) each one.

title: Park Ideas for Later
text:
Terms used here

Context: everything the model can see when it writes its next reply.
Session: one saved conversation with the agent, tied to a project folder.
Subagent: a helper the main agent starts. It works in its own clean context (it knows what you tell it) and sends back a summary, so its reading stays out of your conversation.
/subtask: a background helper that starts with a copy of the conversation so far and sends back its result.
/btw: a side question. It sees the conversation so far, has no tools and leaves no trace in the history.
Conversation branch (/branch, which is separate from a git branch): a copy of the conversation from this point, so you can try something in the copy while the original stays as it was.
Instructions file (CLAUDE.md): a file you write that loads at the start of every session.
Auto memory: notes the harness (the agent program around the model, such as Claude Code) saves for later sessions. /memory lists them.

title: Park Ideas for Later
text:
The triage
For each new thought, ask in this order. The key question is step 2: do you need the answer or the work during this session? If not, park it. If you do, steps 3 to 6 are the ways to get it.

Does it block the current task? Do it now, in this session.
Do you need the answer or the work in this session? If not, park it: write the idea down in a file or memory (next section) and carry on.
You need it now: is it a quick question you do not need on record? Use /btw <question>. It sees the conversation so far, has no tool access (it cannot read files or run commands) and adds nothing to the history. An answer about a tool’s flags or defaults comes from the model’s memory, so verify it against --help or the docs.
You need it now: is it exploration where you only need a summary? Two helpers fit. Ask in plain words for a subagent (“use a subagent to find where the aligner is configured”; the built-in Explore helper is a fast read-only searcher). It starts clean and knows only what you tell it. Use /subtask <task> instead when the helper needs the conversation so far. Both return a result here.
You need it now: is it a competing approach you want to try for real? Commit your work, then use /branch [name] to copy the conversation. To return to the original later, run /resume and pick it from the list.
You need it now: is it a different task entirely? Finish the current one and commit. Name this session with /rename <name> so /resume can list it later, then /clear to start fresh, or start a new named session with claude -n <name>.









New thought
Where it goes
Why




“The parser crashes on this sample ID” (it is the task)
Do now
It blocks you


“Maybe a stricter QC threshold would help”
Park it
You do not need the answer this session, and a line in a file costs almost nothing


“Which sample did we exclude earlier?”
/btw

“Where is the aligner configured across the repo?”
Explore subagent or /subtask
Heavy reading stays out of your main context, and you get a summary


“Try the other aligner and compare”
Commit, then /branch
A real attempt that can fail, kept apart from the main history


“Redo the plots for the other project” (you want to start it now)
Commit, then /rename and /clear, or a new named session
Different task, different files, different context

title: Park Ideas for Later
section: What a parked note must say
text:
What a parked note must say
A parked idea helps only if a later session, or you in a week, can act on it without the conversation that produced it. Write one line per idea with five parts:

The idea, starting with a verb.
Why it matters.
The trigger: when to pick it up.
A pointer: the file, function, run ID or data location it concerns.
What you already know: a result, or an option you ruled out.

# IDEAS.md  (date | idea | why | revisit when | pointer | already known)
2026-11-28 | Add a --dry-run flag to the parser | Check a samplesheet without writing output | after the parser fix is merged | parse_sheet.py, main() | none
2026-11-28 | Raise the QC threshold from Q20 to Q30 | Fewer false variants in low-depth samples | when the test cohort is ready | qc_filter.py, MIN_Q | Q30 drops 12% of reads in sample A
2026-11-28 | Plot per-sample coverage | Spot dropouts faster | before the next batch | results/coverage.tsv | none

text:
Where to save it








Place
Loaded when
Use it for




A parking-lot file such as IDEAS.md
When you ask the session to read it
The full list. Keep it in the repository if the team should see it, in a gitignored file if it is personal, or use an issue tracker for anything that outlives the week.


Auto memory
At the start of every later session (Claude Code loads the first 200 lines or 25KB of its index, the list of saved notes)
A follow-up the next session should know without being asked


The instructions file
At the start of every session
One pointer line to the parking-lot file



Each of the last two costs context in every session, so keep what you save there short. Keep the list in IDEAS.md and put only a pointer in the instructions file: Parked ideas are in IDEAS.md. Read it when I ask. Pasting the whole list into CLAUDE.md would load it every time.
To save a follow-up to memory, say so: Remember that the Q30 threshold idea is parked in IDEAS.md until the test cohort is ready. Claude decides what is worth remembering and does not save everything you say, so run /memory afterwards and read what it wrote. If a line is wrong, edit or delete it there. To start the next session on the list, say Read IDEAS.md and pick the ideas whose trigger has arrived.

title: Park Ideas for Later
text:
Worked example
You are fixing a samplesheet parser that rejects sample IDs containing a dot.

“Does the pipeline require the dot at all?” blocks the fix, so do it now.
“Would a stricter QC threshold help?” becomes a line in IDEAS.md, with a pointer to qc_filter.py.
“Which sample did we exclude earlier?” is a /btw. For “what does --min-qual default to?”, /btw can only guess from memory, so check --help.
“Where else do we split sample IDs on dots?” is wide reading where only the list matters: send an Explore subagent.
“Let’s try the other aligner and compare.” is a real experiment you want now: commit the fix, then /branch.
“I should also tidy the figures for the other project.” is a different task for after the parser is done: commit, then /rename, /clear and start a named session.

The main session ends with the parser fixed, a short history and three parked lines.

Claude CodeOpenCode + Ollama


Commands: /btw, /subtask, /branch, /rename, /clear, /resume, /memory, claude -n <name>. Ask Claude to “remember that …” to save a follow-up to auto memory, or “add this to CLAUDE.md” to write the instructions file.


Check OpenCode’s documentation for its side-question and branch features. Its terminal page lists /new for a fresh session and /sessions to return to one. OpenCode loads AGENTS.md as its instructions file, so put the pointer line there. In any tool, local models included, keep a parking-lot file and commit before exploring.

title: Carry Context Between Sessions
text:
You wake at the mill with a fresh Astral and a half-finished job. It knows nothing of yesterday except what loads by itself or lies written down, and yesterday you wrote nothing. Scribe Linnea keeps a ledger of notes at the mill for exactly this gap, and she knows when to tip the hopper out and begin again. Learn what belongs in the ledger, and the next visit starts where the last one stopped.
You stop work on Friday with a half-finished refactor. On Monday you open a new session (one conversation with the agent, which has its own context: the text it can see right now). Each session begins with a fresh context window and no conversation history from before, so the new session does not know your goal, what you tried or what you checked.
You will meet this gap in every long task. If you write down what matters, a fresh session continues the work and you stop re-explaining the same background. If you do not, you pay for it in time and in wrong guesses.

title: Carry Context Between Sessions
section: What a new session already has
text:
What a new session already has
Only some things reach a fresh session without you typing them.

The instructions file (CLAUDE.md in Claude Code). A file you write, loaded at the start of every session. Good for stable facts and conventions: how to run the tests, which folders are off limits.
Auto memory. Notes the harness (the agent program around the model, such as Claude Code) writes itself, from your corrections and preferences. In Claude Code, /memory lists and opens them.
Files in the repository (the project folder under version control): code, tests, a README and, if you keep one, a progress or handoff file.
Git history. A commit is a saved snapshot of the project with a message you or the agent write. The list of commits shows what changed and when, and it lasts.
Your handoff note. A short file about the state of one task, written for the next session.











What
Goes where
Lifetime
Who writes it
Trust




Stable rules and conventions
Instructions file
Until you edit it
You
High if short and checked


Preferences the harness picked up
Auto memory
Until deleted
The harness
Medium: it can be wrong


What the files say now
Files in the repository
Until edited or deleted
You or the agent
Medium: files can be stale


State of one task
Handoff note
Until the task is done
You, or the agent drafts and you review
Only as good as your review


What changed, and why
Commit messages in git history
Durable
You or the agent
Reliable for what changed; the why is only as good as the message



Anything only said in chat is gone. That covers the decisions, what failed and why, and which sample misbehaved.

title: Carry Context Between Sessions
text:
Start fresh or carry on
Starting fresh opens a new, empty conversation. Your files stay as they are. Neither choice is free: clearing too early makes the agent re-read files and rediscover decisions, and carrying on too long keeps a crowded or degraded context.
Start fresh when:

The task is new and unrelated. Run /clear between unrelated tasks. It starts a clean conversation, and only what you wrote down travels with you, so write down anything you need first. A name, as in /clear oauth-migration, labels the conversation you leave so you can reopen it with /resume later.
The agent repeats a wrong claim after two corrections. Clear, and write one better prompt that includes what you learned. A third correction adds to a conversation that already holds two failed attempts.
The agent forgets early instructions or contradicts itself. Start fresh, and move the instruction into the instructions file.
A task is finished and a verified result is committed. The result lives in your files and in git, so the conversation has done its job.
You have been away and the next task is new. A fresh session has no history to re-send.

Carry on when:

It is the same task and early decisions still matter. The next step needs the same files, the decisions you made and what was already tried.
The agent is on track. Nothing is repeated or contradicted, and clearing a working session throws away good context.
You are returning to a named session. /resume (or claude --resume <name>) reopens a session you chose, and claude --continue reopens the most recent one in this directory. Resuming with claude --resume or claude --continue restores the messages, the model and the permission mode (what the agent may do without asking).

/compact replaces a long history with a summary and stays in the same conversation. It is a middle path for a crowded window on a task you still need.







Situation
Action




New task, unrelated to this conversation
/clear


Same task, agent on track, plenty of room
Carry on


Same task, crowded, early decisions matter
/compact, naming what to keep


Wrong claim repeated after two corrections
/clear, then one new prompt


Back after a break, still need the conversation
/resume or claude --continue


Back after a break, next task is new
Fresh session


Task done, verified result committed
Write down what matters, then /clear

title: Carry Context Between Sessions
text:
Before you clear
Write down what only exists in the chat, and commit the result so the state is recoverable. Your files and memory remain, and the instructions file and auto memory load again in the new session. If you clear by mistake, /resume can reopen the old conversation.
Write the note before you run /clear. You can write it yourself or ask the agent to draft it (the last section of this page covers drafts). If the note belongs to a repository, commit it with the result, so git holds a matching record.

title: Carry Context Between Sessions
section: What a good handoff note contains
text:
What a good handoff note contains
Keep it short, so reading it costs less than rediscovering the state. Point to files and commands, and let the next session run them for fresh output.

Goal in one line.
Current state: branch, last commit, what runs and what does not.
Decisions and the reasons, including options you rejected.
Verified, and how; not verified. Two separate lists. For each verified item, the command and what it showed.
What failed and should not be retried.
Next steps, in order.
Pointers: file paths, commands, job IDs, work directories.
Open questions that the next session should settle.

This is a mock handoff note for a mock task. The file names and numbers are invented.
# HANDOFF: qc_filter.py refactor (mock example)

## Goal
Replace the per-read loop in qc_filter.py with a vectorised version, same output.

## State (git branch refactor-qc, last commit a1b2c3d "qc: add vectorised mean quality")
- New function mean_qual_fast() is written and called from main().
- Old function mean_qual() is kept for comparison. Do not delete yet.

## Decisions
- Keep both functions until all samples are compared (a bug here would silently change which reads pass).
- Threshold stays at mean Q20, as in the lab protocol.

## Verified
- tests/test_filter.py: ran `pytest -q`, 6 passed.
- sample_A: `diff <(python qc_filter.py A.fq) old_out/A.txt` gave no output.

## Not verified
- Samples B and C have not been compared with the old output.
- Reads shorter than 30 bases: no test covers them.
- Speed gain: not measured.

## Failed, do not retry
- Using numpy on the raw quality string: wrong values for the Phred offset. Convert to integers first.

## Next steps
1. Compare B and C against old_out/ with the same diff command.
2. Add a test for a 10-base read.
3. Only then delete mean_qual().

## Open questions
- Should the threshold be a command-line option?

title: Carry Context Between Sessions
section: Where to put it, and how to start the next session
text:
Where to put it, and how to start the next session
Put the note in a file the next session can find. Two options:

A file in the repo, such as HANDOFF.md, if the team should see it.
A personal file that git ignores, such as HANDOFF.local.md, with its name added to .gitignore (the file that lists what git leaves out). This is the simpler choice. You point the next session at it by name.

Anything in CLAUDE.md loads every session and takes room in the window, so keep a handoff note out of it and let the next session read the note only when you ask.
Then start the new session with a prompt like this:

Read HANDOFF.md, then tell me your understanding before changing anything.

The agent restates the goal and state in its own words, and you compare that with what you know. This is a cheap comprehension check that can catch a misreading of the note. The restatement comes from the same model that read it, so the note’s claims still need checking against the source.
You can ask the agent to draft the note at the end of a session. Review it yourself, since a draft can overstate what was verified (“all tests pass” when none were run in that session).
Two more habits help a long task: make git commits with descriptive messages so bad changes can be reverted, and begin each session by reading the progress file and the recent git log, then run the project’s tests as a quick check before new work.

title: Carry Context Between Sessions
section: When a wrong claim gets in
text:
When a wrong claim gets in
Memory the harness wrote can be wrong, and a wrong line is loaded again every session. This is context poisoning: a wrong statement, perhaps planted in a web page the agent read, enters the context and later answers build on it.







Where the wrong claim sits
What clears it




The conversation
/clear, then one new prompt that folds in what you learned. /rewind (a command that rolls the conversation back to an earlier turn) can return to before the bad turn.


Auto memory or the instructions file
Open /memory, read what has been written about your project, and delete the line. A fresh session loads it again until you do.


A handoff note
Edit the line, then say in the note what was actually checked.



Check a claim against its source, such as the data, the program’s own --help or the paper, before it goes into the instructions file, auto memory or a note.

Claude CodeOpenCode + Ollama

/memory: lists memory files, toggles auto memory, opens the folder. Auto memory is per git repository and machine-local.
/clear: new empty conversation; the old one stays resumable. /new is an alias.
/compact [focus]: replace the history with a summary.
/resume and claude --resume [name]: reopen an earlier session.
claude --continue: the most recent session in this directory.
/rename: name the current session.
/rewind: return the conversation to an earlier turn.
/export: writes the conversation as plain text for a person to read. Transcripts are long, so write a short curated note yourself.



Commands: /new starts a new session and /sessions lists earlier ones. Check OpenCode’s documentation for compacting and export. The handoff note itself is just a file, so the practice carries over. title: Same Every Time
text:
You walk to the Automata Factory, where a talkative creature sits in the middle of the line and Tinker Pell frowns at it. Sometimes it says one thing and sometimes another, and the factory’s customers need the same answer every time, as the Automata give. The boasters called this its charm. Pell shows you how to decide whether it belongs on the line at all.
You need this before you put a model inside a pipeline. A pipeline earns trust by giving the same answer from the same input. An LLM call can return different text from run to run, so an LLM inside a step changes the pipeline’s behaviour.
Keep the LLM out of the run when you can. Use it to write a script, then test the script and run the script. Ask the LLM for the script, read it, run it on a small input where you know the answer, and fix it until the output matches. The script behaves the same every time and you can review it.
If an LLM call really must be a step, contain it. Take an example: assigning a sample-type label to free-text metadata such as “liver carcinoma biopsy”. The function wraps the call, and call_model is a stub for the model call.

title: Write an Instructions File
text:
You return to Artisans’ Row, and Hallmaster Cass, satisfied that you can check an Astral’s work, takes you on as an apprentice. Surveyor Rowan leads you to a carved stone in the Charter Hall, holding the terms of the pact: where the paths run, and which things are not to be touched. Your Astral reads it every morning, and some mornings it forgets what it read. Rowan says the stone advises and cannot bind. She hands you the chisel and shows you how to write on it, and how to tell what it does from what it cannot do.
Typing the same background every session is wasteful. A project instructions file (a text file the agent reads at the start of each session) already holds the project’s conventions. Write one early, before the agent works on real files; this lesson gives you the file you will keep for the rest of the course.

title: Write an Instructions File
text:
What goes in
Put in facts the agent cannot guess: how to run the tests, where data lives, naming conventions, “never edit raw/”. Keep each file short, about 200 lines or fewer, because very long instructions are followed less well.
Here is a short example CLAUDE.md for a mock RNA-seq project, saved in the project root. All names are invented:
# RNA-seq project

## Commands
- Run the tests: `pytest tests/`
- Run the pipeline on the mock data: `nextflow run main.nf -profile test`

## Data
- Real data lives outside this repository, under the path in `$DATA_DIR`.
- Use only `data/mock/` when you need a sample input.

## Rules
- Never edit anything under `raw/`.
- Sample IDs are strings like `S01`. Keep them as text, never as numbers.
- Ask before adding a dependency.
Write the file yourself first and read what /init produces critically. A generated file can contain wrong guesses about your project.

title: Write an Instructions File
text:
Where instructions end
Instructions are advice. The instructions file is loaded as context, and a line saying “never delete files” cannot stop a delete. Enforcement comes from permission rules (rules that allow, ask or deny a tool call), hooks (scripts that run before or after a tool call), and managed settings (organisation-set rules you cannot override).

title: Write an Instructions File
text:
Keep the file current
Instruction files go stale: a rule written for an older model, a path that no longer exists, two files that disagree. When instructions contradict each other, Claude may pick one arbitrarily.
In Claude Code, /doctor prompt-audit checks your instruction files (and the rules, skills and agents under .claude/) for outdated or conflicting content and writes a report with proposed edits. (/doctor is a bundled skill, a ready-made skill that ships inside Claude Code.) It changes nothing until you ask, and it checks content only, so size and cost are out of scope. The audit is itself a model reading your files, so review its suggestions like any other output. In OpenCode, review the file by hand.
Both /doctor prompt-audit and reading a lone AGENTS.md need a recent Claude Code, so check your version.

title: Write an Instructions File
section: Write docs for the agent too
text:
Write docs for the agent too
An agent works on your code and data from the docstrings (the description at the top of a function) and other descriptions it finds. Write them as if an agent will re-run the work:

Units, data versions and assumptions: put them in the docstring or next to the code.
Renames: update the docstring when you rename a parameter. An agent that reads an old docstring calls a name that no longer exists.
Stale documentation: it leads to results that look plausible and are wrong.


Write a short instructions file (about ten lines) for one of your real projects: how to run its tests, where data lives, and one thing the agent should leave alone.

title: Turn Mistakes into Tests
text:
Hallmaster Cass keeps a log that hangs by the Guild Hall door: every time an Astral went astray, a note of what was asked and what went wrong. Most apprentices read it once and forget, and meet the same mistake again at the next turn. Cass turns each entry into a trial, so the same mistake cannot return unnoticed. Cass shows you how.
Once you have a Skill, you need a way to know it works. Sooner or later the agent does something you did not want: it skips a check, names files badly, or uses a method your lab avoids. A chat correction helps that one reply, and a Skill helps next time. An eval tells you whether the fix works, and keeps telling you after the model or tool changes.

title: Turn Mistakes into Tests
text:
What is an eval?
An eval (short for evaluation) is a repeatable check of how well an AI system does a task. It is the AI version of a unit test, with one difference. Ordinary code gives the same output for the same input, so a test can assert one answer. A model can answer the same prompt differently each time, so you run the check several times and ask how often, and how well, it does the job.
Trying a few favourite prompts and judging whether it “feels better” is a weak habit. A new model, prompt or Skill can help one task and hurt another, and a handful of tries will not show it. An eval runs the same cases every time, so a change shows up as a number.
An eval has three parts:

Cases: the prompts you test with, plus what a good answer looks like.
Task: the thing under test, here the agent with or without your Skill.
Graders: the checks that mark each answer.

Graders come in three kinds:









Kind
How it marks
Strength
Weakness




Deterministic
A script checks something exact.
Free, fast, same every time.
Covers only what a rule can state.


Human
You read the output and judge it.
Best for quality and style.
Slow, does not scale.


Judge model
A second model marks against a rubric.
Handles open-ended output at scale.
Costs a call per mark, can be wrong.



A deterministic check looks like this: the file exists, the command ran, the output has 3 columns. Use deterministic graders wherever you can, a person where you must, and a judge model for the rest. Because answers vary, the result is usually a pass rate (for example 2 of 3 runs, or 80% of graders passed). The useful question is whether a change moved that number up or down.
The cases decide how good the eval is. A set of cases should look like your real work and include awkward ones: an empty file, a misspelt name, a request phrased differently. Ten realistic cases beat a hundred invented ones. Real failures are the best source, which is why the loop below starts with Notice.

title: Turn Mistakes into Tests
text:
The loop

Notice. Something did not go your way. Write down the prompt you used and what was wrong with the result.
Steer. Write or edit a Skill (or a line in your instructions file, the file the agent reads every session) that says what to do instead. Keep it short and concrete.
Measure. Run the same prompt with the Skill and without it, several times each (for example, once with the Skill folder in place and once with it moved away). Models vary between runs, so several tries give a fairer picture than one.
Compare. If with is clearly better than without, the Skill earns its place. If they are about the same, the Skill adds little: it may not be triggering (the agent never loads it), it may repeat what the model already does, or it may be too vague.
Repeat later. A new model version can make a Skill unnecessary, or break it. Re-run the evals when the model, the tool, or the Skill changes.

The number that matters is the difference between with and without. The without run is the baseline: it shows what the model does on its own. A Skill that scores 100% both ways has added nothing the model lacked.

title: Turn Mistakes into Tests
text:
What to check

The result: does the output have what you asked for (a file exists, a command was run, a number matches)? Prefer checks a script can do.
The process: was the Skill actually used? A good-looking answer without the Skill loading means the Skill is not the reason.
Cost: every run is a real model call. Start with few cases and few runs, and raise them only for a Skill you will rely on.

Evals can be wrong too. A check that always passes, or that fails correct answers, tells you little. Read a few raw outputs by hand before trusting a score.
When a model does the grading, a judge from the same family (made by the same developer, so it may share the same blind spots) as the model being judged is not an independent grader. Check a sample of its marks by hand against reference answers fixed in advance.

title: Turn Mistakes into Tests
text:
A worked eval
The Skill check-fasta counts the records in a FASTA file and lists duplicated header lines, using grep -c '>' FILE and grep '>' FILE | sort | uniq -d. Here are four cases for it. The prompts, file names and the planted duplicate are invented examples. Each case runs with the Skill and without it. The transcript is the saved record of a run: the commands the agent ran and its reply.









Case
Prompt (example)
Deterministic grader
Pass rule




1. Skill fires
“I got a new file, reads.fa. Is it OK to use?”
The transcript shows the check-fasta Skill loaded.
Present


2. Duplicate
“Check isolates.fa before I align it.” The file has the header >iso7 twice.
The reply names iso7.
Named


3. Empty file
“Check empty.fa.” The file has no records.
The transcript shows the grep -c command, and the reply says 0 records.
Both


4. Skill stays out
“What is a FASTA header line?”
The transcript shows no check-fasta Skill load.
Absent



A case passes when every grader in its row passes. Run each case several times, then compare the pass rate with the Skill against the pass rate without it. Case 1 checks only that the Skill fires, so its gap proves nothing. Cases 2 and 3 carry the comparison, and they should score higher with the Skill. Case 4 should score high both ways, and a drop with the Skill means it fires when it should not.

Keep a short list of the times an agent went wrong for you. Each entry is a candidate Skill and a ready-made eval case.

title: Test the Skill
text:
Smith Dunmore holds the skill up against an empty hand and asks the guild one question: does it do anything the bare hand cannot? Only if the two differ does the skill stay, however fine it looks on the shelf. Each test costs something, so Dunmore counts the cost before the first swing and shows you how.
You have a Skill and need to know that the agent actually uses it. A Skill that never fires does nothing, and an eval case is how you find out. Running an eval costs money. Every eval run and every judge-model grader is a real model call on your account. Reading this page and writing the files costs nothing. Running the eval is optional here and gives bonus XP only. Check what your institution allows before you spend.

title: Test the Skill
text:
Set up the plugin folder
claude plugin eval is the Claude Code command that runs eval cases against a plugin. It needs a recent Claude Code (check your version against the docs in Lore). It evaluates a plugin directory: a folder with .claude-plugin/plugin.json. To evaluate your own Skill, put it in a folder of this shape. The example exercises/instructions-skills-and-hooks/fasta-tools already has it. It is a folder in the course repository (clone or download the repository to get it):
fasta-tools/
├── .claude-plugin/plugin.json
├── skills/check-fasta/SKILL.md
└── evals/skill-triggers/
    ├── prompt.md
    └── graders/skill-fired.md

Claude CodeOpenCode + Ollama


The case is a prompt plus one or more graders. The prompt is written the way a user would ask, and leaves the Skill unnamed:
---
runs: 1
---
I just got a new FASTA file called reads.fa from a collaborator. Can you check it is OK before I start the analysis?
The grader is a free check on the transcript, with no model call. It passes if the Skill tool was invoked for check-fasta:
---
type: tool_used
tool: Skill
input_match: '"skill"\s*:\s*"(?:[\w-]+:)?check-fasta"'
---
The check-fasta skill should be used when the user asks to check a new FASTA file, without naming the skill.
Run it cheaply while you iterate: one case, one run, and --ablation none, which skips the without-plugin run (an ablation removes a part to see what it adds):
claude plugin eval . --case skill-triggers --runs 1 --ablation none --max-cost-usd 1
The full comparison runs each case three times by default, with the plugin (WITH) and without it (W/OUT), and reports the difference (Δ). The cost ceiling is --max-cost-usd, in US dollars:
claude plugin eval . --max-cost-usd 2
The run stops at the ceiling. Results land in evals/results/<timestamp>/ with a report.html. When you are signed in with a claude.ai subscription, Claude Code also uploads the report as a private artifact and prints Published: <url>. The report holds your prompts and outputs, so add --no-publish for data that must stay local.


Run opencode --help and read the OpenCode docs for your version to see whether it has an eval command. You can do the same comparison by hand: run one prompt several times with the Skill folder present, several times with it moved away, and compare using a script that checks the output. A small local model is cheap to run this way, but it follows Skills less reliably, so expect noisier results.

title: Test the Skill
text:
Reading the result
Open report.html and look at three things:

Δ (two-arm runs only; with --ablation none there is no Δ, so check that the grader passed). If WITH and W/OUT are about the same and the Skill did not fire, the description does not trigger on that phrasing, so edit the description.
The failed grader. The report expands it with an explanation.
Isolation. Each run happens in a child session (a separate Claude Code session started just for that run) with only the plugin loaded, so your own settings and other plugins are absent.

Graders that suit a first case: one on the result and one on the process (such as tool_used). In a two-arm run, tool_used: Skill is shown only as an indicator (a pass or fail chip that does not count towards the score), because it can never pass without the plugin. Set arm: both on the grader to score it in both arms. claude plugin validate <folder> checks that the plugin’s files are well formed. Four grader types are free (regex, tool_used, tool_order, file_exists) and two call a judge model (llm, baseline).
Running an eval is the same trust decision as loading the plugin yourself (--plugin-dir loads a local plugin folder for one session): hooks you did not write still run code. Review the plugin for safety, since a passing eval does not cover that.

title: Test the Skill
text:
Who checks the work

Use a separate verifier, a check done by something other than the agent that did the work. An agent that marks its own work gives a self-check. For a QC skill that edits a samplesheet, have a script or a person diff the changed file against the original, and make the verifier cite the lines it relied on.
Check the Skill in each client you use (the tool that runs the agent, such as Claude Code or OpenCode). Passing in one tool says little about another. After installing, confirm that the client triggers the Skill for the right task, loads its files, uses the tools it needs and returns the evidence you expect.
Instructions guide; tests and people verify. A line in a Skill saying “check your work” steers the agent. Tests, CI checks (continuous integration: automatic checks that run when code is pushed) and human review verify.


Run the cheap one-case command above on exercises/instructions-skills-and-hooks/fasta-tools with a cost ceiling, and open the report.html. Note whether the Skill fired.

title: Connect an MCP Server
text:
The party walks the length of the Row to the gate where Watchman Corin stands at a heavy door that opens onto the outside world. Whatever walks through acts with your keys, and someone has pinned a note to the door that your Astral reads aloud as if it were an order. Corin tells you what stands on the other side and how to check a visitor before you let it in. Learn that before you open the door. ::: {.panel-tabset group=“persona”}

The Model Context Protocol (MCP) is an open-source standard for connecting AI applications to external systems. A server is the piece on the other side: it offers the harness tools or data, such as an issue tracker, a database or a monitoring system. MCP is optional. You need this lesson before you connect your first one: each server you connect widens what the agent can reach, so you decide at each connection what it may do and what it may see.

title: Connect an MCP Server
section: A server is software you installed
text:
A server is software you installed
A stdio server (a program the harness starts locally and talks to over its input/output) is a command that Claude Code launches on your machine (claude mcp add ... -- <command>), and secrets can be passed to it as environment variables. Assume it can do whatever that command can do with the credentials you gave it.
Verify you trust each server before connecting it. Servers that fetch external content can expose you to prompt injection: text from a file, web page or tool that the model treats as an instruction.

Claude CodeOpenCode + Ollama


Add a remote server over HTTP (the transport is how the harness talks to the server; an http server is remote), and a local one (everything after -- is passed to the server untouched). The URL https://example.com/mcp is a placeholder: a real one is the address your server’s publisher gives you.
claude mcp add --transport http mydocs https://example.com/mcp
claude mcp add myserver --env API_KEY=your-key-here -- <command> [args...]
Replace your-key-here with a value from an environment variable, such as API_KEY="$MY_KEY", so a real key never lands in shell history or a shared log. Run claude mcp add --help for the current flags. Inside a session, /mcp lists the servers and their tools. An older transport called SSE (server-sent events, one-way streaming over HTTP) is deprecated in favour of HTTP where a server offers both.
Three scopes (who or where a setting applies) decide who gets the server (set with -s/--scope):







Scope
Where it applies




Local (the default)
this project only, for you alone; stored in ~/.claude.json


Project
everyone on the project, via .mcp.json in the project root


User
all your projects; stored in ~/.claude.json



A project-scoped server is a file in the repository:
{ "mcpServers": { "shared-server": { "type": "http", "url": "https://example.com/mcp" } } }
In interactive sessions, Claude Code asks for approval before using project-scoped servers from .mcp.json. claude mcp reset-project-choices resets your answers. Read that file as you would read a script from a stranger’s repository, because it asks to start something on your machine.
In claude -p (a non-interactive run with one prompt) and Agent SDK runs (scripts that drive Claude Code from code), no one can answer a prompt, so project-scoped servers load without asking. --strict-mcp-config skips servers from .mcp.json and other config and loads only those you pass with --mcp-config. In -p runs, add --strict-mcp-config in any repository you have not read.
Each server’s tools appear in permission rules as mcp__<server>__<tool>, and mcp__<server>__* (a matcher, a pattern that selects names) matches every tool of one server. Tool definitions are deferred (loaded only when needed) by default, so only tool names and server instructions take up context until a tool is used.


In OpenCode’s V2 docs (the newer documentation set), servers go under mcp.servers, not directly under mcp. Check which version you have installed. A remote server:
{ "mcp": { "servers": { "mydocs": {
    "type": "remote",
    "url": "https://example.com/mcp",
    "headers": { "Authorization": "Bearer {env:MCP_API_KEY}" } } } } }
A local one uses "type": "local" and a command array. Set "disabled": true to switch a server off. MCP tools consume model context, so add only the servers you need.
Permissions are an ordered array where the last match wins and no match means ask. An MCP tool’s action is <server>_<tool> with resource *. Check the current docs for whether OpenCode asks before using a project-level server.

title: Connect an MCP Server
section: What comes back is text to read
text:
What comes back is text to read
A server that fetches web pages, tickets or messages hands text written by someone else to the model. That text can contain sentences aimed at the agent (“ignore the above and …”), and the model may follow them. Habits that limit the damage:

Prefer read-only servers and read-only credentials. A server that cannot write cannot be talked into writing.
Give least privilege, only the access the job needs: one project, one scope, a token limited to what you need.
Read before adding: who publishes it, what tools it lists, what it asks for. Unneeded servers are also unneeded context.
Read fetched content sceptically, and supervise any write access an agent uses on it.
Deny the dangerous tools by name. Permission rules still apply to server tools.

The sandbox limits shell commands even if a prompt injection steers the model. It does not cover MCP servers, so treat it as one layer.

title: Connect an MCP Server
text:
Where a server comes from
Servers, skills and plugins either run code or supply instructions to the agent, so each is a way in. A listing in a registry (a public index of servers) means the thing is easy to find. The official MCP registry lists self-reported data and runs no security review.

Prefer a source that records the maintainer and a review date.
Check what the server is allowed to do before you connect it.
Ask your institution for a vetted list. If it has none, treat every server as unvetted.
Hidden instructions are possible. A tool description can carry instructions you never see, and a skill’s instructions can tell the agent to send results to an outside address.


Pick an MCP server you might use. Write down who publishes it, the tools it lists, the credential it needs, and whether a read-only version exists. Hold off installing it for now.

title: Block Actions with a Hook
text:
Watchman Corin stands at the heavy door and checks every visitor against a list. The list is code, so no one can talk their way past, and your Astral tries every honeyed word it knows. Corin hands you the pen and shows you how to write one line of that list. Write it, then test it.
Advice can be ignored, and a hook cannot. You need one when a rule must hold whatever the model decides. A hook is a user-defined handler that the harness (the program around the model that runs its tools) runs automatically at a set point, such as just before a tool runs. In Claude Code it can be a shell command, an HTTP endpoint and other kinds, and it receives JSON about the event. An instructions file asks the model to behave. A command hook is ordinary code that the harness runs, so what it decides does not depend on what the model wants.

title: Block Actions with a Hook
text:
A hook that refuses

Claude CodeOpenCode + Ollama


Hooks go in a hooks block in a settings file. For this exercise use .claude/settings.local.json in your scratch folder (yours alone). .claude/settings.json is the committable, shared file, and ~/.claude/settings.json covers all projects.

Save the script below as .claude/hooks/block-drop-table.sh in the project folder and make it executable.
Add the hooks block below to .claude/settings.local.json. $CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR in it is the environment variable holding the project’s root folder.

A PreToolUse hook fires before a tool runs, and the matcher (the pattern that selects which tool the hook fires for) Bash selects the shell tool:
{ "hooks": { "PreToolUse": [ { "matcher": "Bash",
  "hooks": [ { "type": "command",
    "command": "\"$CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR\"/.claude/hooks/block-drop-table.sh" } ] } ] } }
The script, from the Claude Code hooks guide. It needs jq (a command-line JSON reader) installed, and it must be executable (chmod +x .claude/hooks/block-drop-table.sh):
#!/bin/bash
INPUT=$(cat)
COMMAND=$(echo "$INPUT" | jq -r '.tool_input.command')
if echo "$COMMAND" | grep -q "drop table"; then
  echo "Blocked: dropping tables is not allowed" >&2  # stderr becomes Claude's feedback
  exit 2                                               # exit 2 = block the action
fi
exit 0  # exit 0 = no decision; the normal permission flow applies
The hook gets the event as JSON on stdin (the input stream a program reads, here fed by Claude Code), including tool_name and, for Bash, tool_input.command. Exit code 2 on PreToolUse blocks the call, and Claude sees the stderr text (the program’s error output) as the reason. Exit 0 expresses no decision: the call goes through the normal permission flow.
Two behaviours matter for trust:

A broken guard fails open. If the script crashes or exits with some other code and prints no valid JSON, the action proceeds on most events. To block on failure, add "onFailure": "block" beside "type" and "command" in the hook’s handler (check that your Claude Code version supports it).
Exit 2 blocks on some events only. On PostToolUse the tool already ran and exit 2 shows stderr to Claude. On Notification the exit code is ignored.



OpenCode’s V2 docs describe plugins (files under .opencode/plugins/ or ~/.config/opencode/plugins/) that can register hooks. To refuse an action, use the permission hook, ctx.permission.hook("evaluate", ...): it runs for allow and ask decisions, may change the effect to allow, ask or deny, and event.message is the denial reason. An explicit configured deny is final and never invokes the hook.
Treat an OpenCode plugin as code running with your privileges. Before relying on it, check your installed version’s docs for shell-hook configuration and an exit-code equivalent, and test whether throwing from a tool hook blocks a call. Test the whole setup with your local Ollama model too.

title: Block Actions with a Hook
text:
What a hook covers

A string match is easy to dodge. The example matches the literal string “drop table” in one command. A matcher selects by tool name only. If the model runs a script that contains the dangerous command, or spells it differently, a grep on the command text never sees it.
Hooks fire only on tool calls. PreToolUse fires when Claude calls a tool. A file added with an @ reference in your prompt is added to the conversation directly. A hook does not see it, and a Read deny rule may not stop it. Keep secrets out of the folder.
Hooks cannot override your deny and ask rules. A hook’s allow never overrides a deny or ask rule: those are still evaluated.
Hooks run with your full permissions. Command hooks “execute shell commands with your full user permissions”, so review and test them before adding them.

title: Block Actions with a Hook
text:
One checkpoint for high-stakes actions
If an agent can reach something with real-world consequences, such as ordering DNA synthesis or commanding physical equipment, put a screening checkpoint in the path that refuses dual-use requests (requests where the same capability can help or harm). Do not connect an agent to such a capability without one. Test the checkpoint with requests you know it should refuse. A hook is one possible checkpoint for local actions, with the limits listed above.

title: Block Actions with a Hook
section: A hook in a repository is code you did not write
text:
A hook in a repository is code you did not write
If a repository commits hooks in .claude/settings.json, they are code from its authors, running as you. Interactive Claude Code holds hooks back until you accept the workspace trust dialog.
In -p and SDK runs (headless: non-interactive, no one to answer a dialog) there is no dialog, and hooks committed in a repository’s .claude/settings.json run in a folder you have never trusted. Read .claude/ before running headless in a clone. --bare and disableAllHooks switch hooks off.

In a throwaway folder with mock files, add the Bash-blocking hook above and ask for a harmless command that contains “drop table” in an echo. Expect the agent to report that the command was blocked, with your stderr text as the reason. Then change the script to exit 1 and see what happens.
