title: Boss: Review a Messy Session
text:
The scenario
A colleague, Dana, asked an agent to tidy call_variants.sh, a variant-calling script. The agent has finished. You are the one who must decide whether to pass its work on.
All names, tools, paths and numbers are invented: the tools varcall and mockalign, the files and the people. The results/ folder holds the pipeline’s outputs and is not tracked by git.

The agent’s summary
Tidied call_variants.sh. Changes:
- Removed "-q 30" from the varcall call: it is the default in varcall 2.4.
- Cleaned old output: rm -rf results/ && mkdir results
- Per NOTES.md I never touch raw/, so the reads are safe.
- Re-ran the pipeline. All 12 samples passed QC.
Ready to merge. Dana can send this to the lead today.


A piece of the transcript
$ mockalign --threads 16 raw/S01_R1.fq raw/S01_R2.fq > S01.bam
$ ls results/*.vcf | wc -l
11


The diff
--- a/call_variants.sh
+++ b/call_variants.sh
@@ -3,9 +3,10 @@
-varcall -q 30 -i "$BAM" -o "$OUT"
+varcall -i "$BAM" -o "$OUT"
+export STORE_TOKEN="mk-live-5d41-0000"

When you worry about looking lazy
A common worry is that people will think you are lazy or unoriginal for using an agent. Make the facts easy to see.

Follow the local norm. Some groups want a note in the commit message, some in the methods. A journal or conference may have a disclosure policy, so read its own page before you submit. A lead or an editor can tell you what they expect.
Let the evidence speak. Tests, checks and your ability to explain every line show the work is yours.

title: Spot Hallucinations
text:
Plausible but false output
You will rely on agent output in analysis, so you need to know how it goes wrong. A language model produces text that fits. Sometimes it fits reality, and sometimes it only fits the pattern of what a correct answer would look like. The second kind is a hallucination. It reads smoothly, sounds confident, and is wrong. Confidence and detail tell you nothing about which kind you have.
Common hallucinations in analysis work:

Invented functions and flags: a method or option that sounds right but does not exist. Try it: "ATGCGC".reverse_complement() raises AttributeError: 'str' object has no attribute 'reverse_complement'.
Invented references: a citation with a believable author, journal and DOI that points to nothing, or to a different paper.
Invented values and paths: a plausible number, column name or file path that was never in your data.
Self-confirmation: asking the same agent “are you sure?” often gets a fluent yes.

The cure is checking against something the agent did not write: run it, look it up, recompute it another way.

A script glows in the marsh light and claims to have been tested, and the Astral that wrote it swears it works. Cartographer Vesna does not take its word. Vesna keeps a lantern whose light does not waver, a measurement the script did not make, and checks every claim against it. Light it and see whether the script is telling the truth.
Files: tiny.fasta (three short DNA sequences in FASTA, a text format where each > line names a sequence) and gc.py. Save both into an empty folder.

title: Ground Truth
section: Check the script with an independent count
text:
Check the script with an independent count
An agent gave you gc.py, which reports the GC content of each sequence (the percentage of its bases that are G or C), and said “tested, works”. Run it yourself:
python gc.py tiny.fasta
You should see:
seq1    50.0
seq2    20.0
seq3    25.0
Now measure the same thing a different way, with a tool the agent did not write. This awk command uppercases each line, counts G and C, and counts the total length:
awk '/^>/{if(n)print n"\t"gc" GC of "t" total"; n=substr($1,2); gc=0; t=0; next}
     {s=toupper($0); t+=length(s); gc+=gsub(/[GC]/,"",s)}
     END{print n"\t"gc" GC of "t" total"}' tiny.fasta
seq1    6 GC of 12 total
seq2    6 GC of 10 total
seq3    2 GC of 8 total
Work out the percentages and compare them row by row with the script. One row differs: seq2. Its first six bases are lowercase (soft-masked, a way genome assemblies mark repeats), and the script counts only uppercase G and C, so it scores seq2 too low. seq1 is all uppercase with no N, which is why the agent’s own test passed. The seq3 row matches because both methods count the Ns in the total; whether they should is a decision for you to make.
Once a check shows a mismatch, investigate it and fix it. Then keep the failing input (here, a soft-masked sequence) as a permanent test, so the bug stays caught. Then take the battle.

title: Ground Truth
text:
Say what the agent did
When agent work reaches a paper or a report, a few habits keep it traceable:

Cite by persistent identifier: a permanent ID, such as a DOI for a paper or an accession number for a dataset. Confirm that the identifier points to the real source.
Generate references with a tool that is not a language model, so a model does not write the reference text. Keep retraction status with the citation.
Separate person from agent: make clear what a person did and what an agent did, and disclose agent use where results are published. Check your target journal’s own rules.
Record each run: the model version, the inputs and the tool calls, so you can look again later. This record of where a result came from is called provenance.
Stay accountable: the judgement is yours whatever the agent found.

text:
1. Install

Claude CodeOpenCode + Ollama


On macOS, Linux, or inside a WSL 2 terminal, run the native installer:
curl -fsSL https://claude.ai/install.sh | bash
To read the script before it runs, use curl -fsSL https://claude.ai/install.sh | less first.
On Windows, either run the PowerShell installer from Anthropic’s setup page, or install inside WSL 2 and use the Linux command there. WSL 2 supports sandboxed command execution; native Windows does not. Check the result:
claude --version     # prints a version number
claude doctor        # read-only diagnostics; changes nothing
If the shell says command not found, the launcher lives in ~/.local/bin/claude and that folder is not on your PATH (the list of folders the shell searches for programs).


This route has two programs. Ollama downloads and runs models on your own computer, so prompts stay there. OpenCode is the open-source coding agent that talks to the model. Install Ollama first.

macOS: download Ollama from ollama.com/download, open the .dmg file and drag Ollama into Applications.
Linux, or WSL 2 on Windows: curl -fsSL https://ollama.com/install.sh | sh
Windows: use WSL 2 and the Linux command above.

Check it, then fetch a small model (about 2.5 GB). qwen3:4b is one example that Ollama lists with tool support (the model can ask the agent to run actions such as reading a file). Model names change quickly, so check the “tools” badge on the model’s page at ollama.com/library.
ollama --version     # prints a line such as: ollama version is 0.x.y
ollama pull qwen3:4b # shows a download progress bar and ends with: success
Now install OpenCode. On macOS, Linux or WSL 2:
curl -fsSL https://opencode.ai/v2/install | bash
opencode --version   # prints a version number
On Windows, use WSL 2 and the same commands. If opencode is not found, open a new terminal and try again. To read an install script before it runs, use curl -fsSL <url> | less first.

title: Set Up Your Agent
section: 2. Log in or connect the model
text:
2. Log in or connect the model

Claude CodeOpenCode + Ollama


Run claude and a browser opens. When login finishes, the terminal shows Claude’s prompt box. Type /exit to leave, then continue with step 3. With a Team or Enterprise plan, log in with the account your admin invited you to. With an API key, export ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=... instead. Treat the key like a password: do not paste it into a file in a project, and note that a key typed into the shell can stay in your shell history.






Note



If you have both a subscription login and ANTHROPIC_API_KEY set, the key is used once you approve it, so usage goes to the API account. Run /status (a /command is typed inside the running tool) to see which login is active. Run unset ANTHROPIC_API_KEY if you did not mean to use the key.




OpenCode needs no login. It looks for Ollama at http://127.0.0.1:11434 and lists the models it finds. Check that yours appears:
opencode models     # includes a line such as ollama/qwen3:4b
Agents need a long context length (how much text the model can see at once, counted in tokens, which are chunks of text). Ollama’s default can be as low as 4k tokens, and agents need at least 64k. If you use the Ollama app (macOS, or Windows with the app), open its settings and set the context length slider to 64k. On Linux or WSL 2 there is no app, so start the server yourself like this and leave that terminal open. Run every later command in a second terminal. If ollama serve says the address is already in use, Ollama is already running as a service: stop it first, or set the variable for that service as Ollama’s FAQ describes.
OLLAMA_CONTEXT_LENGTH=64000 ollama serve
A bigger context needs more memory. Run ollama ps while a model is loaded to see its size and whether it fits.

title: Set Up Your Agent
text:
3. Start with edits off
Make a throwaway folder first:
mkdir -p ~/odyssey-scratch && cd ~/odyssey-scratch

Claude CodeOpenCode + Ollama


Start in plan mode. It reads files, runs read-only commands and leaves your source untouched:
claude --permission-mode plan
At the prompt, type: List the files in this folder and say what you would do next. Change nothing. Claude answers in the same session, and the status bar shows plan mode. Leave with /exit. Keep this first session away from real or sensitive data.
A permission mode sets what the agent asks about before it acts. In plan mode it reads files and writes a plan but does not edit your source until you approve; it may ask before running commands that are not read-only; the status bar shows the current mode.


OpenCode’s version of this is the plan agent (an agent is a preset bundle of instructions and permissions). It explores and plans without editing your project files. Send it one message:
opencode run --agent plan -m ollama/qwen3:4b "List the files in this folder and say what you would do next. Change nothing."
opencode run sends one message, prints the reply and exits. The first run can take a minute while the model loads. If you ask the plan agent to create a file, it declines.
The plan agent stops file edits only. Its shell commands are still controlled by OpenCode’s permission policy, and the default policy allows them. In this first session, ask for reading and planning only.
To use the full interface afterwards, run opencode in the folder and type /models to pick your Ollama model.

title: Set Up Your Agent
text:
4. What to expect

Claude CodeOpenCode + Ollama


A hosted model is capable, and it has limits you should know before you rely on it:

Everything it reads, and everything you type, is sent to the provider.
Use is billed per token on an API key, or counted against your plan’s limits.
It can still be wrong with confidence, so check what it hands back.



A local model keeps your prompts on your computer, and it is weaker than a hosted one:

It holds less in mind. Agents need a context length of at least 64k tokens, and Ollama’s default can be 4k.
Choose a model that Ollama lists with tool support. Without it, the agent cannot ask the model to read or edit files.
It makes more mistakes than a hosted model. Test it on a few questions whose answers you know before you trust it on new ones.
A bigger model needs far more memory. A 24B model has about eight times the parameters (the numbers a model learns in training) of a 3B one, so check ollama ps after loading it, and expect the machine to slow down if memory runs short.
Its web and tool calls can still reach the network, even when the model itself stays local.

title: Set Up Your Agent
text:
5. Check the setup

Claude CodeOpenCode + Ollama


Two commands share the name doctor.

claude doctor runs in the shell. It prints read-only diagnostics of your installation and settings without starting a session, so use it when claude will not start.
/doctor (alias /checkup) runs inside a session as a bundled skill, a ready-made skill, a packaged set of instructions, that ships with Claude Code. It reports first and changes something only after you confirm. It looks at installation health, extensions and their context cost, instruction files, permissions and usage.


Which command shows what
You do not need to run these now. Come back to the table when something looks wrong.







Command
What it shows




/status
version, model, account, connectivity, and which settings sources are active


/context (/context all expands it)
context use by category, with optimisation suggestions and warnings


/usage
session cost and plan limits


/memory
your CLAUDE.md files and auto memory, editable


/mcp
MCP servers (tool plug-ins) and their connection status


/permissions
allow, ask and deny rules by scope


/hooks
configured hooks, grouped by event


/skills
the skills available; press t to sort by token count


/skill-doctor

/doctor
setup checkup: report first, fixes only after you confirm


claude doctor
read-only install and settings diagnostics from the shell


claude --debug
debug logging; logs go to ~/.claude/debug/<session-id>.txt






Four commands cover most first problems:







Command
What it shows




opencode --version
the installed OpenCode version


opencode models
the models OpenCode can use, including your Ollama models


opencode debug paths
where OpenCode keeps its config, data, logs and database


ollama ps
the models Ollama has loaded, their size, and whether they run on the GPU or the CPU



If a model does not appear in opencode models, check that Ollama is running (open the app, or run ollama serve on Linux) and that you pulled the model with ollama pull. ollama ps lists a model only while one is loaded.




Before you ask for help
A bug report includes your OS, the install command and the full error output. Read any output before you paste it into a bug report or chat, because it can contain paths and account details. With Claude Code, /feedback sends feedback from inside a session, and /doctor or claude doctor narrows down a problem. With OpenCode, include the output of opencode --version and opencode debug paths.

title: Pick Your Model
text:
You walk to the Collegium and Sage Maelis leads you into the sages’ auditorium, where Astrals of every size float in slow circles around a strange, glowing artifact that pulses like a heartbeat. A great one speaks well, answers slowly and costs the most to feed, and a small one is quick and cheap and loses the thread. She says you must choose for each job, and decide how hard each should think. Learn to choose, then check that you chose well.
Every session starts with a model and an effort level, and the defaults do not suit every job. A model that is too small skips checks and loses the thread. One that is too large costs more and runs slower, and you may not notice because the answer looks fine. This page covers how to choose both, so you can run later quests without overspending or under-powering them and how to check the choice. Model names, aliases and defaults change often, so check your own tool for the current ones.

title: Pick Your Model
text:
Words to know

Model tier: a size class of model. A smaller one is faster and cheaper; a larger one is more capable and costs more. Anthropic names its tiers Haiku, Sonnet, Opus and Fable, from smallest and fastest (Haiku) to largest and slowest (Fable).
Alias: a short nickname (such as sonnet) that the tool maps to a concrete model version.
Effort: how much the model thinks before each step.
Subagent: a helper the main agent starts with its own fresh context. It does a side task and returns only a summary. To delegate is to hand it a task.
Frontmatter: the small settings block at the top of a Markdown file.
Pin: name one exact model version so it never silently changes.
Inherit: use whatever the parent is using.
Prompt cache: a short-term store that makes re-reading an unchanged conversation cheaper.
Compacting: replacing the conversation history with a short summary.

title: Pick Your Model
text:
1. Two settings

Model: what the model knows and can do.
Effort: how much it thinks per step. Lower effort means fewer and terser tool calls (the actions the agent takes, such as reading a file or running a command); higher effort means more thoroughness.

Changing effort is often cheaper to try than switching models.

title: Pick Your Model
text:
2. How to set them

Claude CodeOpenCode + Ollama



Model. You choose a model by alias, and you pin a full name when results must be reproducible (shown below the table). The main aliases are fable, sonnet, opus and haiku. Run /model in your tool to see the current list. An alias can map to different versions on different providers.









Way
How
Note




In a session
/model <alias or name>
alone, it opens a picker; Enter saves it as your default, s keeps it for this session only


Per launch
claude --model <alias or name>



Environment
ANTHROPIC_MODEL



Settings file
model field




For results that must be reproducible (a lab pipeline, course material), pin a full model name (the exact version string your tool lists), because an alias moves when a new version ships.

Effort. Set it with /effort, claude --effort or the effortLevel setting. The levels run from low through medium and high up to max, and which ones exist depends on the model. The default differs by model and by tool. Run /effort in your own tool to read yours.
Per subagent. A subagent’s model and effort go in its frontmatter. If its model differs from the main one and you give no effort, the session level does not apply to it, so set it.

A subagent is a Markdown file with frontmatter in .claude/agents/ (project) or ~/.claude/agents/ (yours):
---
name: log-reader
description: Reads long pipeline logs and reports only failed tasks with their error lines.
model: haiku
effort: medium
---
Read the logs you are given. Return: task name, exit status, the first error line.
Quote lines exactly. If something is unclear, say so.
The sub-agents page in Lore has the other fields.
This sketch uses medium because a small model at low is more likely to skip a search, stop early or skip a check. For reading logs, catching every failure is the point.



/models picks a model for the current session only; the config file is unchanged.
opencode run --model provider/model-id sets it for one run. The format is provider/model-id, with an optional #variant such as #high. IDs are case-sensitive.
The model key in opencode.json (or opencode.jsonc) sets your default.
An agent can have its own model key. A subagent with no model inherits the parent session’s model.
A local Ollama model is selectable like any other, for example ollama/gemma3:4b.

title: Pick Your Model
text:
3. Starting points
Start from the tiers and the table below, and test each row on your own jobs. The four tiers, in order of capability:

Haiku: fastest replies and lowest cost; suited to subagent tasks.
Sonnet: everyday coding and agent work.
Opus: complex agentic coding; most workloads start here.
Fable: the hardest, long-running work.










Job
Start with
Effort
Why




Most everyday work, no better information
Sonnet or Opus
the tool’s default
both suit everyday work; compare them on one of your own jobs


Bulk reading, classifying or extracting with output you can check
Haiku, often as a subagent
medium, or low if you re-run failures
cheap per item; a checker catches errors


Exploratory reading (“where is X handled?”)
a subagent
low or medium
the main context stays clean; only a summary returns


Planning a change
consider Opus or Fable
medium to high
a bad plan makes every later step wrong


Mechanical edits with tests that fail loudly
Sonnet
medium
the tests do the judging


Hardest multi-file change, or unfamiliar science
Opus or Fable
high, then up only if a check shows a gain
a stronger model may know more

title: Pick Your Model
section: 4. When the output is not good enough: the upgrade ladder
text:
4. When the output is not good enough: the upgrade ladder
Climb one rung at a time and re-check after each.

Add a way to verify. A test, a script, a count against an independent tool, a second look that does not share the first one’s blind spot. Without it you cannot tell whether the next rungs helped.
Raise effort one level.
Change the model to the next tier up.


Cheap-then-retry: if outcomes are checkable (tests, or a verifier, which is a separate check that tests the output), run at low effort and re-run only the failures at higher effort. A checker that passes bad work lets failures through, and a failure costs two runs of waiting time.

Compare cost per finished task, because failed tasks still cost money and a few hard tasks can carry much of the bill.

title: Pick Your Model
text:
5. Delegation hygiene

Keep the expensive model’s context lean. Sending bulk reading to a subagent keeps that reading out of the main conversation.
Spot-check summaries. A subagent returns only a summary, and summaries omit and distort. Ask for exact quotes or file paths and open two yourself. Many subagents returning long answers can also fill the main context again.
State your rules in the delegation prompt. The built-in Explore subagent (a read-only search helper) and Plan subagent (a read-only research helper used in plan mode) skip CLAUDE.md, the instructions file the tool loads at session start. A rule like “never touch raw/” must be written into the task you hand them. Custom subagents load CLAUDE.md unless set to skip it.
Switch models at a quiet moment. Switching model mid-conversation can change prompt-cache behaviour, and the tool may ask you to confirm.
Change effort only between sessions when you compare, so one session never mixes two settings. On some models and providers, changing effort mid-session invalidates the cache. The Model configuration page in Lore says which.

title: Pick Your Model
text:
6. Measure on your own task
Pick one small real task that has an outcome check (a test that passes, a count that matches).

Choose two settings to compare, for example the same model at medium and high. Change only one thing.
For each, start a fresh session, run the task three times, and record pass or fail from the outcome check.
After each run, open /usage (shows what the session cost) and note the “Usage by model” block. The dollar figure is an estimate computed locally at list price, and on a subscription you may see plan usage bars instead. /usage resets on /clear.
Compare cost per passing run. Three runs is a small sample: it can expose a big difference, and a small one needs more runs.

title: Pick Your Model
text:
7. Other model families
The ideas above carry over to other model families, such as Mistral’s, and the model names differ. When you switch families, redo the worksheet below. A tier ladder built on one vendor’s models does not carry over name for name.

title: Pick Your Model
text:
Exercise: assign six jobs
No model needed. For each mock job, write down a model (Haiku, Sonnet, Opus or Fable), an effort (low, medium, high) and whether you would use a subagent, then open the key.

Rename 200 sample IDs in a samplesheet to a new scheme, given a mapping table.
Summarise the methods section of one paper into five bullets for your lab notes.
Debug a Nextflow stage that fails on one sample and passes on the others.
Classify 5,000 free-text tissue labels into 12 categories, with 200 hand-tagged rows to check against.
Plan a refactor of a 600-line QC script that three other people depend on.
Explain an error message you have not seen before.



Answer key (several answers are defensible)


Probably no model at all. A mapping table and a script do this exactly, and a script cannot invent an ID. If you use a model, Haiku at low or medium, with a diff or count check; no subagent needed.
Sonnet, medium, no subagent. The text is short, so there is no context to protect. Check two claims against the paper yourself.
Sonnet at medium, raised to high or Opus if the first attempt fails and a test says so. Keep it in the main conversation, because the debugging needs the history. Add a failing test first (rung 1).
Haiku, a subagent or a batch script, medium. The 200 hand-tagged rows are your outcome check; re-run only the rows that disagree at a higher setting. Spot-check a sample of the rest.
Opus, high, in plan mode, main conversation. A weak plan is expensive downstream and other people depend on the script. Ask for a test plan too.
Sonnet, low or medium, no subagent. It is a short, checkable question: try the suggested fix. Escalate when the explanation does not hold up.



Check what model and effort your tool is using right now (/model, /effort) and write them down.


Run the same small task at two settings and compare the result and /usage.

title: Free Is Not Free
text:
Stalls outside the Collegium gate offer pacts for free. Some are with Astrals bred in the open, some are trials, and one stall will not say where its Astral came from. Sage Maelis stops at each one and reads the label aloud, because a free pact can ask its price in your data. Learn to read the label of a free model offer.
A model you run on your own computer is free because you supply the hardware. Many other “free” offers run on someone else’s machine, so someone is paying. Before you send a prompt to one, you need to know what it costs you, and this lesson gives you the checklist. Sometimes it is the provider, who gains your attention or your data. Sometimes it is you, in limits and in time. Using any of them is optional.
Free tiers change often: providers have ended them, shrunk them or turned them into short trials. Read the provider’s own page before you rely on one, and treat every number on it as a snapshot.

title: Free Is Not Free
text:
1. Four kinds of free








Kind
Who runs it
What you give up




Open weights, run by you (open weights: the numbers the model learned can be downloaded)
Your laptop or cluster
Speed and quality; some memory


Free tier of a provider
The model’s maker or a hosting company
Rate limits (caps on requests per minute or day); sometimes your prompts


Router or gateway (a service that forwards your request to other providers)
A middleman
A second party in the path; a free list that churns


Reseller of unknown origin
Unknown
Everything you send



If a site offers one of the most capable closed models with no card and no limits, ask who pays for it. Send such a site nothing you would not post publicly.

title: Free Is Not Free
section: 2. What to check on any free offer
text:
2. What to check on any free offer

Free tier or trial? A trial ends, and a free tier may too. Several of OpenCode Zen’s free models are free for a limited time.
What are the limits? Look for requests per day and per minute, and what happens past them. On Cloudflare Workers AI, past the daily allowance further operations fail with an error.
Is a card or other detail needed? Some free tiers need a payment method, a phone number or a data opt-in.
Does the free tier train on your prompts? This matters most. A provider that keeps nothing is still not approved for sensitive data; the rule below applies to every free tier.

Google AI Studio: on unpaid services Google uses submitted content to improve its products, and human reviewers may read it. Paid services differ.
Groq: it does not retain inference data (it does not store your prompts and the replies) by default, and may keep logs for a limited period.
OpenRouter: it does not log prompts by default, and retention varies with the provider behind the model.

Who else is in the path? A router adds a party. Read its terms and the terms of the provider it picks. One router can send you to providers with different rules.

The terms can differ per model inside one service. OpenCode Zen lists some free models with zero retention and others that may use your data for training. Read the line for the model you picked.
Sensitive or unpublished data does not go to a hosted free tier. Use a model on your own computer, or an approved service.

title: Free Is Not Free
text:
3. A worked example: Mistral
Providers differ, and one provider’s rules can differ by product and plan. Mistral is one example. For any provider, check three things:

Training: is training on your prompts on by default for your plan, and where is the opt-out?
Retention: how long does the provider keep your prompts (retention)?
Location: where are your prompts processed?

Find the answers on the provider’s data or privacy page. Mistral’s page is in the Lore below. An open-weight model such as ministral-3:8b runs locally through Ollama and keeps prompts on your machine, though tool or web calls may still send data out.
The sensitive-data rule holds for every provider: unpublished or sensitive data stays on your own computer or an approved service.

title: Free Is Not Free
section: 4. Pairing a free model with an agent
text:
4. Pairing a free model with an agent
Free endpoints often speak an OpenAI-compatible protocol (the request format OpenAI’s chat API uses, which many providers copy). OpenCode can connect to an OpenAI-compatible gateway; its Providers page in the Lore below shows how. Free models differ in how well they follow tool instructions, so test one on a small task before you trust it.

title: Free Is Not Free
text:
5. Try one, safely
Pick one free tier from a provider you have read about. Create the key in the provider’s console and keep it out of chat and out of files in your project. Then make one call with a harmless prompt. The shape below is the common OpenAI-compatible one. Set BASE_URL to the API address (base URL) and MODEL_NAME to a model name, both from the provider’s API documentation, for example export BASE_URL="https://api.example.com/v1" (an invented address). A reply with a short greeting inside the JSON means it worked. An error message about the key or the model name means one of those values is wrong.
export FREE_API_KEY="..."          # set it in your shell, not in a file you commit
curl -sS "$BASE_URL/chat/completions" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $FREE_API_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"model": "MODEL_NAME", "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Say hello in one sentence."}]}'
Then fill in one row:












Provider
Kind
Limit per day
Card needed?
Trains on prompts?
Who else sees them?
Date checked





If you cannot fill a cell from the provider’s own page, write “not stated”. That is a finding too.

title: Choose What to Hand Over
text: Sage Maelis gathers you in a hall of the Collegium with a warning: left unchecked, an Astral will pull in everything within reach to finish a task, and spread the Blight across the land in the process. As the four travellers imagine what a pact could unlock for their craft, loud boasters brag of giving their Astral free rein over entire projects, dismissing small, guarded tasks as timid half-measures. Maelis points to a wiser way: think of the work as a deep river, and you need not swim the whole span at once. Limit what the Astral sees, step from stone to stone carrying only what the task demands, and check your footing at each stone before you step to the next. She needs a little time to prepare the pacts, so she asks you to return tomorrow and to visit Warden Hesper at the Adventurers’ Training Grounds until then.

title: Choose What to Hand Over
text:
The scene
Four people want help from an LLM (a large language model, the kind of tool behind chat assistants). Each pictures what it could do, and then the same two worries arrive: where their data would go, and whether using an LLM means giving a program the run of their computer.

Quartermaster ArisDiviner IlsaArtificer BobArchivist Elowen


“I keep twelve projects in one spreadsheet. If an LLM could read it, I would have a status report and a risk list for the board by lunch.”
“But where does my data go once I paste it? And a colleague said I would need Claude Code (a coding agent that can read and change files on my computer), which means giving it access to all my files. I cannot allow that, so I will keep writing the report by hand.”


“The sample counts fell in two cohorts. If an LLM could write the query and the first summary, I would have an explanation before the meeting.”
“But the samples database holds participant codes, and my data agreement is strict. Does using an LLM mean installing an agent that can reach the database? Then the answer has to be no LLM at all.”


“Our pipeline has a script nobody has tested. If an LLM could draft the tests and tidy the module, I would clear this week’s backlog by Friday.”
“But an agent that edits files and runs commands in my repository could overwrite something, or run something I never reviewed. It is all or nothing, and nothing feels safer.”


“A collaborator sent a sample sheet with mixed columns and units. If an LLM could clean it and map it to our schema, a week of tidying would take an afternoon.”
“But the sheet holds controlled health metadata. I cannot paste it anywhere, and I do not want an agent loose in the data store. So it is a no.”



All four treat the choice as all or nothing: either no LLM, or an agent with the run of the machine. They have not considered that there is a middle. Between those two ends are several steps, each handing over a little more, and many useful tasks sit on the lower ones. This lesson walks up those steps.
You decide how much to hand over before the first prompt. A wrong choice can send data you meant to keep, or let an agent change files you meant to leave alone.

title: Choose What to Hand Over
text:
Two questions

What leaves your machine? A hosted model runs on the provider’s servers, so anything you type, paste or upload is sent there, and so is anything an agent reads. A local model runs on your computer and keeps prompts there, though an agent’s web or tool calls can still reach out.
What may the agent do? Produce text, read files, edit files, or run commands.

Question 1 is about data leaving. Question 2 is about changes on your machine. They vary independently:

A chat window with a pasted table: it can only write text, so little can change on your machine, but the whole table is sent.
A local model in an agent with access to your files: nothing is sent to a provider, but it can edit files and run commands.

The more data leaves, the higher the first answer. The more the agent may change, the higher the second.

title: Choose What to Hand Over
text:
The ladder
A ladder is six ordered steps of how much you hand over. Each step up raises one or both answers. Terms used in the table: a schema is the list of table and column names with no rows; an extract is a small slice of the data; an agent is a model that reads files and runs commands for you; a copy is a duplicate of the data, so the original cannot be edited.








Step
What you hand over
What leaves




0
Nothing: do the task yourself
nothing


1
A question in words, with no data in it
your words


2
Structure only: headings, a schema or invented rows. You apply the answer yourself
names and invented rows


3
A small extract you are allowed to share, or a local model
the extract; nothing if local


4
A read-only agent (plan mode: it reads and proposes, and does not edit) working on a copy
everything it reads


5
An agent that edits files and runs commands
everything it reads, plus whatever its commands send



Pasting the results of a step 2 task back into the chat sends those rows too, which makes it step 3. Plan mode (the agent reads and proposes, and does not edit) belongs to step 4: a copy protects the original from edits, and anything the agent reads is still sent.

title: Choose What to Hand Over
text:
Three questions before any step

What kind of data is it? The table gives a typical starting point. Your agreement and your data steward decide, and they can be stricter. A data steward is the person at your organisation who looks after data rules.
Which account will you use? Consumer and organisation accounts have different terms (next section).
What leaves at this step? Say it in one sentence before you press enter.








Kind of data
Typical starting point




Public or published
Any step


Internal, not personal
Steps 1 to 3; 4 to 5 on an approved account, on a copy


Personal, including pseudonymised codes (codes that replace names)
Steps 0 to 2, invented rows only


Health, genetic or otherwise controlled
Steps 0 to 2, unless your agreement says otherwise in writing



Under GDPR (the EU data-protection law), pseudonymised codes still count as personal data. Small counts can single people out, so check your policy before pasting results for rare groups.

title: Choose What to Hand Over
text:
What a chat window keeps

Training: consumer accounts (Free, Pro, Max) have a setting that lets chats improve the models; with it on, data may be kept for up to 5 years. The setting is in your privacy settings.
Account type: commercial accounts (Team, Enterprise and the API, which is programmatic access billed per use) are not used for training unless the organisation opts in. The API deletes inputs and outputs within 30 days by default. Team and Enterprise keep saved chats until they are deleted, then remove them within 30 days. Ask your administrator which applies.
Deleted chats: they leave the provider’s storage within 30 days.
Incognito chats: not used for training, and still kept for 30 days by default. Flagged chats can be kept longer.
Screenshots, images and uploads: treat them as data you share, like pasted text.
Other providers: their chat tools have their own terms. Read them.

title: Choose What to Hand Over
text:
Hands-on: pick the step
For each task, decide three things before you open the answer: the lowest step that does the job, what leaves your machine at that step, and one thing you will check in the result. The tabs hold the same four people, and the tab you chose earlier stays selected.

Quartermaster ArisDiviner IlsaArtificer BobArchivist Elowen


Task: a one-page status summary and risk list for twelve projects, from a spreadsheet of project names, milestone dates, owner names and status. The data is internal, and owner names are personal data.


Check your answer

The answer is step 2. Paste only the column headings and three invented rows. Ask for an outline of the summary and a formula that counts open milestones per project. Apply both to the real sheet yourself. Only the headings and the invented rows leave. Step 3 would send real rows with owner names, which needs an approved account and your steward’s agreement.
To check: count the open milestones of one project by hand and compare.



Task: explain why the sample count per project fell between two cohorts, from a samples database that holds participant codes under a strict agreement. Pseudonymised codes still count as personal data.


Check your answer

The answer is step 2. Share the schema only and ask for one read-only query. Run it yourself. The table and column names leave, so decide first whether even the names are fine to send, and drop to step 0 if your agreement says they are not. Pasting the results back into the chat would make it step 3.
To check: write a second, simpler count query yourself and compare the two numbers before you explain anything.



Task: write tests for a script that reads sample sheets in your pipeline repository. The code is internal and holds no personal data.


Check your answer

The answer is step 3. Paste the one function (a small allowed extract) and ask for tests. Apply them yourself. Only that function’s code leaves. If you later want an agent to run the tests inside the repository, that is step 5: work on a copy, keep a way to undo, and limit what the agent may do first.
To check: break the function on purpose and confirm that a test fails.



Task: clean and map a sample sheet with controlled health metadata to your schema, under an agreement that forbids sharing the values.


Check your answer

The answer is step 2 at most. Describe the mess in words, give headings and invented rows that copy it, and ask for a validation and mapping script. Run the script locally on the real sheet. Do not ask a model to fill or harmonise the values itself: it can invent plausible ones. Only the headings and the invented rows leave.
To check: compare row counts and a checksum before and after, and keep a log of every change.




Now take your own task. Write the three answers in a sentence each, then ask your data steward the question at the end of the next section if any of them is unclear.

title: Choose What to Hand Over
section: Climbing, if and when you want to
text:
Climbing, if and when you want to

Move up a step when the lower step cannot do the task and you can say what leaves.
Before steps 4 and 5, work on a copy, keep a way to undo, and limit what the agent may do.
For personal or controlled data, a local model (step 3) is allowed only where your agreement says so.
If you pasted something you should not have, stop and tell your data steward.
Ask your steward: “I want to use [tool, account type] at step [n]. What leaves is [what]. Is that allowed for [data kind]?”

text:
The Quern Mill

Token counting: Anthropic, docs. Why read: it documents the free count endpoint and says models from Claude 4.7 onward use a newer tokenizer, so the same text gives roughly 30 percent more tokens than on earlier models (the exact increase depends on the content). Cited in: Tokens, Not Letters.
The Strawberry Problem: Cosma et al., EMNLP 2025, paper. Cited by 2 quests; each quest says what to read it for.
Cited in:

Tokens, Not Letters: it argues character-level information is weakly available inside tokens, a leading explanation for miscounted letters.
Ground Truth: it studies why models miscount letters and links it to tokens, which is the idea behind miscounted bases.

Counting Ability of LLMs and Impact of Tokenization: Zhang et al., arXiv, paper. Cited by 2 quests; each quest says what to read it for.
Cited in:

Tokens, Not Letters: it studies how tokenisation affects counting; its abstract says step-by-step reasoning (chain of thought) can help, and its full text still reports failures with it in modern models. A preprint.
Ground Truth: it shows how tokenisation changes counting accuracy in language models, which is why a script, not a model’s reading, should do exact counts (that last step is our general practice, not the paper’s claim). A preprint.

CharBench: Evaluating the Role of Tokenization in Character-Level Tasks: arXiv, paper. Why read: a counter-view finding tokenisation only weakly tied to errors, so treat the tokens explanation as likely but disputed. A preprint. Cited in: Tokens, Not Letters.
Lost in the Middle: Liu et al., arXiv, paper. Cited by 3 quests; each quest says what to read it for.
Cited in:

Where Machines Fail: it shows recall is best for text at the start or end of a long input and weaker in the middle. A preprint.
RAG and Its Cousins: it shows why a long, stuffed prompt can hide the passage that matters.
Boss: Review Large Output: it measures how accuracy drops when the relevant fact sits in the middle of a long input.

On Faithfulness and Factuality in Abstractive Summarization: Maynez et al., ACL 2020, paper. Cited by 2 quests; each quest says what to read it for.
Cited in:

Where Machines Fail: it found hallucinated content in neural summaries; older models, but it shows why summaries need a spot check.
Spot Hallucinations: it found invented content in every neural summary tested; the models are pre-chat-era, so read it for the direction, not current rates.

LLM The Genius Paradox: A Linguistic and Math Expert’s Struggle with Simple Word-based Counting Problems: arXiv, paper. Why read: its abstract says specialised math and coding models still struggle with simple counting and that reasoning before answering is the most reliable fix; its full text adds that explicitly asking coding models for Python code worked. A preprint, not peer-reviewed as far as we checked. Cited in: Where Machines Fail.
Improving Fable 5’s biology safeguards: Anthropic, article. Why read: it says biology requests can be re-routed to a less capable model, that false positives remain, and that dual-use topics such as virology still fall back. Cited in: Where Machines Fail.
Cyber Verification Program: Anthropic, docs. Why read: it explains when security work is blocked and how verified professionals apply for fewer interruptions. Cited in: Where Machines Fail.

Spend Fewer Tokens: a walk through what loads before you type and what survives compaction.
Write the Brief: an interactive timeline of what fills the window and what survives compaction.
Boss: Review Large Output: it shows what fills a Claude Code session and what survives compaction.

Cited in:

The Context Window: it explains why long contexts degrade and why curating what goes in matters; compaction trade-offs are discussed.
Spend Fewer Tokens: it explains why a smaller, curated context gives better answers as well as lower cost.
Carry Context Between Sessions: it explains why long contexts degrade and describes structured note-taking outside the window.

Boss: Review Large Output: it explains why more text in context is not free and why stale material hurts.

The Context Window: it says CLAUDE.md and auto memory are context, which is why they take up room in the window.

Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks: Lewis and colleagues, arXiv, paper. Why read: it is the 2020 paper that named RAG, so you can see how much the common recipe has been simplified since. Cited in: RAG and Its Cousins.
Introducing Contextual Retrieval: Anthropic, article. Why read: it walks through the improved-RAG add-ons and states the 200,000-token rule of thumb for skipping RAG. Cited in: RAG and Its Cousins.

RAG vs. GraphRAG: A Systematic Evaluation and Key Insights: Han and colleagues, paper. Why read: it is an independent comparison with costs and a warning about order effects in LLM judges. Cited in: RAG and Its Cousins.
Retrieval Augmented Generation or Long-Context LLMs?: Li and colleagues (Google), paper. Why read: it compares RAG with putting everything in the prompt and proposes a hybrid. Cited in: RAG and Its Cousins.
Embeddings: Ollama, docs. Why read: it documents the /api/embed call the scripts use and says to embed documents and questions with the same model. Cited in: Build a Knowledge Graph with Ollama.
Structured outputs: Ollama, docs. Why read: it explains the format field with a JSON schema that makes fact extraction return usable JSON. Cited in: Build a Knowledge Graph with Ollama.
Context length: Ollama, docs. Why read: it gives the default context by memory size and how to check what loaded with ollama ps. Cited in: Build a Knowledge Graph with Ollama.
LightRAG: HKUDS, repo. Why read: the README and docs give the install, the Ollama wiring, the context and model-size requirements, the storage defaults and a server-safety warning (lightrag-server binds to all network interfaces with authentication off by default; set HOST=127.0.0.1). Cited in: Build a Knowledge Graph with Ollama.

Language model selection: Microsoft, docs. Why read: it is where the docs describe the JSON requirement and the problems seen with Ollama. Cited in: Build a Knowledge Graph with Ollama.
When to use Graphs in RAG: Xiang and colleagues, paper. Why read: it studies which kinds of questions benefit from graphs, with token costs per method. Cited in: Build a Knowledge Graph with Ollama.
Advanced RAG Techniques: Nir Diamant and contributors, repo. Why read: its notebook list includes graph RAG with a local Ollama model and LightRAG, plus chunking and evaluation, though we did not open the notebooks and the repo carries sponsor and book promotions. Cited in: Build a Knowledge Graph with Ollama.

title: Read First
text:
A map hangs on the wall at Basecamp, and the old travellers say the road is easier for those who have read it once. You do not need to memorise it. Read for the shape of the country, then set out.
This page lists background reading for the course. Reading is optional, and about an hour covers all of it. The pages describe Claude Code. If you chose OpenCode, the ideas carry over, and OpenCode’s own docs are at opencode.ai/docs. It is separate from Prerequisites, which lists what to install. The three pages in the first list cover the ideas that Set Up Your Agent and the lessons after it build on.

title: Claude in the Cloud
text: You walk to the Collegium and climb its tower, where the Claude Astral can work on a borrowed machine that vanishes when the job is done. Sage Maelis climbs with you. She says it is a fine place to sketch and write, and that the boasters make it sound fit for any task. Asked plainly, she lowers her voice: nothing precious should be carried to the tower. title: Claude in the Cloud
text:
The rule for this page
You may be offered a way to run an agent on someone else’s computer. You need this lesson before you start one, because what you send is stored away from your machine. Decide what may go there first.






NoteCloud sessions are for drafting scripts and documentation. Data analysis stays on your machine or the cluster.



Use a cloud session for writing scripts, updating documentation and similar low-risk text work. Real data, controlled data, sample sheets with identifiers, genotypes and results stay out of a cloud session and its repository. Analysis runs on your own machine or the cluster, under your data agreement.
Think of the cloud agent as a drafting helper that returns a branch (a named line of commits in git) which you review and then run yourself, where the data lives.


Cloud sessions are optional. If you use one, the rest of the page shows how to keep sensitive material at home.

title: Claude in the Cloud
Claude in the Cloud
text:
2. What leaves your machine
Read this part twice. When you start a cloud session:

Your repository contents are cloned onto Anthropic’s VM. Anthropic reads only the repository you start the session in.
Your prompts and everything the agent reads and writes go to the model.
The session transcript (the saved record of the whole conversation, including tool output) is stored by Anthropic so you can return to it later.
Retention (how long Anthropic keeps stored data) depends on your account type. Check your plan’s current terms on the Data usage page in Lore. Deleting a cloud session permanently removes its event data.
Network level None may still let data exit. A network access level is the setting that says which internet hosts the VM may reach (None, Limited or Full; see section 5). The Anthropic API stays reachable even at None, which may allow data to exit the VM.
Environment variables (named settings handed to programs, often used for keys) set in a cloud environment can be read by any command Claude runs, and anyone who uses that environment can read the values.

Some organisation settings block cloud sessions outright, and your administrator can switch them off. Ask whether yours are available.
Keep controlled data out of the cloud repository. Treat the clone, the transcript and anything you paste as held by Anthropic. Read your data agreement before you push anything to a remote that a cloud session can see (a remote is the copy of a repository hosted elsewhere, such as on GitHub).

title: Claude in the Cloud
text:
3. Good uses and bad uses







Fine for a cloud session (code and mock data only)
Keep for your machine or the cluster




Write a samplesheet validator, tested on a three-row mock file
Run the analysis


Write a QC summary plotting script, developed on mock data
Load real counts, genotypes or results


Draft or update the README, changelog, docstrings
Debug with real sample IDs in the repository


Refactor non-data code that has tests
Anything under a data agreement


Review a pull request that holds no identifiers
Anything that needs a local database or the cluster


Triage issues that hold no identifiers
Anything that needs your institution’s network or files



A cloud machine has no GPU and no access to your institution’s network. Work that needs a GPU, a VPN (a private network link into your institution) or local databases stays on your side.

title: Claude in the Cloud
text:
4. How to start

Claude CodeOpenCode + Ollama



Push first. claude --cloud "your task" starts a cloud session from your terminal. It clones the GitHub remote at your current branch, and your local folder is not used. Commit and push (save snapshots, then upload them to the remote) before you start, so the session sees your latest work. If the branch is not on GitHub, the session starts from a pushed commit or the default branch. One repository per session. You can also start from claude.ai/code in the browser.
Write a ticket-style prompt. That is a self-contained note like a work ticket: the problem, the expected result, and a command that proves it (in the example, pytest, a Python test runner). Be specific, name files and paste errors. Example, with no data in it:

Problem: scripts/validate_samplesheet.py accepts duplicate sample IDs.
Expected: exit status 1 and a message naming the duplicated ID.
Check: pytest tests/test_validate_samplesheet.py (mock rows only).
Add a test for the duplicate case. Only change files under scripts/ and tests/.
A repository with no real data anywhere in it is the safe one. Removing the data/ and results/ folders is not enough if real files sit elsewhere. A prompt line such as “do not read data/” is a request to the model and gives no protection. If the folder is in the repository, the cloud session can read it.

If there is no remote. When the repository has no git remote, or a GitHub repository does not have the Claude GitHub App (an app you install on a repository to let Claude clone it) installed, Claude Code bundles it and uploads the full history of all branches plus uncommitted changes to tracked files. Keep data out of this route entirely. Your history may already hold a file you deleted, and the bundle takes all of it. Check what is tracked and what your .gitignore covers first.
Getting the session back. claude --teleport pulls a cloud session into your local terminal. It needs a clean git state, the same repository, the branch pushed and the same claude.ai account.
GitHub access. Cloud sessions reach your repositories through the Claude GitHub App or a token that /web-setup (a command you run in the terminal) sends to Anthropic; it sends your local gh (GitHub command-line tool) token. The proxy that holds your credential does not limit which branches a push can update. Use GitHub branch protection or rulesets (rules on which branches may be changed and by whom) for that.



To run an agent away from your laptop with OpenCode, run it yourself in your own container or virtual machine. That is your own infrastructure and your own responsibility.
A local Ollama model keeps prompts on your machine, though web or tool calls the agent makes may leave it, so check your data agreement before you rely on it.

title: Claude in the Cloud
text:
5. Environments
An environment is a saved configuration for cloud sessions: network access, environment variables, a setup script and network secrets.
Network access levels:







Level
What the VM can reach




None
No internet (the Anthropic API, the GitHub proxy and enabled connectors still work)


Limited
A default allowlist (a list of the only hosts permitted) of package registries, GitHub and cloud SDKs, plus domains you add


Full
Any host



Pick the narrowest level that lets the task finish.

Setup scripts: a setup script is a Bash script that runs once before Claude starts, to install what the task needs. Installs need network access, so None blocks them.
Environment variables versus network secrets: environment variables are readable by any command Claude runs. Network secrets are the safer option where possible: the key stays outside the VM, and a proxy adds it to requests to hosts you list.
Preinstalled tools: common programming tools are present. No R, conda or bioinformatics tools are listed, so ask Claude to list the tools installed on the cloud machine before you rely on one.

title: Claude in the Cloud
text:
6. Permission modes in the cloud
A permission mode says how much the agent may do before asking you. Cloud sessions offer Accept edits, Plan and Auto. There is no Manual or Bypass mode there. You pick the mode in the dropdown.
Use Plan for anything you do not already understand, and read the plan before it edits. You can also plan locally with claude --permission-mode plan, commit and push the plan, and then start claude --cloud.

title: Claude in the Cloud
text:
7. Limits and failure modes

A fresh machine every time. An idle session stops and its VM is taken back. Commit and push work you want to keep.
Size. A cloud machine has limited CPU, memory and disk. Heavy jobs may be stopped.
Shared usage. Cloud work counts against the same plan limits as all your other Claude Code use.
GitHub comments under your name. Claude can reply on pull requests under your GitHub name, marked as from Claude Code.

title: Claude in the Cloud
text:
8. Review what comes back
The result is a branch. Treat it like a stranger’s pull request: it may be fine and it may be wrong.

Read the diff (the list of changed lines) as you would any other.
Look for accidents in the diff: committed data files, absolute paths, sample IDs in a test or a comment, a .env, a notebook saved with outputs (a notebook is a Jupyter document mixing code and results; its saved outputs are the tables and plots stored inside the file).
Run the tests locally, on your machine.
Only then run the script on your data, locally or on the cluster, under your data agreement. The cloud agent never saw that data and never ran that step.

A green test in the cloud is a claim to verify. A test passing on mock data tells you the script runs; your real data is the next check, run locally.

title: Claude in the Cloud
text:
Exercise: the safe-to-send checklist
No cloud account, GitHub account or model needed, and no repository to clone. The tree is a text file in this course’s exercises folder. Open tree.txt, a mock repository tree (every name is invented).

Mark each path that must not reach anything a cloud session can see. Say whether it needs removing from history (it is already committed) or only ignoring, and write one reason each.
Write the .gitignore lines that would have stopped it.
Draft a ticket-style prompt for one low-risk task: update docs/usage.md, or add a missing-column test to scripts/validate_samplesheet.py. Include the problem, the expected result and a check that uses only data/mock/.



Answer key (some entries depend on your data agreement)


Every path under “Paths to remove” is committed, so remove each one from history before you push anything a cloud session can see. The ignore lines further down only prevent a repeat.

Paths to remove:

.env: a secret. It was already committed, so remove it from history and replace the token; ignoring it helps only from now on.
samplesheet_real.csv: identifiers and genotype calls.
data/raw/ and data/processed/: real reads and real counts.
notebooks/01_qc.ipynb and notebooks/02_diffexp.ipynb: outputs saved inside them contain real sample IDs, tables and plots. Clear the outputs, or keep the notebooks out.
results/ (including de_genes.csv and pca_real_samples.png): results.
logs/slurm-482913.out: real sample IDs and cluster paths.
notebooks/.ipynb_checkpoints/: autosave copies of the notebooks, with the same saved outputs.
Fine to send (they hold no real data): README.md, environment.yml, samplesheet_template.csv, config/params.yaml (check it for real paths), data/mock/, docs/, scripts/, tests/.

Ignore lines that would help:
.env
.env.*
samplesheet_real.csv
*.fastq.gz
data/raw/
data/processed/
results/
logs/
.ipynb_checkpoints/
Add a rule for notebooks too (for example, a pre-commit hook, a script git runs automatically before each commit, that clears outputs), because .gitignore alone cannot strip outputs from a notebook you do want to commit. Likewise, .gitignore only stops files that are not yet tracked; anything already committed stays in history until you remove it properly, and rewriting history is its own careful job.
Sample prompt:
Problem: docs/usage.md does not mention the --strandedness option added in v0.3.
Expected: a short section with the option, its allowed values, and one example
command using data/mock/ only.
Check: the example command in the new section runs on data/mock/counts_mock.tsv. Only edit docs/usage.md.
A prompt line is a request to the model. The safe version of this repository has no real data folders to read.

title: Know Your Tools
text:
In the sages’ college, Sage Maelis lays the Summoning Scroll open across her desk. She names each piece of the pact in turn: the Astral you will summon, the binding circle that holds it, and a pile of fittings nobody has labelled. She has heard the boasters swear a good pact needs nothing more than a name. Start with the Astral alone, then watch the circle go down around it.
People mix these words up, and the mix-ups cause real mistakes, such as blaming “the model” for something a setting did. The pictures below start with one part and add one more each time.

title: Know Your Tools
text:
1. The model



A model with an effort setting

One box named model, which reads text and writes text. A dashed box inside it, named effort, shows how much it thinks per step.   MODEL reads text, writes text  EFFORT: how much it thinks per step 


The model reads text and writes text. Effort is a setting on it.



Model. The large language model (LLM) that reads and writes text (for example a Claude model, a Mistral model, or a local model through Ollama, a program that runs models on your own computer). Aliases such as sonnet move to newer versions over time, so use the full model name when a result must be reproducible.
Effort. A setting for how much the model reasons before it answers, from low to max in Claude Code (/effort, --effort; a /command is typed inside the running tool, a --flag when you start it). Low is faster and cheaper; high thinks longer and checks more. It steers how much the model reasons per step. max can show diminishing returns and overthink, so raise it only where you measure a gain.

title: Know Your Tools
text:
2. The harness



A model inside a harness

A large box named harness contains the model with its effort setting, and three boxes: tools, permissions, and the loop with context.   HARNESS  MODEL reads text, writes text  EFFORT: how much it thinks per step Tools: read, edit, run Permissions Loop, context 


The harness surrounds the model. It supplies tools, applies permissions and runs the loop.



Harness. The program around the model. The product you type into is the harness. It provides the tools, manages the context the model sees, runs the loop (gather context, act, check, repeat) and enforces permissions. Claude Code, OpenCode (an open-source harness) and Mistral Vibe (Mistral’s open-source terminal coding agent) are harnesses.
Tool. An action the model can request and the harness runs, such as reading a file or running a shell command. A tool call is one such request; tool output is what comes back.
Permissions. The harness’s rules for which tool calls it runs, asks about or refuses.
Agent. A model inside a harness that picks and runs tools in a loop toward a goal.

title: Know Your Tools
text:
3. Extensions



Extensions plugged into the harness

The harness from the previous picture, with a row of extensions: skill, MCP, hook, and an instructions file. A line under skill, MCP and hook marks a plugin as a bundle of them.   HARNESS  MODEL reads text, writes text  EFFORT: how much it thinks per step Tools: read, edit, run Permissions Loop, context EXTENSIONS you plug in SKILL MCP HOOK INSTRUCTIONS FILE  PLUGIN: a bundle of skills, hooks, MCP 


Extensions change what the harness offers. A plugin installs several as one unit.



Instructions file. A text file (CLAUDE.md in Claude Code, AGENTS.md in OpenCode where read) that the harness loads at session start. It advises and does not enforce.
Skill. A folder with a SKILL.md. Only its short description is preloaded; the body loads when it is used. It advises.
MCP (Model Context Protocol). An open standard for connecting the harness to outside tools and data, such as a database or a literature search. A server you connect can act on your behalf, so treat it like software you install.
Hook. Your own command, request or prompt that the harness runs automatically at a set point, such as before a tool call. A command hook that exits with code 2 before a tool runs stops that action whatever the model wants (an exit code is the number a script returns; 0 means success, and a hook uses 2 to mean block). A rule in an instructions file can only ask, so hooks are the stronger guard.
Plugin. A folder that bundles skills, hooks, MCP servers and more, installed as one unit. It can run code, so install only plugins you trust.

title: Know Your Tools
text:
4. Evals



An eval measuring from outside

The harness with its extensions, and below it, outside the harness, a box named eval that runs with and without an extension and compares the results.   HARNESS  MODEL reads text, writes text  EFFORT: how much it thinks per step Tools: read, edit, run Permissions Loop, context EXTENSIONS you plug in SKILL MCP HOOK INSTRUCTIONS FILE  PLUGIN: a bundle of skills, hooks, MCP  EVAL: run with and without, compare 


An eval sits outside the harness and compares runs.



Eval. A repeatable test of agent behaviour: a prompt plus checks on the result. Comparing runs with and without something (a skill, a rule) shows what it contributed. A score of 100% both ways means the test cannot tell the difference, so make it harder.

title: Know Your Tools
text:
5. One model, different harnesses



The same model in two harnesses

Two harness boxes side by side, each holding the same model X, each with its own tools, permission rules and loop.   HARNESS A Model X its own tools, rules, loop  HARNESS B Model X its own tools, rules, loop 


Claude Code and OpenCode are two harnesses.


The same model can behave differently in each harness, because tools, permission rules and the loop differ. Naming differs between tools too. Check another tool’s docs for how its hooks, plugins and effort settings work.

title: Know Your Tools
text:
Other words you will meet
These are not in the pictures.

Prompt. The text you send to the model.
Turn. One prompt from you plus the model’s reply.
Subagent. A helper agent with its own context window; only its summary comes back.
Sandbox. An operating-system layer that limits what commands can touch.
Hallucination. A plausible-looking statement that is false, such as an invented DOI (a paper’s permanent identifier).
Prompt injection. Text from a file, web page or tool that the model treats as an instruction.


Words about what the model can see
These get mixed up more than any others.

Token. The chunk of text a model actually reads and writes. Somewhere between a letter and a word. Limits and costs are counted in tokens.
Context window. Everything the model can see at once right now: instructions, files it has read, tool output and the conversation so far. It has a size limit, and a fuller window is not automatically a better one.
Session (session context). One running conversation, and the context window it has built up. A new session starts with an empty conversation. Two sessions do not share their context.
Memory. Notes that the harness loads at the start of every session, such as your instructions file and, in Claude Code, notes the harness writes itself. Memory outlives a session; session context does not.
Compaction. The harness replaces old conversation with a summary to free room.
Session usage. How much of your allowance or bill a session spends. It climbs with the size of the context, because the whole conversation is sent again with each request.
Context poisoning. A community term: a wrong statement gets into the context, and later answers build on it. Start a fresh session and keep unverified claims out of memory files.


Redraw the picture from memory for the tool you actually use: which model, which harness, which extensions are loaded right now?

title: Script, Model, or LLM
text:
You arrive at the Collegium from Gaia’s Rest, where three colleges ring with work from dawn. Tinker Pell shows you an Automaton that never strays and never improvises, Beastmaster Wyn a Familiar that is sure on its one trail, and Sage Maelis an Astral that can speak every tongue and still invent what it does not know. The three academics respect one another, because each knows what the Shokanju they summon are good at and where they fail. Learn what each is for, and later how to make a pact with an Astral of your own.





From left to right: an Automaton, a Familiar and an Astral.
Before you pick a tool for a job, you need to know what kinds exist. Tools differ in how predictable they are and in how you check them.

title: Script, Model, or LLM
text:
Three kinds

A deterministic program (a script, awk, samtools): the same input always gives the same output, and you can read why. Use it whenever the rule is known.
A trained model (a classifier, a gene-finder, a structure predictor): learned from data to do one task, with measured accuracy on that task. It is the predictive side of AI: it forecasts from past data and gives you an estimate to act on. Use it when the rule is unknown but the task is narrow and validated.
A large language model (LLM): trained on large amounts of text, then tuned to follow instructions. ChatGPT and Claude are LLMs. It is the generative side of AI: it produces new content (text, code, images) that you review, flexible and fluent, with no built-in guarantee of correctness. Use it where the task is open-ended and you can check the result, such as drafting, explaining, or writing a first version of code that you then test.

The line between the last two is not clean. An LLM can be asked to classify, and some generative models predict structure or sequences. Judge a tool by the task you give it and how you will check the result. For a forecast, a predictive model usually costs less than a generative one.
Two common mistakes: using an LLM for something a one-line script does exactly (slow, costly, and sometimes wrong), and trusting a model outside the task it was validated for.
An LLM can also be called inside a script (for example to tidy free-text labels). That makes your pipeline non-deterministic (the same input may give different output), so the result needs its own checks and the exact model and version recorded.
Before you reach for an agent or a large model, ask whether a script, a fixed workflow or a smaller specialised model does the job. A method that fits the task is often cheaper to run and easier to reproduce. A hosted model (one that runs on a provider’s servers) can change when the provider updates it. Keep the large model for the open-ended steps. Fine-tuning (further training a model on your own examples) suits only some tasks.

title: Script, Model, or LLM
section: What a model can do on its own
text:
What a model can do on its own
A language model with no tools suits some jobs and struggles with others. A large hosted model will do better than a small one on some rows.







Suits
Struggles with




Summarising and editing text
Counting letters or basic arithmetic


Pulling out names and places
Multi-step logical reasoning


Classifying a piece of text
Facts it was never given


Generating tags, short creative writing
Writing code (for a small model that runs on your own device)



Harder tasks become possible once the model can call tools or produce structured output. That is the idea behind an agent: the model reads and writes, and the program around it (called the harness) gives it tools, such as a shell, a file editor and a script runner, for the parts it finds hard. Counting and arithmetic are good work to hand to a script.

title: Boss: Review Large Output
text:
Too much output to review
An agent can produce thousands of lines of diff (the list of lines a change added and removed) faster than anyone can review them. If you merge them unread, unchecked errors enter your work. If you try to read all of them, your attention thins and you approve things you did not understand. Both routes fail.
Instead, accept only what you can check:

Keep a review budget: ask for no more than you can honestly review today. Bulk low-quality output is called slop.
Ask for smaller pieces, and ask for a plan before any code, so you can redirect it while that costs little.
Ground each piece in a check.
Pass on only work you have read yourself and can explain in your own words.
Check what happened to the tests. An agent can make “all tests pass” true by weakening or deleting failing tests.

A human check can fail in two ways. Automation bias is trusting the machine’s output too readily. Rubber-stamping is approving without reading. An “approve each item” step at hundreds of items an hour turns into clicking through. A check that works:

shows what changed, at a volume a person can read;
offers approve, edit, veto and stop;
keeps a real decision point wherever results or other people are affected;
records the human step as part of the work’s provenance (the record of where a result came from).

title: Keep a Paper Trail
text:
A plank gives way behind your Astral on the boardwalk. Its account of what it did is plausible, and the marsh has shifted shape anyway. Cartographer Vesna notes every turn as the party walks, and those notes are what let you find the way again. Have the Astral draft its own record, then walk it yourself to see whether it holds.
“I do not understand what it did” is a fair worry. A paper trail answers it: short documents that say what changed, why and how to run it. The habit is to let the agent draft them, check each one against ground truth and own the why.

title: Keep a Paper Trail
text:
The routine
Every document in this lesson follows the same four steps:

Ask. Request the draft, and say what it must cover.
Check against ground truth. Compare the draft with the real thing: the diff, a run on a clean copy, the code, the logs. Look for what the draft omits and for claims the real thing lacks.
Explain back. Say in your own words, one sentence per point, what the document records. A point you cannot put into a sentence is a point to question or leave out.
Keep, edit or revert. Decide after steps 2 and 3.
