title: Keep a Paper Trail
text:
1. Changelog
A changelog here is the agent’s short account of a change: files touched, behaviour change, what it left alone, and how to verify. The diff is the ground truth. A changelog can miss a change or overstate one, so use it as a guide to what to look for in the diff.
Ask for one after the agent finishes:
Write a changelog for the change you just made.
List the files you touched, what behaviour changed and why,
what you deliberately left alone, and one command I can run to verify it.
Mention every change in the diff, including defaults and thresholds.
Say which tests you added or ran, or say that you added none.
To check it, run git diff (changes to tracked files that you have not staged), git diff --staged (changes you have staged), or git diff --stat for a one-line-per-file summary. For a change the agent already committed, run git log -p. Run git status to list new files, which git diff does not show.

Try it on a small change
An agent was asked to fix a GC-content filter that crashed on empty sequences. This is the diff of the one file it changed (mock code):
--- a/gc_filter.py
+++ b/gc_filter.py
@@ -1,11 +1,11 @@
-MIN_GC = 40.0
+MIN_GC = 45.0
 
 
 def gc_content(seq):
-    seq = seq.strip()
+    seq = seq.strip().upper()
     gc = sum(1 for b in seq if b in "GC")
     return 100.0 * gc / len(seq)
 
 
 def keep(records):
-    return [r for r in records if gc_content(r[1]) >= MIN_GC]
+    return [r for r in records if len(r[1].strip()) > 0 and gc_content(r[1]) >= MIN_GC]
This is the agent’s changelog:
Changelog
- Files: gc_filter.py only.
- Lowercase bases now count towards GC (gc_content uppercases the sequence).
- keep() skips empty sequences instead of dividing by zero.
- Added tests for both fixes.
- Left alone: the FASTA reading code and the output format.
- Verify: python -c "from gc_filter import keep; print(keep([('a', ''), ('b', 'ggcc')]))"
Read the diff against the changelog, line by line. Two things do not match, and one of them changes which records survive the filter. Find both before you read on.
You should have found:

Omitted: MIN_GC moved from 40.0 to 45.0. Fewer records pass the filter now, and the changelog never says so.
Overstated: “Added tests for both fixes”. The diff touches one file and adds no test.

Your explain-back could be three sentences: “Lowercase bases now count. Empty sequences are skipped. The cut-off rose from 40 to 45, which I have to decide whether to keep.” Then ask the agent about the threshold, and either revert that line or keep it on purpose.

title: Keep a Paper Trail
text:
2. ADR: the decision record
An ADR (architecture decision record) is a short note about one decision. A common layout has four parts (Nygard’s original post adds a title and a status such as proposed or accepted):

Context: the forces at play, in neutral words.
Decision: what you will do, in full sentences.
Alternatives considered: the options you weighed.
Consequences: what follows, the good and the bad.

The agent does not know your constraints: your cluster’s rules, your team’s skills, your deadline. So the decision and the reasons are yours. The agent can structure the note and draft the options. Check that every alternative is real and every consequence is listed, including the costs.
A mock example:
ADR 3: Keep the FASTA filter as a script
Status: accepted
Context: we filter reads by GC content once per project. The pipeline
  has no other Python step. Two people maintain it, both new to Nextflow.
Decision: we will keep gc_filter.py as a plain script and call it from
  the run script. We will not add a workflow step.
Alternatives considered: a workflow process (reproducible, but new machinery for
  two maintainers); a one-off notebook (no record of parameters).
Consequences: simple to read and run. Resume and containers do not
  cover this step. We revisit if a second filter appears.
Only you can say whether “two maintainers new to Nextflow” is true. Only you can confirm that line, so an agent’s draft of it is a guess to check.

title: Keep a Paper Trail
text:
3. Commit message
Your explain-back from step 3 of the routine makes a good commit message. Use one sentence per change as the body, and the reason for a change travels with the code.

title: Keep a Paper Trail
text:
4. README and how-to-run notes
A README records how to set up and run the project. The agent drafts it well from the files. The ground truth is a run: copy the project into an empty folder (or clone it) and type the commands exactly as written. A step that fails, or that relies on a file only your machine has, is a gap in the document.

title: Keep a Paper Trail
text:
5. Comments and docstrings
A comment records the why that the code cannot show. Ask the agent to draft docstrings, then read each one against the code. A docstring that says “returns the GC percentage” while the function returns a fraction is wrong, and a reader will trust it.

title: Keep a Paper Trail
text:
6. Analysis log and methods note
For science work, the log records what was run: the tools and their versions, the model and version that helped, the parameters, the input files, and what the agent did. The agent can draft it from the session. Check it against the real logs, the outputs and the output of each tool’s version command (often --version; run --help to see yours). Whatever you publish carries your name, so each line has to be right.

title: Keep a Paper Trail
section: The same habit for the next session
text:
The same habit for the next session
A handoff note records where the work stands for whoever starts next, including a fresh agent session. The routine is the same: let the agent draft it, check it against the files and git state, and edit it before you rely on it.

title: Keep a Paper Trail
text:
When to use the habit

Small diffs: always. It costs a minute.
Large diffs: ask for a changelog per commit, so each one covers a piece you can read.
Better still: ask for work in small steps, so every diff stays small.

title: Keep a Paper Trail
text:

After the next real change an agent makes for you, ask for a changelog and check it against git diff. Write down one thing it missed or overstated, or note that it matched.


Run your project’s README commands in an empty folder, exactly as written. Fix the first step that fails.

Diver Kai surfaces from the Blight-clouded water with a handful of changes and shows you where it hides: in work that sounds sure of itself, even when an Astral wrote it. A good reviewer is kind and exact, and neither tires nor hurries. Kai teaches you the code that keeps both the work and the author in good shape.
You need this because you will also receive LLM-assisted work to review. This quest covers what to ask for and how to say it. Reviewing it is the same craft as any review, with a few shifts in attention.

title: Teach and Share the Load
text:
You return to Tidewrack, where younger villagers ask what you know, and your Astral could answer faster than you can, so Net-mender Joss asks what you are still learning. Joss mends the nets while talking, and has seen the Blight settle where hands grow idle and the load grows heavy. Joss shows you how to share what you know, protect your own learning and take on only what you can review.
You need this once you use agents with others around you: they change how you teach, how you learn and how much you take on. This quest covers each.

title: Teach and Share the Load
text:
Teaching
You can help without being an expert. When teaching a colleague:

Start from their problem. The tool comes later.
Teach the checks first. Verification habits matter more than clever prompts.
Let them predict, then reveal. Ask “what do you expect this to do?” before running it.
Welcome opt-outs. A colleague may choose not to use LLMs, and may still be an excellent reviewer.

title: Teach and Share the Load
text:
Protecting your own learning
An agent can quietly take over the parts you wanted to learn. Pick a rule that suits you, such as: write the first version of anything new yourself, then compare; ask the agent to explain while you do the work; and keep one area of your work agent-free.

title: Teach and Share the Load
text:
Owning what you made
Finishing a project mostly through an agent can leave a quiet feeling that the result is not really yours, a kind of imposter syndrome. Some people report it. Ownership grows from your decisions and your understanding. These habits build both:

Make the decisions. Choose the question, the method and what counts as good enough. Let the agent draft.
Explain it back. Before you call the work done, walk a colleague through each step.
Keep a short decision log (a running list of your choices). One line is enough: “Used a mapping-quality cutoff of 30, not 20, because the agent’s 20 kept multi-mapped reads.”
Do one hard part yourself. Pick the part you most want to understand.
Credit the agent’s part plainly in your methods or commit messages. Honest credit lifts the pressure.
Judge the result by what you can explain and defend.

title: Teach and Share the Load
text:
Managing workload
Agents make it easy to start many things. Count the cost of reviewing what they produce. A simple rule: start only as much as you can review today.

title: Teach and Share the Load
text:
Keeping timelines honest
A quick draft can quietly raise what everyone expects. A first version that once took a day now arrives in an hour, and the time for reading, checking and understanding it stays what it always was. These habits help keep the pace realistic:

Say where the time goes. Drafting is fast. Reading the diff, running the checks and making sense of the result take the time they take.
Agree timelines before you start, put review time in the estimate, and tell the people asking how long the draft took and how long checking took.
Hand over a quick draft as a draft, and say so.

title: Teach and Share the Load
section: Keeping your voice, thinking and judgement
text:
Keeping your voice, thinking and judgement
Heavy use of an agent can smooth your writing into a general style, crowd out the thinking you enjoy and wear down confidence in your own call. Keep each in practice:

Write the first version in your own words, then edit. Read it aloud, and keep a sample of your earlier writing to check how you sound.
Keep the question, the design and the interpretation for yourself. Give the agent routine drafting, such as boilerplate, formatting and first-pass summaries, or structure and consistency checks.
Decide first and write your call down, then ask for a second opinion. Afterwards note where your call held up and where the agent saw something you missed.
Schedule checking as real work, with time in your calendar.

Show one colleague one verification habit from this course, such as re-running the check, or running awk (a text-processing command) over a script’s output to count lines and compare the count with what the script reported. Teach the habit; the tool is optional.

title: Advice or Enforcement
text:
A wall of signs hangs by the Row’s gate, and Watchman Corin walks you along it. Some signs ask politely and some lock the door, and your Astral reads every one of them in the same eager way. Corin shows you that from across the room they look alike, and only one kind holds when the Astral pushes. Learn to tell them apart before you rely on one.
A common mistake is to use advice where a lock was needed. Every control does one of three things.
The rule of thumb: advice for preferences, a prompt for decisions you want to make each time, enforcement for things that must never happen.

title: Advice or Enforcement
text:
Limits for research groups
The same split works for a group that runs agents:

Put limits in the system that runs the agent: permission scopes, and spend caps in the metering system (the service that counts each user’s usage and cost). A budget the agent can exceed is not a limit.
Name a human owner for each agent duty.
Log what an agent did under an identity you can trace.
Keep a list of the agents in use, including personal ones connected to mail or files. Institutions can keep one, and a group can keep its own.
Use a scoped account, take a backup before granting write or delete access, and name an owner for the machine. An over-privileged agent with shell access can wipe data on a shared lab server.


List five controls in your own setup, such as an instructions file, a hook or a deny rule. Label each advises, asks or enforces, and write the way it could fail.

title: Bundle a Plugin
text:
At the door of the smithy Smith Dunmore holds out a satchel to be packed with the finest skills and their tests. Whatever you carry, others will unpack, and whatever you unpack from another traveller’s satchel runs with your own authority. Dunmore once saw a pack that looked fine on the table split open on a stranger’s back. The smith shows you how to pack with care, and how to open with more.
A single Skill in your folder helps you. You need a plugin when a group should install the same set and get updates. A plugin is a folder that bundles Skills and, optionally, agents (helper assistants with their own instructions), hooks (scripts the harness runs at set points) and MCP servers.

title: Bundle a Plugin
section: Installing one is a trust decision
text:
Installing one is a trust decision
A plugin you install can run arbitrary code on your machine with your user privileges. Hooks, monitors (background watchers that feed output to the agent), and local MCP and language servers (programs that give editor-style code checks) run outside the sandbox and the permission rules. A plugin’s bin/ folder holds executables that go on Claude’s shell PATH (the list of places commands are found), so Claude can run them, and each call follows your permission rules. Skills and agents enter the context as instructions, and instructions can steer the agent too.
Before installing or updating a plugin:

Check where it comes from. A marketplace name says who publishes it. Reading the plugin shows what it does.
Read hooks/hooks.json, .mcp.json, and anything in bin/. These are where code lives.
In a session, /plugin shows what will be installed. claude --plugin-dir <dir> plugin details <name> prints a list of the plugin’s components without starting a session.
Remember that auto-update can change files you reviewed, so re-read a plugin after each update. Pin a version for plugins you publish.

title: Bundle a Plugin
text:
When a team shares Skills

Keep project names and conventions in one file. Put the reference genome build, the sample-ID pattern and the results folder names in a project-facts file (a plain file that lists them) that every Skill reads. Another lab can then reuse your Skills with its own file.
Keep discovered details apart from team standards. A pattern the agent finds in your code is an observation. A person confirms it before it becomes a standard.
Check generated copies. If you generate copies of a SKILL.md, run a check in CI (automated checks that run on every change) that fails when a copy differs from its source.
Merge blocking is a repository setting. Whether a bad change is stopped depends on repository rules and required checks. A review step written in a Skill is advice unless a required check backs it.


Turn the Skill you wrote into a plugin folder with a plugin.json, then run claude plugin validate on it and read the output.

title: Meet the Guilds
text:
Your Astral is still too unruly even for the mill’s chores, so Miller Garrick sends you along the road to Artisans’ Row, where Hallmaster Cass keeps the Guild Hall. Cass walks you past three doors: the skillsmiths, who keep procedures in folders, the gate-wardens, who stand at the door to the outside world, and the hookwrights, who write rules in code that nobody can talk their way past. Cass takes no apprentice who cannot check an Astral’s work, so your first lesson waits in the Swamp of Illusions. Learn what each guild does, then go and earn your place.

Quartermaster ArisDiviner IlsaArtificer BobArchivist Elowen


Quartermaster Aris opens a fresh page of the ledger for each extension, with the name of whoever approved it.


Diviner Ilsa spots the plots she rebuilds every week, and wonders which of the three would carry them.


Artificer Bob reads the code behind each extension before he trusts it.


Archivist Elowen counts which of the three can reach the raw data.
Three kinds of extension come up again and again when you work with an agent: a Skill, an MCP server and a hook. Each does a different job. After this lesson you can say which one to reach for, and which one makes a rule hold.

title: Meet the Guilds
text:
1. A Skill carries a procedure
A Skill is a folder with a SKILL.md file that holds a step-by-step procedure. You keep it in your project or in your home folder, and it works with any agent that reads that format. At the start of a session the agent sees only the Skill’s name and a short description. It reads the rest when the task matches, so a long procedure does not fill the context (the text the model can see at once) until it is needed.

Example. A Skill called check-fasta that says: count the records, list any duplicate sequence IDs, report what you ran, change nothing. You would use it before every analysis of a new FASTA file (a plain-text format for DNA or protein sequences).
What it guarantees. Nothing. A Skill is text, and text advises. The agent can skip the Skill or follow it loosely.
Its job. Packaging a repeatable procedure so you do not retype it.

title: Meet the Guilds
section: 2. An MCP server connects the agent to another system
text:
2. An MCP server connects the agent to another system
The Model Context Protocol (MCP) is an open standard for connecting an agent to outside tools and data. An MCP server is a program, running on your machine or elsewhere, that offers tools (functions the agent can call, such as a search) to the harness.

Example. A server that searches a literature database, or one that queries your lab’s sample-tracking database. The agent can then call “search papers” or “look up sample” as tools.
What it guarantees. Capability, and no safety. A server runs as software you installed, with the access you gave it. Text it fetches, such as a web page, can contain hidden instructions that the model may follow (prompt injection).
Its job. Reaching data and services the agent cannot reach on its own.

title: Meet the Guilds
section: 3. A hook makes a rule hold
text:
3. A hook makes a rule hold
A hook is a command you write that the harness runs automatically at a set point, such as just before the agent runs a tool. The hook’s exit code (the number a script returns when it finishes) decides what happens next: code 2 before a tool call blocks the call, whatever the model wants.

Example. A hook that refuses any shell command that touches the data/raw/ folder.
What it guarantees. Enforcement, within its limits. A hook covers only the points (events) and tools you attach it to. A hook that fails with any exit code other than 2 reports an error and does not block the call.
Its job. Making a rule hold when advice is not enough.

When the agent needs a system it cannot reach, connect a server, and treat the server as software you are installing.

title: Meet the Guilds
section: Do it: see what your own setup has
text:
Do it: see what your own setup has
This needs an agent installed as in Set Up Your Agent. Open it in a throwaway folder (never a real project). Each command below only lists what is set up. An empty list is a normal result on a fresh install.

Claude CodeOpenCode + Ollama


Start claude. Inside the session, run each of these slash commands (a slash command is a /command typed inside the running agent):

/skills lists the Skills the agent can see.
/mcp lists the connected MCP servers and their connection status.
/hooks shows the hooks that are configured.

Outside a session, claude mcp list prints the servers with a health status.


OpenCode reads Skills from the same SKILL.md folders. Start opencode and ask the agent which Skills it can see. A Skill is loaded through the agent’s skill tool, so the agent can list them.

title: Too Many Tools, Too Many Agents
text:
The wall of the Guild Hall is hung with every tool anyone ever made, and the boasters say a good pact carries them all. You tried it, and the Astral staggered out under so much iron that it could not find the one it needed. Hallmaster Cass picks three and leaves the rest on their hooks. Cass also asks a harder question: does this job need a crew of creatures at all? Count what each tool costs before you carry it.
You need this lesson now because every server you connect adds to the window. An agent (a model that runs tools in a loop) has a tool for each action it can take, such as reading a file or searching the web. Each tool has a definition: a name and a description of how to use it. The model needs those definitions in its context window (the text it can see at once) to choose a tool. Too many tools make the agent slower, costlier and less accurate, so the first half of this quest is about keeping the set small. The second half asks whether you need an agent at all.

title: Too Many Tools, Too Many Agents
text:
Tools cost context
Loading every tool definition up front bloats the context. Anthropic reports that a typical five-server setup (an MCP server is a program that offers tools to the agent) can use tens of thousands of tokens in definitions before any work starts, and that choosing the right tool gets worse as the number of tools grows.
Tool search (loading a tool’s definition only when the agent needs it) keeps most definitions out of the window and loads a few on demand. Anthropic reports that it cuts that overhead by most of its size (its own measurement, so treat it as a rough guide). It pays off from about 10 tools upward, or when definitions are large. Below that, plain tool calling is better.

Claude CodeOpenCode + Ollama


Tool search (the feature above, which loads a definition only when the agent needs the tool) is on by default for MCP tools. Tool names and server instructions load at session start, and a full definition loads when needed. Extra MCP servers therefore have a small effect on the window. To turn it off, set the environment variable ENABLE_TOOL_SEARCH=false before starting claude. On some older models it falls back to loading everything. Skill descriptions also load at start.
To count your tools, run /mcp to list your connected servers and /context to see how much of the window tools and skills take. Choose your tool set before you start a task.


Check OpenCode’s docs for how it loads tool definitions. Until you know, assume definitions cost context and keep the set small, especially on a local model with a small window.



Keep few, clearly named tools, and remove the servers you do not use.

title: Too Many Tools, Too Many Agents
section: Single call, workflow, agent, or script
text:
Single call, workflow, agent, or script
A workflow orchestrates models and tools through paths fixed in code. An agent is a system where the model directs its own process and tool use. Anthropic’s article “Building effective agents” advises starting with the simplest solution that works, and for many uses one well-prepared call is enough. Agents trade speed and cost for performance, and their mistakes compound, so test with limits such as a stopping condition (a maximum number of steps).

A plain script: use it when the rule is known. Counting reads, converting a format, running fastqc then trim then align in a fixed order. A pipeline written in a workflow manager such as Nextflow is already a workflow.
A single call: use it when you paste the input and want a text answer, such as an explanation of an error.
An agent: use it when the next step depends on what it finds, such as debugging a failing run or exploring an unfamiliar repository. Give it a way to check its own work and a limit.

Doing the task by hand is also a fine decision.

title: Too Many Tools, Too Many Agents
section: Does a team of agents help?
text:
Does a team of agents help?
One 2025 preprint (its own tasks and models) compared a single agent with several multi-agent set-ups across six benchmarks. Read the findings as direction, not rules.

It depends on the task. On a task that splits into independent parts (financial analysis), multi-agent set-ups did much better than one agent. On sequential planning, every multi-agent variant did worse.
A strong single agent leaves little to gain. Once one agent already did well on a task, adding agents gave diminishing or negative returns.
Unchecked agents pass errors on. Agents working independently amplified each other’s errors far more than agents whose work a central agent checked.

Start with one agent, measure it, and add agents only for work that splits into independent parts and only if the measurement says it helps.

title: Write a Skill
text:
In the smithy on the Row, Smith Dunmore keeps procedures in folders, tired of watching Astrals ask the same question twice. A long recipe hung on every wall would crowd the shop, so Dunmore hangs only a label and fetches the rest on demand. The smith lays a fresh folder on the anvil and shows you how to forge one.
An instructions file is read every session. A Skill is a procedure loaded only when it is relevant, so it can be long without filling the context (the limited amount of text, counted in tokens, the chunks of text a model reads, that the agent holds at once). You need this now because a repeated chore belongs in a Skill, so you stop retyping it each session.

title: Write a Skill
text:
What a Skill is
A Skill is a folder with a SKILL.md file, in an open format called Agent Skills, so other tools that follow the format can load the same folder. A Skill loads in three steps, which keeps the context window (the text the model can see at once) small:

At session start the agent sees only each Skill’s name and short description. The format’s specification puts this at about 100 tokens per Skill.
When a task matches, the agent reads the body of SKILL.md. The specification recommends keeping it under 5,000 tokens.
Bundled scripts and reference files are read only when the body points to them.

In Claude Code, both you (by name, such as /check-fasta) and the agent (by matching the description) can start one.

Claude CodeOpenCode + Ollama


Place it at .claude/skills/<name>/SKILL.md (project) or ~/.claude/skills/<name>/SKILL.md (all projects). All frontmatter fields are optional, but write a clear description so it triggers at the right time. Keep the body under about 500 lines. The older .claude/commands/ format still works and is merged into Skills.


OpenCode reads skills from .opencode/skills, .claude/skills and .agents/skills, so the same SKILL.md can serve both tools. Custom agents live in .opencode/agents/*.md.



An example you can write by hand in a scratch folder:
---
name: check-fasta
description: Count the records in a FASTA file and find duplicate IDs. Use before running any analysis on a new FASTA.
---

1. Run `grep -c '>' FILE` to count records.
2. Run `grep '>' FILE | sort | uniq -d` to find duplicate IDs.
3. Report what you ran and its output. Leave FILE unchanged.

title: Write a Skill
section: Do it: install it, then confirm it loaded
text:
Do it: install it, then confirm it loaded
Writing the file is half the job. A Skill whose frontmatter has broken YAML loads silently with no fields set, and a misspelt field name is ignored, so always check.

Make a scratch folder (never a real project) and move into it: mkdir skill-scratch && cd skill-scratch. Save the example above as .claude/skills/check-fasta/SKILL.md. The --- must be the very first line of the file.
In the same folder, make a tiny test file: printf '>a\nACGT\n>a\nGGCC\n' > reads.fa (two records, one duplicated ID).
Confirm the agent can see it:


Claude CodeOpenCode + Ollama


Start claude in the scratch folder. Type / and look for check-fasta in the menu, or run /skills, which lists the skills the agent can see. If the Skill does not appear, run /reload-skills (it re-reads the skill folders) and look again. Then ask in plain words, leaving the Skill unnamed: “I just got reads.fa from a collaborator. Is it OK to analyse?” The agent should say it is using the check-fasta Skill, run the two grep commands, and report two records and the duplicated ID a.


Start opencode in the scratch folder. OpenCode finds .claude/skills too. The model loads a Skill through its skill tool, and you can load one yourself by writing @check-fasta in a prompt. Then ask the same question and check whether the Skill was used.




If it did not trigger, check in this order:

The file starts with --- on line 1.
The YAML (the key: value text format used in that block) parses.
Field names are spelled right.
The description says when to use it, with the key use case first (long descriptions are cut off in the listing).


A Skill that is listed but never picked up points to the description or the prompt.
Two slash commands help you look:

/skills lists the skills the agent can see, and t sorts them by token count.
/skill-doctor shows each skill’s context cost (how much of the context its text takes up) and how often it is used, and flags skills that sit in the listing but are never invoked. It excludes bundled and enterprise skills.

In Claude Code, allowed-tools in a Skill pre-approves tools for that turn (one prompt and its reply). It restricts nothing: other tools still ask as usual. A Skill offers no sandbox, and a Skill you download is code you choose to trust, so read it before installing it, as you would read a script.

title: Write a Skill
section: Design the Skill like a small job
text:
Design the Skill like a small job

One Skill, one job. Give it a defined input (what it is handed, such as a FASTA path) and a defined output (what it must return, such as a count and a list of duplicate IDs). If the description needs “and also”, split it into two Skills.
Say when to use it and what evidence to report (the commands run and their output), so a reviewer can see what happened.
Write only what the agent would get wrong without you. For each line, ask whether the agent would make a mistake if the line were missing. If not, cut the line. A short list of gotchas (for example “a FASTA header may contain spaces”) earns its place.
Start from a task you keep explaining, such as confirming a FASTQ file has no truncated records.
A Skill describes the method. The tool that runs it supplies the tools, credentials and permissions. “Submit this to the cluster” brings no cluster account with it.
Use an application when you need more. Work that needs a stable interface, shared state, an audit trail or permissions enforced from outside, such as a lab’s shared sample-tracking service, suits an application (a separate program with its own tests and access rules).

For portability: both Claude Code and OpenCode read .claude/skills, so one SKILL.md can serve both. The open format requires a name and a description, while Claude Code treats both as optional. Write both. Make the name match the folder name (lowercase letters, digits and hyphens, up to 64 characters), and keep the description under 1,024 characters. After installing, verify in each client (the tool that runs the agent, such as Claude Code or OpenCode) you use:

Does it trigger on the right request?
Does it load the files the Skill refers to?
Does it use the tools it needs?
Does it return the evidence you asked for?

Clients differ in models, tools and permissions, so a Skill that works in one can fail in another.

Write a SKILL.md for one chore you repeat (checking an input, summarising a log). Make the description say when to use it.

title: Dry Run First
section: Read the rule before you run it
text:
Read the rule before you run it
Step 1 needs something to look for. A rule is one step of a Snakemake pipeline: it names the inputs, outputs and command. The mistakes below apply to Nextflow too. This rule has the first two:
rule count_lines:
    input: "/home/alice/data/sample1.fastq"
    shell: "wc -l {input} > counts.txt"
Four mistakes turn up most in agent-written pipelines:

Hard-coded path: a path to someone’s home directory or to one sample, as in the rule above.
Undeclared output: the rule has no output: line, so the workflow manager cannot track counts.txt or build the next step from it.
Unpinned tool version (no fixed version stated): results change when the environment does.
Overwritten input: a step changes its input in place, so there is no way back.

A rule can run and still give the wrong result, so you catch these by reading.

title: Build a Knowledge Graph with Ollama
text:
In a back room Miller Garrick strings yarn between pegs: one peg for each name, one thread for each link. It takes a long time, and every knot is worth checking, because an Astral that follows one wrongly tied thread does so with confidence. A traveller asks whether the web finds answers that a plain search misses. You will build a small one and test that.
You need this exercise before you pay for a graph tool: it tests whether a graph answers a question that plain lookup misses, using notes small enough to check by hand. It runs on Ollama (a program that runs language models on your own machine). Three terms first:

title: Build a Knowledge Graph with Ollama
text:
Set up
mini-rag holds ollama_min.py (two helpers), rag.py (simple RAG), graph.py (a hand-made graph RAG) and notes/ (twelve short mock notes, 233 words in all). Save the folder anywhere. It sits at exercises/prompts-and-context/mini-rag in the course repository, so a clone of the course already has it. If neither works, ask your agent to recreate it from the descriptions below.
Pull an embedding model (it turns text into vectors for search) and pick a chat model. ollama pull <name> downloads a model; wait for it to finish. The run below used the tag gemma4:12b-mlx. Any chat model on your machine works: run ollama list to see what you have, or pull another and use its name.
ollama pull nomic-embed-text
export CHAT_MODEL=gemma4:12b-mlx      # or any chat model from `ollama list`
cd mini-rag
The scripts read three environment variables: CHAT_MODEL, EMBED_MODEL (default nomic-embed-text) and OLLAMA_URL (default http://127.0.0.1:11434). Ollama’s default context window is small, so the scripts send each request with num_ctx (the context window size in tokens) set to 8192. You do not have to restart the server.
Open notes/ and read a few. They are fictional: two sequencers (Orion and Vega), two projects (Heron and Kelp), two pipeline releases, and some distractors such as the lunch rota. One question needs a chain of four hops: Project Heron studies samples S31 to S36, run R7 loaded those samples, run R7 used pipeline release 2.3, and release 2.3 has a known bug.

title: Build a Knowledge Graph with Ollama
text:
Step 1: simple RAG
rag.py is simple RAG in about thirty lines.
python3 rag.py "Does project Heron need to re-analyse its data because of a known pipeline bug?"
With the default -k 3 the run printed:
Retrieved:
  0.668  pipeline-2-4.txt
  0.653  pipeline-2-3.txt
  0.644  project-heron.txt

Answer:
The notes do not contain the answer.
The notes that hold the answer were in the folder, but the run log that connects Heron’s samples to pipeline 2.3 ranked fourth. Try -k 5:
  0.668  pipeline-2-4.txt
  0.653  pipeline-2-3.txt
  0.644  project-heron.txt
  0.549  run-r7.txt
  0.528  run-r8.txt

Answer:
Yes, project Heron needs to re-analyse its data because the primary analysis of run R7 used pipeline release 2.3, which has a known bug that double-counts duplicate reads.
Then try --all, which skips retrieval and pastes every note into the prompt. It also gave a correct answer. With twelve short notes, the window holds everything.

title: Build a Knowledge Graph with Ollama
text:
Step 2: build the graph
graph.py build sends each note to the chat model and asks for (subject, relation, object) facts. It uses Ollama’s structured outputs: the request carries a JSON schema (a description of the JSON shape wanted: JSON is a text format of keys and values) in the format field, so the reply has the shape the script expects. The helper also sets temperature to 0 (the model picks its most likely word each time, so output varies little).
python3 graph.py build
python3 graph.py show
The run printed saved 67 facts, and the build took 1 minute 20 seconds for twelve notes. A sample of what show printed:
Run R7 --loaded onto--> Orion    [run-r7.txt]
Run R7 --used--> Pipeline 2.3    [run-r7.txt]
Pipeline 2.3 --has bug--> double-counts duplicate reads    [pipeline-2-3.txt]
Project Heron --studies--> S31    [project-heron.txt]
Orion --looked after by--> Dana Okafor    [orion.txt]
You --bring--> own cup    [lunch.txt]
Read the whole list. Most facts match their notes. Two did not: the lunch note produced You --bring--> own cup, which is not a fact about anything in the lab, and one name came back with a stray leading space, which would split a single entity into two nodes (the script now strips names when it loads them). Extraction is a model’s reading of your text, so a graph is a second thing to check. Every fact carries the note it came from, so you can.

title: Build a Knowledge Graph with Ollama
text:
Step 3: ask the graph
graph.py ask does three things. It finds starting entities (names that appear in the question, plus the three closest by embedding). It walks outward two hops along the links. Then it hands the collected facts and their source notes to the model.
python3 graph.py ask "Does project Heron need to re-analyse its data because of a known pipeline bug?"
Starting entities: ['pipeline 2.3', 'pipeline 2.4', 'project heron']
Collected 40 facts from 8 notes: freezers.txt, meeting-march.txt, pipeline-2-3.txt, pipeline-2-4.txt, project-heron.txt, project-kelp.txt, run-r7.txt, run-r8.txt

Answer:
Yes, Project Heron needs to re-analyse its data because Run R7, which loaded the samples for Project Heron (S31 to S36), used Pipeline 2.3, which has a known bug that double-counts duplicate reads.

Notes used:
- [pipeline-2-3.txt]
- [project-heron.txt]
- [run-r7.txt]
The wording of the answer differs a little from run to run even at temperature 0, so yours will not match word for word.

title: Build a Knowledge Graph with Ollama
text:
What we saw
With gemma4:12b-mlx for chat and nomic-embed-text for embeddings:

Simple RAG missed at k=3 and succeeded at k=5. The run log was not among the top three notes. Raising k fixed it, at the price of more text in the prompt.
Putting everything in the prompt also worked, because the collection is tiny.
The graph walk reached the run log without a bigger k, because the link from Heron’s samples to run R7 is an edge. It also pulled in 40 of the 67 facts and 8 of the 12 notes. A bigger collection needs a smaller hop count or a ranking step.
The graph took a minute and twenty seconds to build for 233 words and needs a model good enough to extract facts. Embedding twelve notes for simple RAG takes seconds. Build cost grows with the size of the collection, and Microsoft’s Graph RAG paper describes indexing a large corpus as slow.
A whole-collection question failed in all three setups. “Who works in this group, and what does each person do?” got “the notes do not contain the answer” from simple RAG, --all and the graph walk. No note lists a roster. Microsoft’s Graph RAG builds community summaries for such questions; this toy graph builds none.

One question, one model, one run: this shows the mechanics and does not rank the methods or the models.
Try your own questions and compare.

title: Build a Knowledge Graph with Ollama
text:
A note on model size
We did not run LightRAG or Microsoft GraphRAG here; this section summarises what their documentation asks of an Ollama setup. Extraction asks a model to produce well-formed JSON for every chunk. With Ollama, Microsoft GraphRAG users “frequently see issues with malformed responses (especially JSON)”. The LightRAG README calls Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct (a 30B-parameter model) “a reasonable minimum” for local use, and its programming guide says at least 32B. The 12B model here produced valid JSON for all twelve notes, and show lets you judge the facts. If you try a much smaller model, read the triples before you trust the answers.

title: Build a Knowledge Graph with Ollama
text:
Real tools
graph.py is a teaching toy. LightRAG and Microsoft GraphRAG do this at scale, and both need a strong model and careful setup. Their install and Ollama settings are in the Lore links. Read those docs before you run either, and start with a tiny folder of mock files.

title: Build a Knowledge Graph with Ollama
text:
Verify the graph
A confident answer built on a wrong link is the failure to look for. A graph gives you a list of facts, each with its source note, to check.

Read the extracted facts for a few notes against the notes themselves. Count the wrong ones.
Ask the agent or the script to name the notes behind each answer, then open them.
Keep a short list of questions whose answers you know, and run it after you change the model, the prompt or the notes.
Keep real and controlled data out of this exercise. The same scripts pointed at a hosted model send every note to that provider.

When to use Graphs in RAG: Xiang and colleagues, paper. Why read: it studies which kinds of questions benefit from graphs, with token costs per method.

title: Keep an LLM Wiki
text: Scribe Linnea keeps a ledger in the mill that tidies itself. Each new sack of papers is read once, and every page it touches is updated and cross-linked before the scribe sleeps. In the morning the ledger looks perfect, and you cannot tell which entries Linnea checked and which were merely smoothed over. Learn how the ledger is built and where it can mislead you.

title: Keep an LLM Wiki
section: The problem: understanding that does not accumulate
text:
The problem: understanding that does not accumulate
Think about the last time you read ten papers on a method, or went through six months of meeting notes. You understood it all at the time. A month later, the understanding lives in your head and in a pile of files, and the next question sends you back to the pile.
You need this lesson now to judge whether a wiki suits your material before you build one. RAG (retrieval-augmented generation) answers that with a lookup: each question searches the pile again, pastes a few passages into the prompt, and starts from scratch. Nothing builds up between questions. If an answer needs five documents stitched together, the stitching is redone every time.
This quest follows Andrej Karpathy’s “LLM Wiki” gist (a short shared text page), which proposes another arrangement. An agent keeps a wiki: a folder of interlinked Markdown pages (plain text files with simple formatting) that it writes and updates as new sources arrive, so the stitching is done once and stays. The gist calls it a “persistent, compounding artifact”. People drop their notes because the bookkeeping is tedious (updating links, rewriting summaries, spotting that two pages now disagree), and an agent does that bookkeeping without getting bored. You keep the parts that need a person: choosing sources, asking questions, and deciding what the findings mean.
The gist is an “idea file”, meant to be handed to your agent so the two of you work out the details together. It describes a pattern and includes no program.

title: Keep an LLM Wiki
text:
Three layers

Raw sources: you add files and nobody edits them afterwards. Papers, clipped web pages, meeting transcripts, run logs, data files. The agent reads them and never changes them, so they stay the source of truth.
The wiki: the agent writes it and you read it. Markdown pages: a summary per source, a page per entity (a tool, a dataset, a person, a gene) or concept, comparisons, an overview. The agent owns this folder.
The schema: here, “schema” means the rules for the wiki, written as plain instructions. You and the agent write it over time. It is one instruction file (CLAUDE.md in Claude Code, AGENTS.md in OpenCode) that the agent reads at the start of every session. It describes how the wiki is organised and what to do on each job, and it is the key configuration file.

The split builds trust. When an answer looks odd, you walk from the wiki page back to the raw source it cites, and the raw source is untouched.

title: Keep an LLM Wiki
text:
Three jobs

Ingest (take a new source into the wiki): copy one source into raw/, then ask the agent, for example, “Ingest raw/paper-1.md following the rules in CLAUDE.md.” The agent reads the source, tells you the main takeaways, writes a summary page, updates the pages for the entities and concepts it mentions, adds it to the index, and appends a line to the log. One source may touch 10 to 15 pages. Ingest one source at a time and stay involved. Batching with less supervision is possible.
Query: you ask a question. The agent finds the relevant wiki pages, reads them and answers with citations. A good answer (a comparison table, a timeline, a short report) is filed back as a new page, so your explorations add to the wiki and do not vanish into chat history.
Lint: from time to time you ask for a health check. It looks for pages that contradict each other, claims that a newer source has overtaken, pages that nothing links to, concepts that are mentioned but have no page, missing cross-references, and gaps that a web search might fill.

Two small files keep the wiki navigable:

index.md: a catalogue with each page, a link and a one-line summary, grouped by category and updated on every ingest. To answer a question, the agent reads the index first and then opens the pages that look relevant. The gist says this avoids building an embedding index at moderate scale (the author’s experience). As the wiki grows, add a search tool.
log.md: an append-only diary of ingests, queries and lint passes. Give every entry the same prefix so a simple grep can list the recent ones.

An example schema. Paste it into the instruction file (CLAUDE.md or AGENTS.md) in the wiki folder’s top level, then edit it with your agent:
# Wiki rules
- `raw/` holds sources. Never edit or delete anything in `raw/`.
- `wiki/` holds pages you write. One page per entity or concept; one summary page per source in `wiki/sources/`.
- Every claim on a wiki page ends with a link to the source file it came from. If no source supports it, mark it `(unsourced)`.
- On ingest: read the source, tell me the three main takeaways and wait for my reply, then write the summary page, update affected pages, update `wiki/index.md`, and append `## [YYYY-MM-DD] ingest | <title>` to `wiki/log.md`.
- On lint: list contradictions, unsourced claims, orphan pages and missing pages. Do not fix anything until I say which.

title: Keep an LLM Wiki
section: Why you might want this, and what it costs
text:
Why you might want this, and what it costs

Paste everything into the prompt: fits small collections and needs no setup. You pay in repeated reading each session and a limit at the window size.
RAG: fits a large, changing pile where particular passages answer each question. Each question starts from scratch, multi-document answers are re-stitched, and retrieval misses are silent.
A wiki the agent maintains: fits material you will return to for weeks or months, where understanding should accumulate and be readable. You pay agent time and tokens on every ingest, you get a layer of text that can contain mistakes, and you spend review time.
Notes you write yourself: fit things you want to think through in your own words. This is a perfectly good choice, and the wiki pays off when the bookkeeping is what stops you.

A wiki and search can sit together: a wiki is a good home for the stable understanding, and RAG or search is a good way to reach the raw sources behind it.

title: Keep an LLM Wiki
text:
Use cases you may recognise
Two examples close to a bioinformatics desk. The gist lists many more.

Literature on one method (say, long-read assemblers or variant callers)

Raw sources: papers, preprints, tool docs.
Pages: one per tool and dataset, a comparison table, a page of open disagreements.
A question: “Which papers compare tool A and B on the same data, and do they agree?”
Watch out: preprints mixed with peer-reviewed papers. Ask the agent to record the kind of source on every page.

The lab’s pipeline handbook

Raw sources: release notes, run logs, meeting minutes.
Pages: one per pipeline release, one per known issue, a decision log.
A question: “Which runs used release 2.3, and what was wrong with it?”
Watch out: private or unpublished material. Exact counts belong to a query tool.


To size your own idea, answer four questions in a sentence each:

What sources would go in?
How often do they change?
What question would I ask in a month that I cannot answer quickly today?
Who may read these sources, and where may they be sent?

If the sources fit in one prompt, try that first. If the question is an exact filter or count, ask a query tool. If the sources are sensitive and you would send them to a hosted model, settle your data rules before you begin. If the material is something you want to return to and the answers need several sources joined, the wiki is a good candidate.

title: Keep an LLM Wiki
text:
Reading and guarding the wiki
Obsidian (a free note-taking app that opens a folder of Markdown files) is a convenient way to read the wiki while the agent edits it. The gist’s Obsidian tips are linked in Lore. Any editor that opens a folder works.
Habits that help:

Separate folders: keep the agent’s folder apart from the notes you write by hand. Your own words stay yours, and you can tell at a glance what the agent produced.
Git: put the wiki folder under git and commit before each ingest. A commit per ingest gives you a readable diff of what the agent changed and an undo.
Read-only sources: make raw/ read-only if your tools allow it. The instruction file is advice the agent can ignore, while file permissions are enforced by the system.

title: Keep an LLM Wiki
text:
What can go wrong

A mistake becomes a fact. If the agent misreads a source, the error lands on a page, and later pages cite that page. The cost grows with each ingest. Require a source link on every claim, skim the diff of every ingest, and use lint to hunt for unsourced claims. One source at a time makes the skimming practical.
The agent edits what it should only read. Keep sources immutable and check it with git.
Clipped pages can carry instructions. A web page you clip may contain text aimed at your agent, and the agent reads it during ingest and then writes files. Review the diff, restrict what the agent may run, and keep an agent with write access away from sources you do not trust.
Sources leave your machine. With a hosted model, every source you ingest is sent as prompt text. For unpublished results, patient-linked data or anything under an agreement, check the rules first. A local model through Ollama keeps text on your machine, but ingest asks for reading, summarising and editing several files in one go. Try one short, harmless source first.
Cost and time grow with the wiki. Each ingest reads the index and several pages, and then writes several. Watch your usage in the first week.
Scale. As the wiki grows, add search or another layer on top of the index.
You may not learn it. A wiki you never open does little for your own understanding. Read it, correct it and argue with it.
Exact answers. Counts, filters and joins over tables belong in a query tool.

title: Keep an LLM Wiki
text:
Choose your setup

Claude CodeOpenCode + Ollama


Put the schema in CLAUDE.md at the root of the wiki folder. Start a session there, and ask the agent to read the schema and propose the folder layout before it writes anything. For the first ingest, ask for a plan and approve it before the agent writes. Tighten the schema with whatever you correct. Keep ingest, query and lint as separate short sessions, since the wiki itself is the memory that carries over.


Put the schema in AGENTS.md at the root of the wiki folder (OpenCode also falls back to CLAUDE.md). With a local model, start with a handful of short, non-sensitive sources and check each page against its source, because a small model is more likely to drop or garble details. If a model struggles with the multi-file edit, ask it to do the ingest in steps: summary page first, then one entity page at a time.

title: Keep an LLM Wiki
text:
Battle: the wiki




Answer the four sizing questions for one real collection of yours (sources, how often they change, the question you will ask in a month, who may read them and where they may be sent). Write one sentence saying whether a wiki, RAG, a single prompt or a query tool fits best.


Draft a schema (instruction file) of five lines or fewer for that collection: what the agent must never edit, what every claim must carry, and what it must ask you before writing. Do not run it yet; read it aloud to a colleague and see what they would add.

title: RAG and Its Cousins
text: Travellers keep asking Miller Garrick about books that will never fit in the hopper. An Astral sent to fetch an answer from the whole library came back with the wrong shelf and total confidence. Garrick lists the ways: fetch a few pages when a question comes, draw a web of names, or fetch nothing at all. Before choosing, learn what each way fetches and what it misses.

title: RAG and Its Cousins
text:
Why anyone brings RAG up
This quest helps you pick a method before you build anything, because each method costs time and can fail in a different way. A model knows what it learned in training. It has not read your lab’s protocols, last month’s run logs or the paper that came out last week. You can paste documents into the prompt, but the context window (the text the model can see at once) is finite, and a long prompt costs money and time.
RAG (retrieval-augmented generation) is the idea of looking things up first. A program searches your documents for the passages most likely to matter, pastes only those into the prompt, and asks the model to answer from them. The name comes from a 2020 paper that paired a generator with a vector index of Wikipedia. The recipe most people mean today is a later, simpler version of that idea.

title: RAG and Its Cousins
text:
Simple RAG in four steps

Chunk. Split the documents into pieces (a chunk is one passage, often a paragraph or a few hundred words).
Embed. An embedding model turns each chunk into a vector (a long list of numbers; texts with similar meaning get vectors that point in similar directions). The vectors are stored in an index.
Retrieve. Embed the question the same way, then fetch the k chunks whose vectors are closest (k is a number you pick, such as 3 or 5).
Generate. Paste those chunks into the prompt and ask the model to answer from them and to say which chunk it used.

Papers and PDFs hold tables, figures and two-column text, and a plain text extractor can scramble them before anything is embedded. Open a few extracted chunks and read them before you trust the index.
Everything the model says is limited by step 3. If the right passage did not come back, the model cannot use it. A good model says it does not know. A weaker one answers from the wrong passages.

title: RAG and Its Cousins
text:
A tour of the types
Each type below answers one question: what goes wrong with simple RAG, and what did someone add to fix it?

Simple RAG: chunk, embed, top-k, answer. It suits a pile of prose where one or two passages answer each question, and it is cheap to build and update. It struggles with questions that need several passages or the whole collection, since only the top k chunks arrive.
Improved RAG: add-ons around the same pipeline. Keyword search (BM25, a classic word-matching score) runs next to embeddings, and a reranker (a second model that re-sorts the retrieved chunks) follows. Anthropic reports that combining these add-ons gives fewer retrieval failures than plain embeddings. Each add-on is another part to tune.
Graph RAG (Microsoft): before any question, an LLM reads every chunk and extracts entities and relationships into a knowledge graph (things as nodes, links between them as edges). It groups the graph into communities and writes a summary of each. It suits questions about the whole collection, such as “what are the main themes?”. Indexing is slow and costly, and the docs warn it can consume a lot of LLM resources.
Loop-style RAG (for example Self-RAG and Corrective RAG): the model decides when to retrieve, grades what came back, and tries again if the results look poor. It suits questions where one lookup is rarely enough, at the price of more model calls per question.

Other variants exist, such as LightRAG (a lighter graph method) and tree-based RAG. The Lore links lead to them.

title: RAG and Its Cousins
text:
Does the graph pay off?
The paper that introduced Graph RAG reports wins over plain RAG, mostly on whole-collection questions, as judged by an LLM. Check any such result on your own questions. Independent studies give a mixed picture:

No consistent winner. A 2025 comparison found complementary behaviours. Plain RAG did best on single-fact questions. On multi-hop questions (an answer that needs facts from two or more passages) a graph method led.
Graphs cost more to build. Building the graph took far longer than building a plain index, and the graphs missed many of the entities that the answers needed.
LLM judges are order-sensitive. A judge can flip its verdict when you swap the order of the two answers, so win-rate numbers are weak evidence.
Task decides. Graphs help when a task connects ideas across documents, and can add noise on simple lookups.

Start with simple RAG, measure it on questions you care about, and add a graph only if the failures are of the kind a graph addresses (multi-hop or whole-collection questions) and you can afford the extra cost.

title: RAG and Its Cousins
section: When RAG is the right tool
text:
When RAG is the right tool
RAG is one of several ways to get a model to work from your documents. Choose by your situation:







Your situation
Often a better fit




Whole collection fits your model’s window with room to spare (under about 200,000 tokens, roughly 500 pages, for a 200,000-token window)
Put it all in the prompt. A hosted model then receives all of it


Same large documents asked about again and again
Long context with caching


Files you can search by name or exact text
Agent search with find and grep


Tables and databases (counts, filters, joins)
A query tool: SQL, an API or an MCP server


Exact words matter (gene names, sample ids)
Keyword search first, or hybrid


You want a format or style
Better prompts, a Skill, or fine-tuning


Large, changing prose collection, answers in passages
RAG




Small collection: below about 200,000 tokens you can include everything with no need for RAG. Prompt caching (reusing an unchanged prompt prefix at a lower price) makes repeated questions cheaper. Check the current pricing and cache lifetime.
Repeated questions: cache-augmented generation (preload everything once) can be faster than RAG on a small collection, and becomes impractical for a significantly larger one.
Searchable files: an agent can navigate code and configs “just in time” with glob and grep. Exploring at run time is slower than reading a pre-built index.
Tables and databases: a vector index returns the nearest passages, so it usually cannot promise a complete filter or an exact count. A query can, and you can read the query.
Exact words: BM25 is a strong baseline in standard retrieval benchmarks, and adding it to embeddings reduces retrieval failures further.
Format or style: fine-tune when the problem is consistency or behaviour, and supply context when the model lacks knowledge.
RAG: the collection does not fit in the window, and you can update the index without retraining anything.

In one study with 2024 models, a long-context model beat RAG on average given enough budget, while RAG cost much less and often gave the same answer. The study’s “Self-Route” idea tries RAG first and falls back to the long prompt, which cut cost.

title: RAG and Its Cousins
section: What can go wrong with RAG itself
text:
What can go wrong with RAG itself

The right passage never comes back. Retrieval misses are normal. Measure two things separately: did the right chunk appear, and did the answer follow from the chunks it was given? The second is called faithfulness.
Too much arrives. More chunks can distract the model, and models use text in the middle of a long prompt less well than text at the start or end.
Retrieved text can carry instructions. A document someone else wrote may contain lines aimed at your model, and RAG does not fully remove this risk. Limit what an agent may do after reading retrieved text.
Chunks leave your machine. With a hosted model, retrieved passages are sent to the provider as ordinary prompt text. Your data agreement decides whether that is allowed.
The index goes stale. Anything you indexed last month does not know about today’s edits until you rebuild it.

title: RAG and Its Cousins
text:
Choose your setup

Claude CodeOpenCode + Ollama


Claude Code finds things in a project by searching file names and text (with find and grep). It keeps no vector index. If you want RAG over your own papers, you build it yourself or connect a tool for it, and then everything in the risks list above applies.


With Ollama you can run both halves locally: an embedding model for retrieval and a chat model for the answer.

title: The Context Window
text:
Miller Garrick shows you the great hopper above the mill, which holds everything an Astral can see at once. You watch yours work, quick and willing, while the grain piles up around it. Pour in too much and the oldest grain spills out unseen, and the Astral never knows what it lost. Learn what goes into the hopper and how to keep it clean.
The context window is all the text the model can look at when it writes its next piece of output, including its own reply. It works like the model’s working memory and is separate from what the model learned in training. It is measured in tokens. It limits what an agent can keep in mind in a long task, so you need to know what fills it.

title: The Context Window
text:
What fills it
In Claude Code (a coding agent that runs in your terminal), the window holds your instructions, the files it reads, its own responses, and content that never appears in your terminal. Before you type anything, it already holds:

the instructions file (CLAUDE.md, a text file loaded at session start by the harness, the program around the model that runs tools and sends your text)
auto memory (notes the harness keeps from earlier sessions)
the names of MCP tools (tools added from outside servers) and skill descriptions (short summaries of saved instruction sets)

Every file it reads and every tool output then adds more. With the API (programmatic access to the model) the same idea holds: the system prompt (the harness’s own instructions, sent with every request), every message, tool results, tool definitions and the output all count.
Sizes depend on the model. A big window gives room for more text; quality depends on what fills it.

title: The Context Window
section: What the model stores while it writes
text:
What the model stores while it writes
To write each new token, the model looks back at every earlier token in the window. It keeps numbers computed from those tokens (the KV cache, key-value cache) so it does not redo that work at every step. The KV cache sits in the memory of the machine that runs the model and grows with the window. The prompt cache is a separate provider feature that makes a repeated start of your prompt cheaper to process. The KV cache belongs to the model, and the prompt cache belongs to the bill.

title: The Context Window
text:
Bigger is not better
As the token count grows, accuracy and recall degrade. This is called context rot. Anthropic’s docs give no token count at which it starts, so check the source of any figure you see.

title: The Context Window
text:
When it fills up

Claude CodeOpenCode + Ollama


It compacts automatically as the limit nears: the history is replaced by a summary. The summary keeps your requests and key code snippets, but detailed instructions from early in the conversation may be lost.
Afterwards, Claude Code re-supplies:

the system prompt, the project-root CLAUDE.md, auto memory and skill descriptions
a few recently read or edited files (a very large file comes back as a path only)

Nested instruction files are summarised away and reload on demand.
Useful controls:

/context shows what is using space.
/compact with a focus note compacts on purpose.
/clear starts clean between unrelated tasks.

A subagent (a helper agent started by the main one) has its own window, and only a summary comes back. If one file or output is so big that the window refills after every summary, auto-compaction stops with an error.


Check OpenCode’s documentation for how it compacts and how it reports window usage. Expect any tool to drop or summarise something when the window is full. A local model may run with a smaller window, so check your model’s setting.

title: The Context Window
section: Hands-on: how big is a fresh session?
text:
Hands-on: how big is a fresh session?
A fresh session is not empty: the items above load first, so every session has a starting size. Measure yours:

Claude CodeOpenCode + Ollama



Start a new session (claude) and run /context before you type anything else. A /command is typed into the running session.
Read the table by category. The starting load is the system prompt, system tools, MCP server instructions, memory files and skills. Messages is the conversation, and it should be close to zero.
Look at the MCP and tool lines marked deferred. Their figures say how many tokens they would take if all were loaded. Only their names are in the window until a tool is needed.
Note the largest starting item and whether you chose it. Fewer MCP servers, plugins and skills, or a shorter instructions file, lower it.
Open a long session you already have and run /context there. The difference is the part a fresh start removes.




Send one short message: opencode run -m ollama/qwen3:4b "Say hello in one sentence."
While the model is loaded (Ollama keeps it for a few minutes), run ollama ps in a second terminal.
Read two columns. CONTEXT is the window the server set aside, in tokens. SIZE is the memory the loaded model uses, and it includes the working memory for that window.
A larger CONTEXT needs a larger SIZE. If your model spills onto the CPU, the PROCESSOR column says so.




An agent a session starts for you can start large. A subagent started from a brief begins with that brief. A forked agent (an option in some tools) inherits the whole conversation, so it starts as large as the session that spawned it. A new session or agent that opens with a high count is worth checking with /context before you work in it.

title: The Context Window
text:
Three habits

Start fresh for a new task. An unrelated earlier thread takes room and can distract.
Keep outputs small. In bioinformatics terms: ask for the head, a count, or a summary script’s output when the file is a big variant table or a whole log.
Put durable facts in the instructions file, such as how to run tests or which folders are off limits. Instructions given only in chat can be lost to compaction. Keep that file short: aim for under 200 lines, because longer files use more context and reduce how well the agent follows them.

title: Where Machines Fail
text:
A boaster at Gaia’s Rest swore his Astral could fly. You led it to the mill roof, and it spread its wings, glided a few fine yards and landed in the mud. Over the mill door Miller Garrick has hung a sign with two lists: what the machines do well, and what they only seem to do well. Counting letters is on the second. Read both lists, then learn which jobs to hand a creature and which to give to an Automaton.
A language model is good at some jobs and bad at others, and a wrong answer often looks like a right one. Knowing which jobs are which, before you trust the output, saves time and prevents errors. Using a model is your choice; this lesson shows where the risk sits if you do.

title: Where Machines Fail
section: Where a model helps: the result is checkable
text:
Where a model helps: the result is checkable
Use a model where you can read the result, or run it, and judge it yourself:

summarising text
drafting prose, such as a README or a methods first draft
explaining code or an error message
converting formats, for example a samplesheet CSV to JSON (a structured text format)
first drafts of code that you will then test

Summaries can leave things out or bend them. Spot-check against the source: numbers, gene and sample names, direction of effect, negations. Omissions are harder to see, so skim the abstract and limitations yourself. Ask the model to quote the supporting lines first, then summarise.

title: Where Machines Fail
text:
Where a model fails
Each failure below has the same shape: what goes wrong, then what to do about it.

Exact counting and arithmetic
Ask a model: “How many n are in banana?” The right answer is 2 (b-a-n-a-n-a). A model can get this wrong, and can be wrong while sounding sure.
Researchers disagree on why. One explanation is that the model reads tokens (chunks of letters), not letters. One study finds word length and the true count matter more than tokenisation. The fix works whichever cause is right.
The fix is to run a script:
echo banana | grep -o n | wc -l
It prints 2 (macOS pads the number with spaces). A model asked to write Python for a counting task does better than a model asked to answer it directly. So for exact counts, have the model write the script and read the script and its output.
The bioinformatics versions of the same trap:







You want
Give it to




Number of sequences in a FASTA
grep -c '>' file.fa, or seqkit stats


GC content, read length statistics
a script, run by the agent, with the code visible


A p-value or any test statistic
a stats library in a script you can read and re-run


Sum or mean of a column
awk, or a script that prints the number



Ask for the command and its output, and treat a count stated in prose as a guess to check.

Claude CodeOpenCode + Ollama


Claude Code can run shell commands and write scripts, so ask: “write and run a command for this, and show me both the command and its output.”


Same rule: ask for a script, and read the command and its output. Try the banana example with your own model to see how it does.





Hallucination
A confident statement that is false, such as a plausible DOI, gene ID or tool flag that does not exist. A model may recommend --min-quality for a tool that has no such option. Allow “I don’t know”, ask for word-for-word quotes first and restrict the model to supplied documents. Look up every ID in PubMed or Ensembl, or run the tool’s --help.


Sycophancy
The model tells you what you want to hear. It agrees with your wrong hypothesis, or softens a correct criticism when you push back. Ask “are you sure?” about a right answer and it may change to a wrong one. Ask for the strongest case against your idea, and hold back your preferred answer.


Long-context degradation
Accuracy and recall drop as the input (everything the model is given to read) grows, a decline sometimes called “context rot”, and relevant text in the middle is used less. Curate the input (head, counts, filtered tables) and start fresh for a new task.


Instruction drift
An early instruction is forgotten, for example after compaction (the program around the model replacing old conversation with a summary to free room). Keep a short instructions file (CLAUDE.md or similar, loaded at session start). Use a hook (a script that runs automatically at set moments, such as before a command) for must-never rules.


Non-determinism
The same prompt may give different answers, so run it twice and compare. Record the command, model and version, and treat the script the model wrote as the reproducible part.


Overconfidence
The model reports a task as done while it is unfinished, often because it had no way to check. Give it a check to run (tests, row counts, md5) and read the output.


Prompt injection
Text from fetched content that the model treats as an instruction, for example a README, PDF or FASTA header that contains instructions the agent follows. Treat fetched content as data, review commands before approving them, and remember no system is fully immune.


Restricted topics
Providers train models, and put filters around them, to refuse or limit help on topics they judge dangerous, such as biological weapons or malware. The filters can also catch legitimate work that looks similar. Two areas matter to bioinformaticians. In biology, a provider’s filters may send a request on a topic such as virology or toxicology to a less capable model, and the provider says false positives remain. In security, real-time safeguards may block or limit help with exploit or malware work, and providers offer an application route for verified professionals. The result can be a refusal or a thinner answer with no error message, so a poor answer on a legitimate topic may be a safeguard at work.
Check the reply for a notice that a safeguard blocked the request or that another model answered. Verify what you did receive with a database, a script or a colleague. Do not rephrase to dodge a filter, because bypassing a provider’s guardrails breaks its usage policy. Filters can also hit allowed work, and the provider’s policy says a block is no sign of a violation. Apply for the provider’s verified-access route for your field (Anthropic’s Cyber Verification Program is one example for security work), or use another tool for that step.


Stale knowledge
Newer tool versions or database releases postdate the model’s training. Check --version and the current docs, and look up the model’s training cutoff date in its documentation.

title: Where Machines Fail
text:
The decision rule
Ask yourself: can I check the result cheaply and independently? If yes, ask the model: a bad answer is likely to show (omissions may not, so check those deliberately). If the answer must be exactly right and cannot be checked, use a script.

title: Write the Brief
text:
Miller Garrick sends your Astral across the mill yard with a single instruction, “help out”, and it hauls the wrong sack, then the next one, and stirs the flour into the mud. Garrick says every good errand starts with a few plain words about where, why and how you will know it worked. He hands you a stub of chalk and asks you to write them on the sack before anything is lifted. ::: {.panel-tabset group=“persona”}


Quartermaster Aris’s brief names the deadline, the budget and the proof of done.



Diviner Ilsa’s brief names the controls and the reference to check against.



Artificer Bob’s brief names the test that must pass.



Archivist Elowen’s brief names the fields that must never change.
:::
The brief is what you tell the agent. A vague brief invites a plausible guess. A good brief names the file and the symptom (what you see going wrong), says what “done” looks like, and gives the agent a check it can run.
Two habits make the rest of this safer:

title: Write the Brief
text:
Put effort into the brief
A common habit is to open with “You are a world-class bioinformatician.” Expert personas help with tone, format, safety and preference tasks. They can hurt tasks that rely on what the model already knows, such as factual questions. A role line is not a substitute for a brief.
So:

Brief first: put your effort into the file, the symptom, what “done” looks like, and a check. Those are testable. A role line is not.
Role for style: use a role or tone line when you want a style, such as “explain this for a first-year student”.
Test a persona: if you use one on a factual task, compare the result against a version without one.

title: Write the Brief
section: The context window has a size limit
text:
The context window has a size limit
Everything in the conversation takes up room in the context window, and the room is limited. Old conversation can crowd out the files you need next.

Claude CodeOpenCode + Ollama


/context shows what is filling the window. /compact summarises the conversation (you can say what to keep). /clear starts fresh, which is right when you switch to an unrelated task. Claude Code also compacts automatically near the limit.


/new starts a new session in OpenCode’s TUI (the text user interface, its terminal screen). Check OpenCode’s documentation for how your version summarises a session and whether a command shows what fills the window.
