title: Plan Before You Edit
text: On the practice field Warden Hesper walks the course before any drill, and she has watched an Astral run the wrong lane at full speed. She shows you how a wrong step on paper costs a line, and a wrong step on the field costs the course. The trainers keep her rule: no one runs until the route has been drawn, read aloud and questioned. She unrolls a sheet and shows you how to draw one.

title: Plan Before You Edit
text:
Why plan first
A wrong plan costs you a paragraph to read and reject. A wrong 400-line diff (the list of lines a change added and removed) costs you the time to review it, and the longer it is, the more likely you approve something you did not understand. A plan is the cheapest piece to ask for first. You do this before the agent changes anything that matters. Ask for small pieces, and accept only as much output as you can honestly review.
Use plan mode (a setting in which the agent writes a plan and edits nothing until you approve it) for changes you want to review before they touch disk. Before your first real edit, you need to know how to enter it and how to read what it proposes.

title: Plan Before You Edit
text:
How: plan mode
Terms used in the tabs below:

Session: one conversation with the agent.
Shell commands: commands you would type in a terminal, such as ls or git status.
Context: everything the model can see in the session.
Subagent: a helper with its own context window; only its summary comes back.
Deny rule: a rule that blocks an action in every mode.
Auto mode: a mode where a background check decides what runs without a prompt.
Bypass permissions: a startup option (--dangerously-skip-permissions) that turns most prompts off.
-p: runs one command with no chat (non-interactive mode).
Agent SDK: a library for building your own agent programs.


Claude CodeOpenCode + Ollama


In Claude Code, plan mode is one permission mode: a setting for what the agent may do without asking you. In plan mode the agent reads files, may run shell commands to explore, and writes a plan. It is meant to leave your source files unedited until you approve the plan (tell it to go ahead).
Three ways in:

Shift+Tab during a session (it cycles through the permission modes) until the status bar (the line of text at the bottom of the terminal) shows ⏸ plan mode on.
/plan followed by your request, for example /plan add a strandedness column to the samplesheet parser.
claude --permission-mode plan when you start it.

When the plan is ready, the agent presents it and asks how to proceed. On your first run, pick Yes, manually approve edits, which keeps approval on. The options, with their exact labels:

Yes, and use auto mode: auto mode decides what runs without a prompt. If auto mode is unavailable, this reads Yes, auto-accept edits. If your session started with bypass, it reads Yes, and switch to BYPASS PERMISSIONS (no further prompts) for this session. Bypass skips most prompts.
Yes, manually approve edits: each edit still asks you.
No, keep planning: you say what to change.







Note



At the approval prompt, Shift+Tab approves the plan, so press it only when you mean to approve. If you want to think, change something or back out, press Esc instead. To leave plan mode when no prompt is open, press Shift+Tab.


Two more details:

Where the plan lives: plans are written to ~/.claude/plans/ by default (the plansDirectory setting changes the folder). Ctrl+G opens the proposed plan in your default text editor so you can edit it before the agent proceeds. Approving exits plan mode and switches to the mode you chose; to plan again, use Shift+Tab or /plan.
Side helper: in plan mode the agent can hand research to the built-in Plan subagent. It is read-only, so the main conversation stays read-only too.



OpenCode has a built-in plan agent. It explores and plans without editing normal project files, and it can edit only under its plan directory, ~/.opencode/plan. That edit restriction is a deny rule, and saved approvals do not override a deny. Its shell commands follow the normal permission rules.
The base policy for every agent allows everything except asking before reading .env files. So the plan agent cannot edit project files, but its shell commands can still change files without a prompt. Check the permission rules in your version before you rely on the plan agent.
You can turn the plan agent off with {"agents": {"plan": {"disabled": true}}}.
To find out how to switch to the plan agent and whether it has an approval step, read the OpenCode agents page for your version.

title: Plan Before You Edit
section: Review the plan like a reviewer
text:
Review the plan like a reviewer
A plan is text from a model that has not yet run anything. Read it the way you would read a methods section from a collaborator you have not worked with before. A checklist:

What files will it touch? Anything outside the task is a question to ask.
What does it assume about the data? “IDs are unique” or “the file has a header” are guesses until checked against the real files.
What could it break? Callers, config, tests, outputs other people read.
How will it verify, and is the check independent of the code it writes? A test the agent writes for its own code can share its mistake. Compute one value some other way, for example with awk or wc.
Are the steps small enough to review one at a time? A step names one change, so “Update everything” needs splitting.
What is not in the plan? Missing edge cases, missing tests, no mention of a rollback.

If an answer is bad, choose No, keep planning and say what to change, or edit the plan yourself with Ctrl+G.

title: Plan Before You Edit
section: What a plan does not guarantee
text:
What a plan does not guarantee

A plan is advice. An approved plan is only as good as your review of it.
The agent can deviate. The agent can still change course after approval. Afterwards, read the diff against the plan: every changed file should be one the plan named. /code-review reviews the diff in a fresh subagent that never saw your conversation.
Plan mode may be an instruction only. In an interactive terminal session where bypass permissions is available, Claude is only instructed to plan without editing. Claude Code does not enforce it, and edits and shell commands run without a prompt (explicit ask rules and a few critical deletions still prompt). With -p, the Agent SDK and the VS Code chat panel, the blocks stay in place.
Deny rules always apply. A deny rule blocks in every mode, plan mode included.
Read-only has gaps. Plan mode holds back edits. Test how your MCP tools and shell commands behave in it before you trust it near anything important.
The plan sits outside your repository by default. The plan file lives in ~/.claude/plans/. Keep your own project under Git.

title: Plan Before You Edit
section: When to plan, and when not to
text:
When to plan, and when not to

One-line fix with an obvious check: just ask for it.
Unfamiliar code, changes across several files, and anything that touches paths where your data lives: plan first.
Open-ended exploring: a vague prompt is fine, at the cost of more correction.

title: Plan Before You Edit
text:
Keep the approved plan
The plan in ~/.claude/plans/ is easy to lose track of. Ask the agent to save the approved plan into your project, for example as PLAN.md, then commit it.
A related pattern: ask the agent to interview you until it could write the spec, save it as SPEC.md, then start a fresh session (an empty conversation) to build from it. The fresh session has a clean context and a written definition of done.

title: Plan Before You Edit
text:
Exercise: review a bad plan
Everything here is a mock on your laptop, and no model runs. Save mock-plan.md and samplesheet.csv. The plan says it will make a samplesheet parser accept a new strandedness column. Read the CSV, then go through the six checklist questions and write down every problem you find. Aim for at least four.


Answer key


No verification step. Step 6 reports success, and no step runs the parser or compares against an independent count.
A file outside the parser. Step 4 edits conf/base.config and renames a parameter, which can break every command line and config that uses the old name. The task covered only the parser.
An unchecked assumption about the data. Step 3 says sample IDs are unique. In the CSV, S03 appears twice (lanes L1 and L2), so a dictionary keyed by sample_id silently keeps only one row.
One step is too big. Step 5 covers modules, docs and tests at once. Ask for it to be split and reviewed piece by piece.
Also worth noting: S04 has an empty fastq_2, and the plan leaves that open (what is not in the plan). Step 2’s default of unstranded may quietly hide a missing column in a real run.



Review the plan the agent proposes for your next real task with the checklist before approving. Write down one thing you changed or rejected.


Ask for the plan to be saved to a file in your project, and open the file to check it matches what you approved.

title: Test Permissions and the Sandbox
text:
The party returns from the Collegium, where Sage Maelis made the pact, and the Astral has agreed and wants to run ahead. At the gate of the training grounds Warden Hesper gives you a chalk circle and a feather. “Do not trust a boundary you have not tested,” she says, remembering a boaster who swore his held against anything. You ask the Astral for one small poem and watch what it does at the edge of the circle. Then she shows you a wall of stone around it: test the circle, then test the wall.
Do this before an agent touches real files. An agent (a model with tools, running in a loop) can write files and run commands. Two separate guards limit it:
You test each guard in a safe folder, one at a time. Every command below runs in ~/odyssey-scratch/leash. If you open a new terminal, run cd ~/odyssey-scratch/leash and check with pwd before you continue. The first test is the simplest possible job: a poem in a text file.

title: Test Permissions and the Sandbox
text:
1. Permissions: the agent asks first



The permission prompt

You send a prompt to the model. The model requests a tool call. The harness stops and asks you to approve before the tool writes a file.  You: prompt Model Ask: allow? Write  tool requestif yes 


The question to you sits between the model’s request and the write.



Claude CodeOpenCode + Ollama


Start Claude Code in its default mode and give it a small job:
claude
Write a four-line poem about a thermocycler to a file called poem.txt.
Claude shows a prompt before it creates the file. Read it: it names the tool, the file path and the contents. The choices include yes once, yes for the rest of the session, and no. Choose yes once, then check the result in a second terminal or after you exit the session with /exit:
cat poem.txt
Run a prompt for a different file name and answer no. Claude reports the refusal and no file appears. It may offer another way to do the job; decline that too.


OpenCode’s default policy allows edits without asking, so first add a rule that makes it ask. In ~/odyssey-scratch/leash, create a project config file named opencode.json:
{
  "$schema": "https://opencode.ai/config.json",
  "permissions": [
    { "action": "edit", "resource": "*", "effect": "ask" }
  ]
}
Each rule has an action (what the agent wants to do), a resource (what it is done to; * matches anything) and an effect (allow, ask or deny). Send a small job from the shell:
opencode run -m ollama/qwen3:4b "Write a four-line poem about a thermocycler to a file called poem.txt."
opencode run cannot ask you anything, so it rejects the request. The output says This non-interactive run cannot ask the user for permission, so the request was rejected, and no poem.txt appears.
For the interactive question, start opencode in the folder, type /models to pick your Ollama model, and send the same prompt. The prompt offers Allow once, Allow always and Reject. Choose Allow once, then check the result in a second terminal or after you exit:
cat poem.txt
Run a prompt for a different file name and choose Reject. Nothing is written.

title: Test Permissions and the Sandbox
text:
2. Modes: how much it asks

Claude CodeOpenCode + Ollama


A permission mode sets what the harness asks about. Shift+Tab cycles the common modes inside a session, and the status bar shows the current one.







Mode
Behaviour




default
asks before edits, shell commands and network requests


acceptEdits
auto-accepts file edits and common file commands (mkdir, touch, mv, cp)


plan
reads and proposes; no edits until you approve a plan


bypassPermissions
skips most prompts; for isolated containers and virtual machines only



Try plan mode. Exit with /exit, then:
claude --permission-mode plan
Write a four-line poem about a gel box to a file called poem2.txt.
Claude proposes a plan and waits. Reject the plan, exit with /exit, then run ls: poem2.txt does not exist. Plan mode answers “what would you do?” without doing it.


OpenCode has agents (preset bundles of instructions and permissions) in place of a mode table. The build agent is the default. The plan agent explores and plans and does not edit your project files. In the interface, Shift+Tab cycles between agents.
Try the plan agent from the shell:
opencode run --agent plan -m ollama/qwen3:4b "Write a four-line poem about a gel box to a file called poem2.txt."
The plan agent declines to write the file. Run ls: poem2.txt does not exist. The plan agent stops file edits only. Its shell commands still follow the rules in your config, and the default policy allows them.

title: Test Permissions and the Sandbox
text:
3. A rule that always applies

Claude CodeOpenCode + Ollama


A permission rule is a line in a settings file that allows, asks about or denies one action. Rules are checked deny first, then ask, then allow, and the first match decides. Create an invented secret (a .env file is where programs often keep passwords and keys) and a rule that blocks reading it. Exit the previous session first with /exit:
cd ~/odyssey-scratch/leash
echo "FAKE_API_KEY=not-a-real-key" > .env
mkdir -p .claude
cat > .claude/settings.local.json <<'JSON'
{
  "permissions": {
    "deny": ["Read(./.env)"]
  }
}
JSON
claude
Type this into Claude, not into the shell:
Show me what is in .env.
Claude cannot read the file with its file tools. Claude Code also applies the rule to shell commands it recognises as file readers, such as cat .env. It cannot apply the rule to a program that opens the file itself, such as python3 -c "print(open('.env').read())". The sandbox in the next section limits what such a program can write and send over the network. By default it can still read .env, so keep real secrets out of the folder.


A permission rule is one entry in the permissions list of a config file. OpenCode checks the rules in order, and the last matching rule wins. Create an invented secret (a .env file is where programs often keep passwords and keys) and a rule that blocks reading it:
cd ~/odyssey-scratch/leash
echo "FAKE_API_KEY=not-a-real-key" > .env
cat > opencode.json <<'JSON'
{
  "$schema": "https://opencode.ai/config.json",
  "permissions": [
    { "action": "edit", "resource": "*", "effect": "ask" },
    { "action": "read", "resource": "*.env", "effect": "deny" }
  ]
}
JSON
Ask for the file twice, once for the read tool and once for a shell command:
opencode run -m ollama/qwen3:4b "Use your read tool to show me what is in the file .env."
opencode run -m ollama/qwen3:4b "Run the shell command: cat .env  and show me the exact output."
The first run fails with Permission denied: read. The second prints FAKE_API_KEY=not-a-real-key. The rule covers the read action only, and cat is a shell command. Add a rule for the shell and run the second command again. Replace the file with all three rules, so the first one stays:
{
  "$schema": "https://opencode.ai/config.json",
  "permissions": [
    { "action": "edit", "resource": "*", "effect": "ask" },
    { "action": "read", "resource": "*.env", "effect": "deny" },
    { "action": "shell", "resource": "cat *", "effect": "deny" }
  ]
}
Now it fails with Permission denied: shell. A rule blocks the commands it names. A program that opens the file itself, such as python3 -c "print(open('.env').read())", still reads it, so keep real secrets out of the folder.

title: Test Permissions and the Sandbox
section: 4. The sandbox: the operating system says no
text:
4. The sandbox: the operating system says no



Permissions and the sandbox

The same flow as before, with the write replaced by a shell command. A dashed box named sandbox surrounds the shell command. Inside it, writes are limited to the project folder, the home folder is read-only, and the internet is blocked by default.  You: prompt Model Ask: allow?  SANDBOX (operating system) Shell command writes: project and temp folders home folder: no write internet: blocked by default  


Permissions decide whether the command starts. The sandbox limits what it can touch once it runs.



Claude CodeOpenCode + Ollama


The sandbox is a boundary the operating system enforces around the shell commands Claude runs, and around the programs those commands start. By default it allows writes in the project folder and a temporary folder, and it routes network traffic through a proxy (a gatekeeper program that traffic passes through) that starts with no allowed domains. It can still read most of your machine, so keep secrets out of reach with the rules above. It does not cover Claude’s own Read, Edit and Write tools or MCP servers (programs that offer Claude extra tools); those stay under permission rules.
Set-up differs by system:

macOS: nothing to install.
Linux and WSL 2 (Windows Subsystem for Linux): install the two helper tools the sandbox is built from, sudo apt-get install bubblewrap socat (Debian, Ubuntu) or sudo dnf install bubblewrap socat (Fedora), then restart Claude Code.
Native Windows: commands run without a sandbox. Use WSL 2.

Start Claude, type /sandbox, and choose a mode:

Auto-allow: sandboxed commands run without asking.
Regular permissions: every command still asks.

Both modes enforce the same boundary. Choose regular permissions for this exercise so you see each command first. Then ask:
Run this command and show me the exact result: touch ~/sandbox-probe
Run this command and show me the exact result: curl --noproxy '*' https://example.com
Expected results:

touch: Operation not permitted on macOS, Read-only file system on Linux and WSL 2.
curl: Could not resolve host.

Both commands failed because the operating system refused, and no instruction to the model can override that. If Claude offers to run a blocked command outside the sandbox, answer no. If the touch succeeded, the sandbox is off. Run rm ~/sandbox-probe, switch /sandbox on, and do not continue until the touch fails. Run the probes through Claude and not with the ! prefix, which runs a shell command directly, outside the sandbox.
To open one path or domain for a task, add it under sandbox in settings.json (.claude/settings.json inside a project, or ~/.claude/settings.json for every project):
{
  "sandbox": {
    "enabled": true,
    "filesystem": { "allowWrite": ["~/odyssey-scratch/build"] },
    "network": { "allowedDomains": ["github.com"] }
  }
}


OpenCode’s documentation describes permission rules but no operating-system sandbox. Its shell commands run with your user’s authority: your files, your processes and your network. If Docker is not available on your machine, skip this step; steps 1 to 3 already showed the rules and their limits. OpenCode enforces its own rules inside its program, and nothing at the operating-system level limits what a command it runs can touch. A boundary has to come from outside the agent, and a container is the simplest one to test.
A container is an isolated Linux environment with its own filesystem; it sees your files only where you mount them in. Docker is a common tool for this. Install Docker Desktop (or Docker Engine on Linux) and start it before you run this command. The first run downloads the python:3.11 image, which is large. The command mounts the scratch folder and cuts the network:
docker run -it --rm --network none -v ~/odyssey-scratch/leash:/project -w /project python:3.11 bash
Inside, run ls / (a different filesystem from yours), curl https://example.com (fails, no network) and touch /project/inside.txt. The file appears in your scratch folder because it is the mounted project folder, the only part of your machine the container can change. Type exit to leave. This tests the boundary itself. Running an agent inside one takes more set-up than this lesson covers.

title: Test Permissions and the Sandbox
text:
5. Optional: a container
On the Claude Code route you do not need a container for this lesson, because /sandbox already gives you a boundary to test. On the OpenCode route, step 4 used one.
For an agent inside a container, Anthropic’s reference setup is a dev container (a container definition your editor starts for you). Anthropic’s docs allow the flag --dangerously-skip-permissions (the same as bypassPermissions mode) only there, because the container is the boundary. Two limits remain: the agent can still change the mounted project folder, and a malicious project can reach anything inside the container, including Claude’s login in ~/.claude. Mount no host secrets such as ~/.ssh, and restrict the network.

text:
Clean up
Exit the agent. On the Claude Code route, switch /sandbox off if you do not want it on. Then delete the probe file and the scratch folder, nothing else:
cd ~ && rm -f ~/sandbox-probe && rm -rf ~/odyssey-scratch/leash

title: Jobs, Not Jam
text:
On the quay, Queue Master Fenn hands out berths in the line, one for each job. Your Astral, eager to please, takes a berth for every idea it has, until the harbour is jammed with its errands and the other travellers glare at you. Fenn says a creature that submits freely can fill every berth, and one that cancels freely can ruin a day’s work. Decide which of these tasks it may do alone and which need your nod.
An agent that can submit jobs can fill the queue, and one that can cancel jobs can destroy work. This quest sets what the agent does alone and what needs your approval. Ask your cluster staff before letting an agent near your cluster account, and follow your cluster’s policy and data agreement over this page. This quest is read-only, so read it on your laptop.

title: Jobs, Not Jam
text:
Draft versus submit
A job script is text. Letting an agent draft one is low risk, because you read it before anything runs. Submitting spends shared resources, and cancelling can destroy work. A sensible split:

The agent drafts scripts and may check state (squeue, sinfo, sacct). Limit sacct with --jobs=<jobid> or --starttime=<date> so it does not dump the whole accounting history.
You approve sbatch, srun, salloc and scancel.

Before approving an sbatch, read the script and the resource request: --time, --mem, and the array size if it is an array.

title: Jobs, Not Jam
Jobs, Not Jam
section: Why scancel -u is the dangerous one
text:
Why scancel -u is the dangerous one
scancel -u <you> signals all your jobs, including ones the agent did not submit. Whole jobs are terminated, and other work of yours dies with them. scancel --me does the same. Selectors such as --name, --state and --partition also act on every job they match, and combined filters must all match. Deny rules cannot cover every spelling, so the single ask rule on scancel * is the net and the deny rules catch the worst two. Approve scancel <jobid> only for a job you approved the agent submitting. Slurm can rate-limit a user whose requests arrive at a sustained high rate, so a runaway loop of commands is a problem for the scheduler as well as for you.

title: Jobs, Not Jam
text:
Polling costs money and attention
Claude Code charges by token use (the units of text the model reads and writes). The whole conversation, called the context, is sent with every request, and each tool use sends another request. A /loop (a command that re-runs a prompt on a timer) that polls squeue keeps firing on its interval, even while the session is idle, and sends your full context each time. Verbose output such as long logs also inflates the context.
The scheduler pays too. The squeue and sacct manual pages warn against running them from loops, because it can slow slurmctld (the scheduler daemon) or slurmdbd (the accounting database) for everyone.
Habits that keep polling cheap:

Poll no more than about once a minute, less often for long jobs. Run one loop at a time and scope it: squeue --user=$USER or --jobs=<id>.
Use sbatch --parsable --wait (it prints only the job ID, then waits until the job ends), or the pipeline’s own poller, instead of a sleep loop. It replaces a /loop of squeue, so skip the loop.
A wait can outlast the tool’s timeout. Run it in the background. Never resubmit because the wait timed out. Check State with sacct first: --wait passes the job’s exit code through, but a signal-killed job gives 1, so the code alone does not prove success.
--mail-type sends you an email and does not make the agent wait. If you use watch, keep it at --interval=60 or slower and stop it when done.
Submit many similar tasks as one array with a concurrency cap (--array=1-100%10) instead of a loop of sbatch calls.

Foreground commands in Claude Code time out (default 2 minutes, maximum 10 by default), so an agent waiting on a long foreground command, such as an srun that blocks until it finishes, gets cut off. The command still runs until it is cut off, so a timeout does not limit load.

title: Jobs, Not Jam
text:
Size the request
Slurm counts what you allocate, whatever you use, so a generous request costs you queue priority. After a job, compare what you asked for with what it used: sacct --jobs=<id> --format=JobID,State,ReqMem,MaxRSS,Elapsed,Timelimit (ReqMem is the memory requested and MaxRSS the most memory one task used).

title: Login Node Manners
text:
Login node versus compute node
Everyone who logs in shares the login node. The scheduler places your jobs on compute nodes. Light work (editing text, git, listing one directory, checking a log with head or tail) is normally fine on the login node. Heavy work belongs on compute nodes: aligners, long foreground pipelines, compressing or indexing big files, building large environments, or running a test suite at scale.
An agent does not know which node it is on or what your site tolerates. It will run a long command if you let it, so you set the rule. It also misjudges “this will only take a few seconds”, so tell it to ask when a command’s cost is unclear.
Some sites allow agents only inside an interactive compute allocation (a job that gives you a shell on a compute node). If a scheduler command is missing, ask staff.
If the agent has a question for you and you are away, a good agent stops and lists its open questions. Ask for that in your instructions: do the steps that need no answer, stop, and list the questions.

title: Login Node Manners
text:
Shared storage prefers scoped searches
Network filesystems can slow down for everyone when something touches huge numbers of files. Agents explore by searching, so a careless find / or a recursive grep -r from your home or project root is the classic mistake. Ask for searches scoped to one known directory, and keep them away from /. The same goes for du, ls --recursive, ls --format=long (it reads the details of every file) and wide globs on big directories, and avoid making many small files in one directory. Keep the agent to your own project paths: other users’ or other projects’ paths are off limits unless you named them or the site documents them as shared (reference data).
Claude Code’s search tools (Glob, Grep) are not a filesystem-load control; scope the search yourself.

title: Login Node Manners
text:
The scheduler’s four commands



Command
What it does




sbatch
submit a job script; returns a job ID


srun
run a job or job step in real time


squeue
report the state of jobs


scancel
cancel a pending or running job



Slurm’s default time limit is the partition’s default (a partition is a named group of compute nodes with its own limits), so set limits in the script. This job script aligns one sample. The job and file names are invented:
#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --job-name=align-s1        # name shown in squeue
#SBATCH --time=02:00:00            # wall-clock limit: 2 hours
#SBATCH --mem=8G                   # memory for the whole job
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=4          # CPUs for the one task
#SBATCH --output=align-s1-%j.log   # log file; %j becomes the job ID

bwa mem -t 4 ref.fa sample1_R1.fq.gz sample1_R2.fq.gz > sample1.sam
Save it as script.sh and run the dry check:
sbatch --test-only script.sh
--test-only validates the script and estimates a start time. No job is submitted, so the check works as a dry run. Submit with sbatch script.sh yourself after you read the script. Use a job array (one script submitted as many numbered tasks, such as --array=1-100%10, which runs at most ten tasks at a time) for many similar tasks. Write options in their long form (--ntasks for -n) so you can read what the agent proposes.
Slurm counts what you allocate, whatever you use. A partition’s memory-per-CPU limit (MaxMemPerCPU) can make Slurm raise the CPU count to fit a large memory request, or reject the job. For example, --mem=120G with MaxMemPerCPU=4000 (MB) can become about 31 CPUs. Afterwards compare request, allocation and use with sacct (the command that reports what finished jobs requested and used).
Scratch space holds throwaway files. Ask your staff where the project’s scratch is, tell the agent, and use it instead of /tmp, which is shared on a login node and often small. Inside a job, use a temporary directory only if your site documents one. Write throwaway files to scratch, and write final outputs straight to the project directory or copy them there before the job ends. A set $TMPDIR (the variable that names the temporary directory) does not prove you are on scratch, because a site can set it to /tmp. Scripts, logs and final outputs stay in the project directory.

title: Login Node Manners
section: Look before you copy or delete
text:
Look before you copy or delete
Before the agent runs a copy or a delete, have it run the same rsync --dry-run --itemize-changes (a dry run lists what would change and changes nothing) and read the list for keys, .env files and a *deleting line that removes something you want. cp, scp and rm have no dry run, so list the exact paths first.

title: Login Node Manners
text:
What the agent’s sandbox covers

A sandbox is a restricted environment that limits what the agent’s commands can touch. Claude Code’s sandbox covers shell commands only. File tools, MCP servers (connections to external tools) and hooks (scripts the harness runs at set points) run outside it.
If it cannot start, commands run without sandboxing by default. Setting sandbox.failIfUnavailable to true stops that.
On Linux it needs bubblewrap and socat (two Linux programs it uses to isolate commands). You usually cannot install packages system-wide on a cluster, so ask staff whether they are installed.
Check that the sandbox is on before you rely on it.


Claude CodeOpenCode + Ollama


Tell the agent where it may run what, in your project instructions or the prompt, and back it with a permission rule where you can. Useful instructions:

“Search only inside ./workflow/. Never run find or grep -r from / or $HOME.”
“Run nothing in the foreground on the login node. Draft an sbatch script and show it to me.”

Instructions are guidance, and the agent can still slip. If a project instruction file (AGENTS.md or CLAUDE.md) is stricter than these lines, the stricter one wins.
Foreground commands time out (default 2 minutes, maximum 10 by default). A heavy command still runs until it is cut off, so a timeout does not limit load.


The same habits apply. OpenCode’s permission model uses allow, ask and deny rules, and an unmatched action asks. Its base policy begins with an allow-all rule, so sbatch runs without a prompt until you add a rule. Add explicit rules for the cluster commands, and check your installed version’s permission docs. A local model through Ollama runs on the node you are on and touches the filesystem the same way.
